p.seg: 1.1 Mèngzǐ went to see Liáng Huì Wáng.
The King said,
“Venerable sir!
You have not considered a thousand lǐ too far to come;
surely you must have some way to profit my state?”
Mèngzǐ replied,
“Your Majesty! Why must you speak of profit?
There are only benevolence and righteousness, and nothing else.
If Your Majesty says,
‘How can I profit my state?’
the grand officers will say,
‘How can I profit my family?’
and the scholars and commoners will say,
‘How can I profit myself?’
Superiors and inferiors will fight one another for profit,
and the state will be in danger.
In a state of ten thousand chariots,
the one who assassinates his ruler
will surely be the head of a family of one thousand chariots;
in a state of one thousand chariots,
the one who assassinates his ruler
will surely be the head of a family of one hundred chariots.
To have one thousand out of ten thousand,
or one hundred out of one thousand,
is not a small share.
But if righteousness is put last and profit first,
they will not be satisfied without seizing everything.
There has never been a benevolent person who abandoned his parents,
and there has never been a righteous person who put his ruler last.
Your Majesty should also speak only of benevolence and righteousness;
why must you speak of profit?”
1.2 Mèngzǐ went to see Liáng Huì Wáng.
The King was standing by a pond,
looking around at the wild geese and deer,
and said,
“Do the worthy also find pleasure in these things?”
Mèngzǐ replied,
“Only the worthy can find pleasure in these things;
those who are not worthy, even if they have them, do not find pleasure in them.
The *Shī* says,
‘When he planned and began the Língtái,
planning it and designing it,
the common people worked on it,
and in no time they completed it.
In beginning the planning, he told them not to hurry,
yet the common people came like children helping their father.
The King was in the Língyòu,
where the does and stags lay down,
the does and stags so sleek,
and the white birds glistening.
The King was by the Língzhǎo,
oh, how full of leaping fish!’
Wénwáng used the labor of the people to make his tower and pond,
yet the people rejoiced in them,
calling his tower the Língtái,
calling his pond the Língzhǎo,
and finding pleasure in his having deer, fish, and turtles.
The ancients shared their joy with the people,
and therefore they could enjoy it.
The *Tāngshì* says,
‘When will this sun perish?
We will perish together with you!’
Since the people wished to perish together with him,
even though he had towers, ponds, birds, and beasts,
how could he enjoy them alone?”
1.3 Liáng Huì Wáng said,
“As for my relation to my state,
I exert my heart to the utmost.
When there is a famine in Hénèi,
I move some of the people to Hédōng
and move grain to Hénèi.
When there is a famine in Hédōng,
I do the same.
When I examine the government of neighboring states,
there is no ruler who exerts his heart as I do.
Yet the population of neighboring states does not decrease,
and my population does not increase.
Why is this?”
Mèngzǐ replied,
“Your Majesty loves war;
please allow me to use an analogy from war.
The drums beat thunderously,
and the weapons have crossed.
Then, abandoning their armor and dragging their weapons, the soldiers flee.
Some stop after a hundred paces,
others stop after fifty paces.
If those who ran fifty paces laugh at those who ran a hundred paces,
what would you think of that?”
The King said,
“They should not do so.
They merely did not run a hundred paces,
but they fled nonetheless.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“If Your Majesty understands this,
then do not hope for your population to be greater than that of neighboring states.
If you do not interfere with the farming seasons, the grain will be more than can be eaten.
If close-meshed nets are not allowed in deep ponds, the fish and turtles will be more than can be consumed.
If axes and bills enter the mountain forests only at the proper times, the timber will be more than can be used.
When grain, fish, and turtles are more than can be eaten,
and timber is more than can be used,
this enables the people to nourish their living and mourn their dead without any regrets.
To nourish the living and mourn the dead without regrets
is the beginning of the Kingly Way.
Around homesteads of five mǔ, plant them with mulberry trees,
and those of fifty years old can wear silk.
In breeding chickens, young pigs, dogs, and swine, do not neglect their breeding seasons,
and those of seventy years old can eat meat.
On fields of one hundred mǔ, do not deprive them of their labor during farming seasons,
and a family of several mouths can be free from hunger.
Pay careful attention to education in schools,
reinforcing it with the principles of filial piety and fraternal duty,
and those with grey hair will not be carrying loads on their backs or heads on the roads.
When those of seventy years old wear silk and eat meat,
and the common people are neither hungry nor cold,
and yet their ruler does not become a true king,
such a thing has never occurred.
“Your dogs and swine eat the food of humans, and you do not know how to restrict them;
there are people dying of hunger on the roads, and you do not know how to distribute the grain in your granaries.
When people die, you say,
‘It is not my fault; it is because of the bad harvest.’
How is this different from stabbing a person to death and saying,
‘It was not I; it was the weapon.’?
If Your Majesty stops blaming the harvest,
then the people of the world will come to you.”
1.4 Liáng Huì Wáng said,
“I wish to quietly receive your instruction.”
Mèngzǐ replied,
“To kill a person with a club or a blade—
is there any difference?”
The King said,
“There is no difference.”
“To kill a person with a blade or with government policies—
is there any difference?”
The King said, “There is no difference.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“In your kitchen there is fat meat,
and in your stables there are fat horses;
yet the people have the look of hunger,
and there are those dying of starvation in the wilds.
This is leading beasts to devour humans.
Beasts devouring one another
is something that humans hate;
yet if the ruler, being the parent of the people,
administers his government in such a way that he cannot avoid leading beasts to devour humans,
where is his quality of being the parent of the people?
Zhòngní said,
‘Was he who first made wooden images to bury with the dead
left without any descendants!’
This was because he made images of humans and used them.
What then should be thought of
one who causes his people to die of hunger?”
1.5 Liáng Huì Wáng said,
“The state of Jìn
was once the strongest in the world,
as you, venerable sir, well know.
But when it came to my reign,
we were defeated in the east by Qí,
where my eldest son died;
we lost seven hundred lǐ of territory in the west to Qín;
and we were humiliated in the south by Chǔ.
I feel deeply ashamed of this,
and wish to wipe away these stains on behalf of the deceased.
How can this be accomplished?”
Mèngzǐ replied,
“With a territory of only one hundred lǐ square,
one can still become a true king.
If Your Majesty practices a benevolent government toward the people,
reducing punishments and fines,
and lightening taxes and levies,
they will plow deeply and weed thoroughly.
The strong-bodied, in their leisure days, will cultivate filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and trustworthiness.
At home, they will serve their fathers and elder brothers;
abroad, they will serve their elders and superiors.
They could then be made to strike the strong armor and sharp weapons of Qín and Chǔ with simple wooden clubs.
“Those rulers rob their people of their farming seasons,
preventing them from plowing and weeding
to support their parents.
Their parents suffer from cold and hunger,
and brothers, wives, and children are separated and scattered.
They plunge their people into misery.
If Your Majesty goes to punish them,
who could oppose Your Majesty?
Therefore it is said,
‘The benevolent person has no enemy.’
I pray Your Majesty do not doubt this!”
1.6 Mèngzǐ went to see Liáng Xiāng Wáng.
When he came out,
he said to some people,
“When looked at from a distance, he does not look like a ruler of men;
when approached, nothing is seen to inspire awe.
Abruptly, he asked me,
‘How can the world be settled?’
“I replied,
‘It will be settled by being united.’
‘Who can unite it?’ he asked.
I replied,
‘One who does not take pleasure in killing people can unite it.’
‘Who would join such a ruler?’ he asked.
“I replied,
‘There is no one in the world who would not join him.’
“Does Your Majesty know about the sprouts of grain?
During the seventh and eighth months, if there is a drought,
then the sprouts wither.
When clouds dense and dark form in the heavens,
and rain pours down abundantly,
then the sprouts vigorously spring up.
When it is like this,
who can stop it?
Now among the rulers of men in the world,
there is none who does not love killing people.
If there were one who did not love killing people,
then all the people of the world would crane their necks to look toward him.
If it were truly like this,
the people would turn to him
just as water flows downward—
gushing forth with such force, who could stop them?”
1.7 King Xuān of Qí asked, saying:
“Can I hear about the affairs of Huán of Qí and Wén of Jìn?”
Mèngzǐ replied, saying:
“Among the disciples of Zhòngní,
none spoke of the affairs of Huán and Wén,
and so nothing has been handed down to later generations;
I, your servant, have not heard of them.
Since I cannot speak of them, shall we talk about kingly rule?”
The King said,
“What must one’s virtue be like
in order to rule as a king?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“Protect the people and rule as a king;
then no one can stop you.”
The King said,
“Can someone like me protect the people?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“You can.”
The King said,
“How do you know that I can?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“I heard from Hú Hé that
Your Majesty was sitting up in the hall,
when someone led an ox past below.
Your Majesty saw it
and asked,
‘Where is the ox going?’
The man replied,
‘We are going to consecrate a bell with its blood.’
Your Majesty said,
‘Spare it!
I cannot bear its trembling,
like an innocent person going to the place of execution.’
The man replied,
‘In that case, should we abandon the consecration of the bell?’
Your Majesty said,
‘How can it be abandoned?
Substitute it with a sheep!’
I do not know if this really happened?”
The King said,
“It did.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“Such a mind is sufficient to rule as a king.
The common people all thought Your Majesty was being stingy,
but I certainly knew that Your Majesty simply could not bear its suffering.”
The King said,
“Indeed,
the common people truly thought so.
Although the state of Qí is small and narrow,
how could I begrudge a single ox?
It was simply that I could not bear its trembling,
like an innocent person going to the place of execution,
and so I substituted it with a sheep.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“Your Majesty should not be surprised that the people thought you were being stingy.
Since you substituted a small animal for a large one,
how could they know your real reason?
If Your Majesty was pained by its being innocent yet going to the place of execution,
then what was there to choose between an ox and a sheep?”
The King laughed and said,
“What kind of mind was that indeed?
It was not that I begrudged the expense and so substituted it with a sheep,
yet it is only natural that the common people said I was being stingy.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“There is no harm in that.
This is precisely how benevolence works:
you saw the ox, but you had not seen the sheep.
A gentleman’s attitude toward birds and beasts is this:
having seen them alive,
he cannot bear to see them die;
having heard their cries,
he cannot bear to eat their meat.
Therefore, the gentleman stays far away from the kitchen.”
The King was pleased and said,
“The *Odes* (*Shī*) say:
‘Another person has a mind,
and I fathom it.’
This describes you, Master.
For when I did it,
and then turned back to examine it,
I could not understand my own mind.
But when you spoke of it,
something in my heart was deeply stirred.
How is it that this mind is in accord with being a king?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“Suppose someone reported to Your Majesty, saying:
‘My strength is sufficient to lift a hundred *jūn*,
but is not sufficient to lift a single feather;
my eyesight is sufficient to examine the tip of an autumn hair,
but I cannot see a cartload of firewood.’
Would Your Majesty accept this?”
The King said,
“No.”
“Now your kindness is sufficient to reach birds and beasts,
yet your achievements do not reach the common people.
Why should this be?
Therefore, not lifting a feather
is because one does not use one’s strength;
not seeing a cartload of firewood
is because one does not use one’s eyesight;
and the common people not being protected
is because one does not use one’s kindness.
Therefore, Your Majesty’s not ruling as a king
is because you do not do it,
not because you are unable.”
The King said,
“How does the state of ‘not doing’ and ‘being unable to do’
differ?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“If one were to tuck Mount Tài under one’s arm and leap over the North Sea,
and tell people,
‘I am unable to do it,’
this is truly being unable.
But if it is breaking off a branch for an elder,
and one tells people,
‘I am unable to do it,’
this is not doing it,
not being unable.
Therefore, Your Majesty’s not ruling as a king
is not of the category of tucking Mount Tài under one’s arm and leaping over the North Sea;
Your Majesty’s not ruling as a king
is of the category of breaking off a branch.
“Treat your own elders as elders, and extend this to the elders of others;
treat your own young as young, and extend this to the young of others;
and the world can be turned in the palm of your hand.
The *Odes* (*Shī*) say:
‘He set an example for his wife,
and it extended to his brothers,
and so he governed his family and state.’
This means simply taking this mind and applying it to others.
Therefore, if you extend your kindness, it will be sufficient to protect all within the Four Seas;
if you do not extend your kindness, you will not even be able to protect your own wife and children.
The reason why the ancients greatly surpassed others
was nothing other than this:
they were good at extending what they did.
Now your kindness is sufficient to reach birds and beasts,
yet your achievements do not reach the common people.
Why should this be?
“Weigh a thing, and only then do you know its weight;
measure a thing, and only then do you know its length.
This is true of all things,
and especially so for the mind.
I beg Your Majesty to measure it!
“Or does Your Majesty mobilize your armored troops,
endanger your soldiers and ministers,
and incur the resentment of the feudal lords,
and only then find pleasure in your heart?”
The King said,
“No,
how could I find pleasure in this?
I do this only to seek what I greatly desire.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“May I hear what it is that Your Majesty greatly desires?”
The King smiled and did not speak.
Mèngzǐ said,
“Is it because rich and sweet foods are not enough for your mouth?
Or light and warm clothing is not enough for your body?
Or beautiful colors are not enough for your eyes to behold?
Or beautiful sounds are not enough for your ears to hear?
Or favorites and servants are not enough to wait upon you?
Your Majesty’s ministers are all sufficient to provide these for you,
how could Your Majesty be doing this for such things?”
The King said,
“No,
I am not doing it for these.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“In that case, what Your Majesty greatly desires can be known:
you wish to expand your territory,
make Qín and Chǔ pay court to you,
rule over the Central Kingdoms,
and pacify the four barbarian tribes around them.
To seek what you desire by doing what you are doing
is like climbing a tree to seek fish.”
The King said,
"Is it really that severe?"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"It is probably even more severe than that.
If one climbs a tree to seek fish,
although one will not obtain any fish,
there will be no subsequent disaster.
But by doing what you are doing
to seek what you desire,
even if you exert your mind and strength to the utmost,
there will certainly be disaster afterward."
The King said,
"May I hear the reason for this?"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"If the people of Zōu and the people of Chǔ were to fight,
whom does the King think would win?"
The King said,
"The people of Chǔ would win."
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"Thus, the small indeed cannot match the large,
the few indeed cannot match the many,
and the weak indeed cannot match the strong.
Within the seas, of territories
one thousand *lǐ* square, there are nine in total,
and Qí, when combined, possesses only one.
To try to subjugate the other eight with only one,
how is this any different from Zōu fighting Chǔ?
Why not indeed return to the root?
"Now, if your Majesty were to issue government measures and practice benevolence,
it would make all those in the world who wish to serve as officials want to stand in your Majesty's court,
all tillers want to till in your Majesty's fields,
all merchants want to store their goods in your Majesty's markets,
all travelers want to journey along your Majesty's roads,
and all those in the world who hate their own rulers
want to rush and appeal to your Majesty.
If it were like this,
who could resist you?"
The King said,
"I am dim-witted,
and unable to advance to this.
I wish for you, Master, to assist my will
and clearly instruct me.
Although I am not clever,
please let me try."
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"To have no constant livelihood and yet maintain a constant heart—
only scholars are capable of this.
As for the common people, if they have no constant livelihood,
they will consequently have no constant heart.
If they have no constant heart,
they will give way to self-abandonment, moral deviancy, depravity, and wild license,
and there is nothing they will not do.
When they fall into crime,
to then follow up and punish them
is to entrap the people.
How could a benevolent person be in power
and permit the entrapment of the people?
Therefore, an enlightened ruler regulates the livelihood of the people
in such a way that, looking up, they have sufficient to serve their parents,
and looking down, they have sufficient to support their wives and children;
in good years, they are always full,
and in bad years, they escape death.
Only then does the ruler urge them toward goodness,
and thus the people follow him easily.
Now, however, the regulation of the livelihood of the people is such that,
looking up, they have insufficient to serve their parents,
and looking down, they have insufficient to support their wives and children;
in good years, their whole lives are bitter,
and in bad years, they cannot escape death.
Under these conditions, they only seek to escape death and fear they cannot even do that;
what leisure do they have to cultivate ritual and righteousness?
"If your Majesty wishes to practice this,
why not return to the root?
On homesteads of five *mǔ*, plant them with mulberry trees,
and those of fifty years can wear silk.
In the breeding of chickens, young pigs, dogs, and swine, do not neglect their seasons,
and those of seventy years can eat meat.
On fields of one hundred *mǔ*, do not disrupt their agricultural seasons,
and families of eight mouths can be free from hunger.
Pay careful attention to education in the local schools,
reinforcing it with the principles of filial piety and fraternal duty,
and those with grey hair will not be carrying loads on their heads or backs on the roads.
When the elderly wear silk and eat meat,
and the common people are neither hungry nor cold,
for such a ruler not to become king—
there has never been such a thing."
2.1 Zhuāng Bào met with Mèngzǐ and said,
"I, Bào, had an audience with the King.
The King spoke to me of his fondness for music,
and I had nothing with which to reply."
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"How is his fondness for music?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"If the King's fondness for music is deep,
then the state of Qí is perhaps close to being well-governed!"
On another day,
(Mèngzǐ) had an audience with the King and said,
"Your Majesty once spoke to Zhuāngzǐ about your fondness for music;
was there such a thing?"
The King changed color and said,
"I am not able to love the music of the ancient kings;
I simply love the music of the common world."
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"If your Majesty's fondness for music is deep,
then Qí is perhaps close to being well-governed!
Today's music is just like the music of antiquity."
The King said,
"May I hear how that is?"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"To enjoy music alone,
or to enjoy music with others—
which is more joyful?"
The King said,
"It is not as joyful as enjoying it with others."
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"To enjoy music with a few,
or to enjoy music with the crowd—
which is more joyful?"
The King said,
"It is not as joyful as with the crowd."
"Please allow me to speak to your Majesty about music.
Suppose your Majesty is playing music here,
and the common people hear the sound of your Majesty's bells and drums,
and the notes of your flutes and pipes.
They all, with aching heads and furrowed brows, say to one another,
'Our King is so fond of playing music,
but why does he bring us to such an extreme state of misery?
Fathers and sons do not see one another,
and brothers, wives, and children are scattered and separated.'
Suppose your Majesty is hunting here,
and the common people hear the sound of your Majesty's carriages and horses,
and see the beauty of your feathered banners.
They all, with aching heads and furrowed brows, say to one another,
'Our King is so fond of hunting,
but why does he bring us to such an extreme state of misery?
Fathers and sons do not see one another,
and brothers, wives, and children are scattered and separated.'
This is for no other reason than
that you do not share your joy with the people.
"Now, suppose your Majesty is playing music here,
and the common people hear the sound of your Majesty's bells and drums
and the notes of your flutes and pipes,
and they all, with joyful faces and happy expressions, say to one another,
'Our King is probably free from illness,
for how else could he play music?'
Suppose your Majesty is hunting here,
and the common people hear the sound of your Majesty's carriages and horses
and see the beauty of your feathered banners,
and they all, with joyful faces and happy expressions, say to one another,
'Our King is probably free from illness,
for how else could he hunt?'
This is for no other reason than
that you share your joy with the people.
If your Majesty shares your joy with the common people, then you will rule as king."
2.2 King Xuān of Qí asked,
"Is it true that King Wén's park was seventy *lǐ* square?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"It is so recorded in the traditions."
The King said,
"Was it really that large?"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"The people still thought it was small."
The King said,
"My park is forty *lǐ* square,
and yet the people think it is large.
Why is this?"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"King Wén's park was seventy *lǐ* square,
yet those who gathered firewood went there,
and those who caught pheasants and hares went there.
He shared it with the people.
That the people thought it was small—
is it not reasonable?
When I first arrived at the border,
I asked about the major prohibitions of the state,
before I dared to enter.
I heard that within the suburban passes,
there is a park forty *lǐ* square,
and anyone who kills a deer there
is punished as if they had committed murder.
Thus, this forty *lǐ* square area is a trap set in the middle of the state.
That the people think it is large—is it not reasonable?"
2.3 King Xuān of Qí asked,
"Is there a proper way to maintain relations with neighboring states?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"There is.
Only the benevolent are able to serve the small with the large;
therefore, Tāng served Gě,
and King Wén served the Hùnyí.
Only the wise are able to serve the large with the small;
therefore, King Tài served the Xūnyù,
and Gōujiàn served Wú.
Those who serve the small with the large are those who find joy in Heaven;
those who serve the large with the small are those who stand in awe of Heaven.
Those who find joy in Heaven protect all under heaven;
those who stand in awe of Heaven protect their own states."
The *Odes* (*Shī*) say:
‘Awe at the majesty of Heaven,
And thereby preserve it.’"
The King said:
"Great indeed are your words!
But I have a weakness:
I am fond of courage."
Mèngzǐ replied:
"I pray Your Majesty not to be fond of petty courage.
Clutching one's sword and staring fiercely, saying,
‘How dare he withstand me!’—
this is the courage of a common man,
which can only match a single opponent.
Please, Your Majesty, make it great!
The *Odes* say:
‘The King blazed with wrath,
Whereupon he marshaled his hosts,
To stop the march on Jǔ,
To consolidate the blessing of Zhōu,
And to answer the expectations of the world.’
This was the courage of Wén Wáng.
With one burst of anger, Wén Wáng
brought peace to the people of the world.
"The *Book of Documents* (*Shū*) says:
‘Heaven, having sent down the people below,
Appointed for them rulers,
Appointed for them teachers,
With the sole purpose that they should assist Shàngdì in showing them favor.
Throughout the four quarters, whether they be guilty or guiltless, there is only myself here;
How should anyone under heaven dare to transgress his will?’
When one man ran amok in the world,
Wǔ Wáng felt ashamed of it.
This was the courage of Wǔ Wáng.
And Wǔ Wáng also, with one burst of anger,
brought peace to the people of the world.
Now, if Your Majesty also, with one burst of anger,
brings peace to the people of the world,
the people will only fear that Your Majesty is not fond of courage."
2.4 Qí Xuān Wáng received Mèngzǐ in the Xuě Palace.
The King said:
Mèngzǐ replied:
"They do.
If the people do not obtain them,
they will condemn their rulers.
To condemn their rulers because they cannot obtain them
is wrong;
but to be a ruler over the people and yet not share pleasures with them
is also wrong.
When a ruler rejoices in the joy of his people,
the people also rejoice in his joy;
when a ruler grieves at the sorrow of his people,
the people also grieve at his sorrow.
Rejoicing with the whole world,
grieving with the whole world—
that one should do this and yet not become a true king,
has never happened.
"In the past, Qí Jǐng Gōng asked Yànzǐ, saying:
‘I wish to go on a tour of inspection to Zhuǎnfù and Cháowǔ,
and then travel south along the sea,
all the way to Lángyá.
What must I do so that my tour may compare with the tours of inspection of the former kings?’
"Yànzǐ replied:
‘An excellent question indeed!
When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords, it is called a "tour of inspection" (*xúnshòu*).
"Tour of inspection" means inspecting what they are keeping charge of.
When the feudal lords pay court to the Son of Heaven, it is called "reporting on office" (*shùzhí*).
"Reporting on office" means reporting on the duties of their office.
None of these is without a purpose.
In spring, they inspect the plowing to assist those who are lacking;
in autumn, they inspect the harvest to help those who are in want.
A proverb of the Xià dynasty says:
“If our king does not take a tour,
how can we find rest?
If our king does not take his pleasure,
how can we receive aid?”
Every tour, every pleasure-trip,
sets a standard for the feudal lords.’
But now it is not so:
hosts of troops march and consume provisions,
the hungry cannot get food,
and the weary cannot find rest.
They look askance and slander one another,
and the people begin to commit offenses.
Your orders defy destiny and oppress the people,
while food and drink flow like water.
With abandon, you indulge in "flowing, linking, wasting, and ruining,"
which brings grief to the feudal lords.
To float down the stream and forget to return
is called "flowing" (*liú*);
to float up the stream and forget to return
is called "linking" (*lián*);
to pursue game without being satisfied
is called "wasting" (*huāng*);
to indulge in wine without being satisfied
is called "ruining" (*wáng*).
The former kings did not indulge in the pleasures of flowing and linking,
nor in the conduct of wasting and ruining.
It is entirely for you, my lord, to choose which path to follow.’
"Qí Jǐng Gōng was pleased.
He issued a solemn warning throughout his state,
moved out of his palace, and lodged in the suburbs.
Then he began to open the granaries to relieve those who were lacking.
He summoned the Grand Music Master, saying:
‘Compose for me music in which ruler and minister rejoice in each other!’
These were indeed the compositions *Zhǐsháo* and *Juésháo*.
Their lyrics say:
‘What fault is there in restraining one's ruler?’
To restrain one's ruler
is to love one's ruler."
2.5 Qí Xuān Wáng asked, saying:
"Everyone advises me to pull down the Míngtáng.
Should I pull it down, or stop?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"The Míngtáng is the hall of a true king.
If Your Majesty wishes to practice kingly government,
then do not pull it down."
The King said:
"May I hear about this kingly government?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"In ancient times, when Wén Wáng ruled Qí,
the farmers tilled the land on the nine-one system;
descendants of officers received hereditary salaries;
at the border passes and in the markets, there was inspection but no levying of duties;
there were no prohibitions regarding the fish weirs and pools;
and the wives and children of criminals were not implicated.
The old who are without wives are called widowers;
the old who are without husbands are called widows;
the old who are without children are called the childless;
the young who are without fathers are called orphans.
These four classes
are the most destitute of the world's people, having none to whom they can tell their grievances.
When Wén Wáng initiated his government and dispensed benevolence,
he always gave priority to these four.
The *Odes* say:
‘Well off are the wealthy,
But pity these solitary ones who are left alone.’"
The King said:
"Excellent indeed are these words!"
Mèngzǐ said:
"If Your Majesty considers them excellent,
why do you not practice them?"
The King said:
"I have a weakness:
I am fond of wealth."
Mèngzǐ replied:
"In ancient times, Gōngliú was fond of wealth.
The *Odes* say:
‘They piled up stacks, they filled granaries,
They wrapped up dried provisions,
In bags and in sacks.
He sought to unite and make glorious his people.
Bows and arrows were displayed,
Shields and spears, halberds and battle-axes,
Then they commenced their march.’
Therefore, those who stayed at home had filled granaries,
and those who marched had bags of provisions;
only then could they commence their march.
If Your Majesty is fond of wealth,
but shares it with the common people,
what difficulty would there be in attaining kingly rule?"
The King said:
"I have a weakness:
I am fond of beauty."
Mèngzǐ replied:
"In ancient times, Tài Wáng was fond of beauty,
and cherished his consort.
The *Odes* say:
‘Gǔgōng Dǎnfù came in the morning, galloping his horses,
Along the banks of the western waters, till he came to the foot of Mount Qí,
Along with Jiāng Nǚ, they came to inspect the site for their home.’
At that time,
there were no dissatisfied women in private,
nor any unmarried men in public.
If Your Majesty is fond of beauty,
but shares this with the common people,
what difficulty would there be in attaining kingly rule?"
2.6 Mèngzǐ said to Qí Xuān Wáng:
"Suppose a subject of Your Majesty entrusted his wife and children to his friend's care
and went to travel in Chǔ,
and when he returned,
he found that his friend had let his wife and children suffer from cold and hunger—
what should he do with him?"
The King said:
"Cast him off."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Suppose the Shìshī cannot govern his officers—
what should be done with him?"
The King said:
"Dismiss him."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Suppose that within the four borders of your kingdom there is no order—
what should be done then?"
The King looked to the left and right, and spoke of other things.
2.7 Mèngzǐ met with Qí Xuān Wáng and said:
"What is called an ancient state
does not mean it has tall trees,
but that it has ministers of successive generations.
Your Majesty has no intimate ministers now;
those whom you promoted yesterday
have disappeared today without you even knowing it."
The King said:
"How can I recognize their lack of talent and dismiss them?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"When a ruler promotes the worthy, if it cannot be helped,
he will cause the low to overlook the honorable,
and distant relatives to overlook close ones.
How can one not be cautious?
If your immediate attendants all say someone is worthy,
that is not enough;
if the great officers all say someone is worthy,
that is not enough;
if the people of the state all say someone is worthy,
only then should you examine him;
if you find him to be indeed worthy,
only then should you employ him.
If your immediate attendants all say someone is unfit,
do not listen;
if the great officers all say someone is unfit,
do not listen;
if the people of the state all say someone is unfit,
only then should you examine him;
if you find him to be indeed unfit,
only then should you dismiss him.
If your immediate attendants all say someone should be executed,
do not listen;
if the great officers all say someone should be executed,
do not listen;
if the people of the state all say someone should be executed,
only then should you examine him;
if you find that he indeed deserves execution,
only then should you execute him.
Therefore it is said: 'It was the people of the state who executed him.'
In this manner,
one can then be the father and mother of the people."
2.8 Qí Xuān Wáng asked:
"Tāng banished Jié,
and Wǔ Wáng smote Zhòu;
did this indeed happen?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"It is so in the records."
The King said:
"Is it permissible for a minister to assassinate his ruler?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"He who outrages benevolence
is called a robber;
he who outrages righteousness
is called a ruffian.
A person who is a robber and ruffian
is called a mere fellow.
I have heard of the execution of the fellow Zhòu,
but I have not heard of assassinating a ruler."
2.9 Mèngzǐ said to Qí Xuān Wáng:
"If you are building a grand mansion,
you must have the master carpenter seek out large timber.
When the master carpenter finds large timber,
Your Majesty is pleased,
thinking he is competent for the task.
But if the artisan carves and makes it too small,
Your Majesty is angry,
thinking he is incompetent for the task.
Now, when a man has studied something in his youth,
and wishes to put it into practice in his adulthood,
if Your Majesty says to him,
'For now, lay aside what you have learned and follow my instructions,'
how would that be?
Suppose there is a piece of unpolished jade here,
though it be worth ten thousand yì,
you would surely have a lapidary carve and polish it.
But when it comes to governing the state and family,
you say,
'For now, lay aside what you have learned and follow my instructions,'
how is this different from teaching a lapidary how to carve jade?"
2.10 The people of Qí attacked Yān and conquered it.
Xuān Wáng asked:
"Some tell me not to annex it,
while others tell me to annex it.
For a state of ten thousand chariots to attack another state of ten thousand chariots,
and to conquer it within fifty days—
human power alone could not have achieved this.
If I do not annex it, there will surely be heaven-sent calamity.
What if I annex it?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"If annexing it makes the people of Yān pleased,
then annex it.
There were those among the ancients who did this—
Wǔ Wáng was one.
If annexing it does not make the people of Yān pleased,
then do not annex it.
There were those among the ancients who did this—
Wén Wáng was one.
When a state of ten thousand chariots attacks another state of ten thousand chariots,
and the people welcome your royal army with baskets of rice and vessels of drink,
how could there be any other reason?
They are only fleeing from water and fire.
If the water becomes even deeper,
and the fire becomes even hotter,
they will just turn elsewhere."
2.11 The people of Qí attacked Yān
and annexed it.
The feudal lords are planning to rescue Yān.
Xuān Wáng said:
"Many of the feudal lords are planning to attack me.
How should I deal with them?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"I have heard of one with a territory of only seventy lǐ governing the world;
Tāng was such a one.
But I have never heard of one with a thousand lǐ fearing others.
The Shū says,
'When Tāng began his military expeditions,
he started with Gě.'
The world trusted him.
When he marched to the east,
the western Barbarians grumbled;
when he marched to the south,
the northern Dí grumbled,
saying,
'Why does he leave us for last?'
The people looked toward him
as they would look for rain-clouds during a great drought.
Those going to market did not stop;
those tilling the fields made no change.
He punished their rulers and consoled their people,
like the falling of a timely rain.
The people were greatly pleased.
The Shū says,
'We await our sovereign;
when our sovereign comes, we shall be revived.'
Now, Yān oppressed its people,
and Your Majesty went and campaigned against it.
The people thought you were going to deliver them out of water and fire,
so they welcomed your royal army with baskets of rice and vessels of drink.
But if you kill their fathers and elder brothers,
bind and imprison their sons and younger brothers,
destroy their ancestral temples,
and plunder their precious vessels,
how can this be tolerated?
The world already fears the strength of Qí.
Now, you have doubled your territory
but do not practice benevolent governance;
this is to mobilize the armies of the world against you.
Your Majesty should quickly issue orders
to send back the captive old and young,
stop the plundering of precious vessels,
consult with the people of Yān,
establish a ruler for them, and then withdraw.
In this way, you may still be able to avert the impending danger."
2.12 There was a conflict between Zōu and Lǔ.
Mù Gōng asked:
"Thirty-three of my officials died,
but none of the people would die for them.
If I punish them,
they are too numerous to be fully punished;
if I do not punish them,
they will continue to look with anger upon the death of their superiors and not rescue them.
What is the right course to take?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"In years of bad harvest and famine,
among your subjects, the old and weak rolled into ditches and valleys,
while the strong scattered to the four quarters—there were several thousand of them.
Yet your granaries were full,
and your treasuries were well-stocked,
but none of your officials reported this to you.
This is a case of superiors being negligent and cruel to those below.
Céngzǐ said:
'Beware, beware!
What goes out from you
will return to you.'
The people have now indeed paid back their superiors.
Do not blame them, Your Lordship!
If Your Lordship practices benevolent governance,
then these people will love their superiors
and die for their leaders."
2.13 Téng Wén Gōng asked:
"Téng is a small state,
situated between Qí and Chǔ.
Should I serve Qí?
Or should I serve Chǔ?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"This kind of plan is beyond my capacity.
But if you have no choice,
there is one course:
dig deep moats,
build high walls,
defend them together with the people,
and even to the point of death they will not desert you.
This is something that can be done."
2.14 Téng Wén Gōng asked:
"The people of Qí are going to fortify Xuē;
I am very much afraid.
What is the right course to take?"
Mèngzǐ replied, saying:
“In ancient times, when Dàwáng dwelt in Bīn,
the Dí people invaded it.
He left it and went to dwell at the foot of Mount Qí.
It was not that he chose this and took it;
he had no alternative.
If one does good,
among his descendants in future generations there will surely be kings.
A gentleman founds an enterprise and hands down his lineage
so that it may be continued.
As for attaining success,
that is up to Heaven.
What can you do about them?
Strive to do good, and that is all.”
2.15 Duke Wén of Téng asked, saying:
“Téng is a small state.
Even if I exert all my strength to serve the great states,
I still cannot escape calamity.
What course of action should I take?”
Mèngzǐ replied, saying:
“In ancient times, when Dàwáng dwelt in Bīn,
the Dí people invaded it.
He served them with skins and silks,
but could not escape them;
he served them with dogs and horses,
but could not escape them;
he served them with pearls and jade,
but could not escape them.
Thereupon, he assembled his elders and addressed them, saying:
‘What the Dí people want is my land.
I have heard this:
a gentleman does not harm his people for the sake of that which nourishes them.
Why should you, my gentlemen, worry about having no ruler?
I shall leave this place.’
He left Bīn, crossed Mount Liáng,
and founded a town at the foot of Mount Qí to dwell there.
The people of Bīn said:
‘He is a benevolent man;
we must not lose him.’
Those who followed him were like people flocking to a market.
Others say:
‘It is a state to be guarded from generation to generation;
it is not something one can decide on one’s own.
Commit to death and do not leave.’
“Your Highness, please choose between these two courses.”
2.16 Duke Píng of Lǔ was about to go out,
when his favorite, Zāng Cāng, made a request, saying:
“On other days when Your Highness goes out,
you always command the officers where you are going.
Now your carriage is already yoked,
but the officers do not know where you are going.
I venture to ask.”
The Duke said:
“I am going to see Mèngzǐ.”
Zāng Cāng said:
“Why should Your Highness demean your person by being the first to visit a common man?
Do you think he is a worthy man?
Propriety and righteousness proceed from worthy men;
yet Mèngzǐ’s later funeral was more lavish than his earlier funeral.
Your Highness should not see him!”
The Duke said:
“Very well.”
Lèzhèngzǐ went in to see the Duke, saying:
“Why did Your Highness not go to see Mèng Kē?”
The Duke said:
“Someone informed me, saying,
‘Mèngzǐ’s later funeral was more lavish than his earlier funeral,’
and so I did not go to see him.”
Lèzhèngzǐ said:
“What does Your Highness mean by ‘more lavish’?
Was it because the former was with the rites of an officer and the latter with those of a great officer?
Because the former used three tripods, while the latter used five?”
The Duke said:
“No;
I refer to the splendor of the inner and outer coffins, and of the shroud and grave-clothes.”
Lèzhèngzǐ said:
“That is not what is meant by ‘more lavish’;
it was simply a difference in wealth between the two periods.”
Lèzhèngzǐ saw Mèngzǐ, and said:
“I told the Duke about you,
and he was about to come see you.
But among his favorites there was a certain Zāng Cāng who discouraged him,
and so the Duke did not come after all.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“A man’s advancement is sometimes caused by others;
his arrest is sometimes caused by others.
But advancement or arrest is not within human power.
My not meeting with the Marquis of Lǔ
is the will of Heaven.
How could that fellow Zāng
prevent me from meeting him?”
3.1 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked, saying:
“If you, Master, were to obtain office in Qí,
could the achievements of Guǎn Zhòng and Yànzǐ be expected of you again?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“You are indeed a man of Qí;
you know of Guǎn Zhòng and Yànzǐ, and nothing more.
Someone once asked Zēng Xī, saying:
‘Who is the more worthy, you or Zǐlù?’
Zēng Xī looked uneasy and said:
‘He is one whom my late father held in awe.’
The other said:
‘Well then, who is the more worthy, you or Guǎn Zhòng?’
Zēng Xī flushed with displeasure and said:
‘How can you compare me to Guǎn Zhòng?
Guǎn Zhòng possessed the confidence of his ruler so exclusively,
and directed the government of the state for so long,
yet his achievements were so low!
How can you compare me to him?’”
Mèngzǐ continued:
“Guǎn Zhòng was one whom Zēng Xī would not be compared to,
and yet you wish me to be like him?”
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
“Guǎn Zhòng made his ruler leader of all the feudal lords,
and Yànzǐ made his ruler illustrious.
Are Guǎn Zhòng and Yànzǐ still not worthy of being imitated?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“To rule the empire through Qí
would be as easy as turning over one’s hand.”
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
“If it be so,
then the perplexity of your disciple is indeed very great.
Moreover, with the virtue of King Wén,
who lived to a hundred years before he died,
his influence had not yet penetrated the whole empire.
King Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu succeeded him,
and only then did it prevail widely.
Now you speak of ruling as if it were an easy thing;
is King Wén then not worthy of being imitated?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“How can King Wén be compared to anyone?
From Tāng to Wǔdīng,
there arose six or seven worthy and sage sovereigns.
The empire had been attached to Yīn for a long time,
and what has lasted long is difficult to change.
Wǔdīng brought the feudal lords to court
and possessed the empire as easily as turning it in his palm.
The interval between Zhòu and Wǔdīng was not very long;
the ancient families, the traditional customs, the lingering influence, and the good administration were still preserved.
Moreover, there were Wēizǐ, Wēizhòng, Prince Bǐgān, Jīzǐ, and Jiāogé,
all of whom were worthy men,
who joined in assisting him;
therefore, it was only after a long time that they lost the empire.
Not a foot of land but was theirs;
not a single person but was their subject.
Yet King Wén rose from a territory of only a hundred square lǐ;
this is why it was difficult for him.
The people of Qí have a saying:
‘Though you have wisdom,
it is not as good as taking advantage of favorable circumstances;
though you have farming tools,
it is not as good as waiting for the right season.’
Now, the present time is highly favorable:
At the height of the sovereigns of Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu,
the territory of none of them exceeded a thousand lǐ,
and Qí already possesses such a territory.
The crowing of cocks and barking of dogs are heard from one place to another
all the way to its four borders,
and Qí already has such a population.
Without any further expansion of territory,
and without any further gathering of people,
if it practices benevolent government and rules the empire,
no one will be able to resist.
Moreover, there has never been a time when a true king did not arise
for a longer interval than the present;
and the people have never suffered more severely under tyrannical government
than at the present time.
To the hungry, any food is easily made sweet;
to the thirsty, any drink is easily made sweet.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘The influence of virtue spreads
faster than a message carried by post-stations.’
At the present time,
if a state of ten thousand chariots practices benevolent government,
the people will rejoice in it
as if they were delivered from hanging by their heels.
Therefore, with half the effort of the ancients,
the achievement will surely be doubled;
it is only the present time that makes this possible.”
3.2 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked, saying:
“If you, Master, were appointed to the high office of minister or prime minister of Qí,
and were able to carry your principles into practice,
it would not be surprising if through this you made its ruler leader of all the lords, or even king.
If this were so, would your mind be perturbed or not?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“No;
at forty my mind was no longer perturbed.”
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
“If it be so,
then you, Master, far surpass Mèng Bēn.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“That is not difficult;
Gàozǐ attained an unperturbed mind before I did.”
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
“Is there a way to attain an unperturbed mind?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“Yes.
Běigōng Yǒu’s cultivation of courage was like this:
he did not shrink back physically,
and his eyes did not turn away.
He considered the slightest insult from anyone
to be like being beaten in the public marketplace.
He would not accept an insult from a commoner wearing coarse cloth,
nor would he accept it from a lord of ten thousand chariots.
He regarded stabbing a lord of ten thousand chariots
just as he regarded stabbing a commoner.
He stood in no awe of the feudal lords;
if an offensive word came to him,
he was sure to return it.
The way Mèng Shīshè cultivated courage
was by saying,
"To regard defeat just as victory;
to advance only after measuring the enemy,
and to join battle only after calculating the certainty of victory—
this is to be afraid of the three armies.
How could I, Shè, guarantee victory?
I can only be without fear, and that is all."
Mèng Shīshè resembled Zēngzǐ,
while Běigōng Yǒu resembled Zǐxià.
Of the courage of these two men,
it is not known which was superior,
yet Mèng Shīshè held to what was essential.
In the past, Zēngzǐ said to Zǐxiāng,
"Do you love courage?
I once heard about great courage from the Master:
'If, on self-examination, I find myself not to be upright,
even though my opponent be a commoner wearing coarse cloth,
must I not be afraid?
But if, on self-examination, I find myself to be upright,
though my opponents be ten million men, I will go forward.'"
Mèng Shīshè’s preservation of his qi,
was still not as good as Zēngzǐ’s holding to what was essential.
He said,
"May I venture to ask
about your unperturbed mind compared to that of Gàozǐ?
May I hear about it?"
Mencius said, "Gàozǐ said,
'What you do not get in words,
do not seek in your mind;
what you do not get in your mind,
do not seek in your qi.'
'What you do not get in your mind,
do not seek in your qi'
is acceptable.
But 'What you do not get in words,
do not seek in your mind'
is unacceptable.
For the will is the leader of the qi,
and the qi is that which fills the body.
Where the will is directed,
there the qi follows.
Therefore it is said,
'Maintain your will,
and do not do violence to your qi.'"
"Since you say, 'Where the will is directed,
there the qi follows,'
and also say,
'Maintain your will,
and do not do violence to your qi,'
why is this?"
Mencius said,
"When the will is unified, it moves the qi;
when the qi is unified, it moves the will.
Now, stumbling or running
is a matter of the qi,
yet it reacts back and moves the mind."
"May I venture to ask, wherein do you excel, Master?"
Mencius said,
"I understand words,
and I am good at nourishing my vast, flowing qi."
"May I venture to ask, what is this vast, flowing qi?"
Mencius said,
"It is difficult to explain.
As for this qi,
it is exceedingly great and exceedingly strong.
If nourished with uprightness and not harmed,
it will fill the space between heaven and earth.
As for this qi,
it is the companion of righteousness and the Way.
Without these, it starves.
It is produced by the accumulation of righteous deeds,
not by incidental acts of righteousness to seize it.
If one's conduct is not satisfying to the mind,
then it starves."
Therefore I say,
"Gàozǐ has never understood righteousness,
because he treats it as external."
"One must work at it,
but without expectation of instant results;
let the mind not forget it,
yet do not assist it to grow.
Do not be like the man of Sòng.
There was a man of Sòng who was anxious because his sprouts were not growing, so he pulled them up.
Weary, he returned home,
and said to his family,
'I am exhausted today!
I have helped the sprouts grow!'
His son ran to look at them,
and found that the sprouts had withered."
In the world, those who do not try to help the sprouts grow are few.
Those who think it is of no use and abandon it,
are like those who do not weed their sprouts;
those who assist them to grow,
are like those who pull up the sprouts.
Not only is this of no benefit,
but it actually harms them.
"What do you mean by 'understanding words'?"
Mencius said,
"From biased words, I know what they conceal;
from extravagant words, I know wherein they are trapped;
from crooked words, I know how they have strayed;
from evasive words, I know how they are at their wits' end.
Arising in their minds,
they do harm to their government;
manifested in their government,
they do harm to their affairs.
Should a sage arise again,
he would certainly agree with my words."
"Zǎi Wǒ and Zǐgòng were good at rhetoric;
Rǎn Niú, Mǐnzǐ, and Yányuān were good at speaking of virtuous conduct.
Kǒngzǐ combined all these,
yet he said,
'As for diplomatic speech,
I am not capable.'
If so, then are you, Master, already a sage?"
Mencius said,
"Oh!
What kind of talk is this?
In the past, Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ,
'Are you, Master, already a sage?'
Kǒngzǐ said,
'As for being a sage, that I cannot do.
I simply study without satiety and teach without weariness.'
Zǐgòng said,
'To study without satiety
is wisdom;
to teach without weariness
is benevolence.
Being both benevolent and wise,
you, Master, are indeed a sage.'
Even a sage Kǒngzǐ did not claim to be.
What kind of talk is this?"
"In the past, I have privately heard this:
Zǐxià, Zǐyóu, and Zǐzhāng
each possessed a single aspect of the sage,
while Rǎn Niú, Mǐnzǐ, and Yányuān
possessed it in its entirety, though in miniature.
May I venture to ask, which of these do you align yourself with?"
Mencius said,
"Let us put this aside for now."
He said,
"What about Bó Yí and Yī Yǐn?"
Mencius said,
"Their ways were different.
Unless it was his ruler, he would not serve;
unless they were his people, he would not employ them.
When there was good government, he would take office;
when there was disorder, he would retire.
Such was Bó Yí.
'Whomsoever I serve, is he not my ruler?
Whomsoever I employ, are they not my people?'
In times of good government, he would take office;
and in times of disorder, he would also take office.
Such was Yī Yǐn.
When it was proper to take office, he took office;
when it was proper to retire, he retired;
when it was proper to remain long, he remained long;
when it was proper to leave quickly, he left quickly.
Such was Kǒngzǐ.
All of them were ancient sages,
and I have not been able to equal any of their deeds.
But as for my heart's desire,
it is to study Kǒngzǐ."
"Were Bó Yí and Yī Yǐn
on a level with Kǒngzǐ?"
Mencius said,
"No.
Since the birth of mankind,
there has never been another Kǒngzǐ."
"Did they, then, have anything in common?"
Mencius said,
"They did.
If they had obtained a territory of a hundred lǐ and ruled over it,
each would have been able to bring the feudal lords to court and possess the whole empire.
But to commit a single act of unrighteousness,
or to kill a single innocent person,
in order to obtain the empire,
none of them would have done it.
In this they were the same."
He said:
"I venture to ask how they differed."
He said:
"Zǎi Wǒ, Zǐgòng, and Yǒu Ruò
had wisdom sufficient to recognize a sage,
and even when in low positions, they would not stoop to flatter the one they admired.
Zǎi Wǒ said:
'As I view the Master,
he is far superior to Yáo and Shùn.'
Zǐgòng said:
'By seeing his rituals, one knows his government;
by hearing his music, one knows his virtue.
From the distance of a hundred generations hereafter,
if we appraise the kings of those hundred generations,
none will be able to diverge from him.
Since the birth of mankind,
there has never been another like the Master.'
Yǒu Ruò said:
'Is it only among people?
The qílín among beasts of the field,
the fènghuáng among birds of the air,
Mount Tài among hills and anthills,
the rivers and seas among rain-pools in the road
—they are of the same kind.
The sage among ordinary people
is also of the same kind.
But he rises above his kind,
and stands out from the crowd.
Since the birth of mankind,
there has never been one greater than Kǒngzǐ.' "
3.3 Mèngzǐ said:
"He who uses force while pretending to benevolence is a hegemon;
a hegemon must possess a large state.
He who uses virtue to practice benevolence is a king;
a king does not rely on greatness.
Tāng did it with seventy lǐ,
and King Wén with a hundred lǐ.
"When one subdues people by force,
they do not submit in their hearts,
but only because their strength is insufficient;
when one subdues people by virtue,
they are pleased in their hearts and sincerely submit,
just as the seventy disciples submitted to Kǒngzǐ.
The *Shī* says:
'From the west, from the east,
from the south, from the north,
there was not a thought but of submission.'
This is what that refers to."
3.4 Mèngzǐ said:
"Benevolence brings glory,
while non-benevolence brings disgrace.
To dislike disgrace and yet dwell in non-benevolence
is like disliking dampness and yet dwelling in a low-lying place.
"If one dislikes it,
there is nothing better than to honor virtue and respect scholars,
so that worthy men are in high positions
and capable men are in office.
When the state is at leisure and free from trouble,
take advantage of this time to make the government and laws clear.
Even a large state
will surely stand in awe of you.
The *Shī* says:
'Before the sky grew dark with rain,
I gathered the bark of the mulberry root,
and bound tight my windows and doors.
Now, indeed, you people below,
who will dare insult me?'
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Did the author of this poem
understand the Way?
If one can govern one's state,
who would dare to insult them?'
"Now, when the state is at leisure and free from trouble,
they take advantage of this time to indulge in pleasure and idle laziness;
this is seeking disaster for oneself.
There is no disaster or good fortune that is not sought by oneself.
The *Shī* says:
'May you ever match the mandate,
and seek for yourself much good fortune.'
The *Tàijiǎ* says:
'When Heaven sends down calamities,
they may still be escaped;
but when one brings about calamity oneself,
one cannot survive.'
This is what that refers to."
3.5 Mèngzǐ said:
"If you honor the worthy and employ the capable,
so that outstanding talents hold office,
then all the scholars of the world will be pleased and wish to stand in your court.
If in the marketplace, you provide stalls but do not levy taxes on goods,
or enforce the regulations without taxing the stalls,
then all the merchants of the world will be pleased and wish to store their goods in your marketplace.
If at the border passes, there is inspection but no toll levied,
then all the travelers of the world will be pleased and wish to travel on your roads.
If for the tillers, they perform mutual assistance but are not taxed,
then all the farmers of the world will be pleased and wish to plow in your fields.
If in the dwellings, there is no individual tax or neighborhood tax,
then all the people of the world will be pleased and wish to become your subjects.
"If you can truly practice these five things,
then the people of neighboring states will look up to you as their father and mother.
If they try to lead their children to attack their own father and mother,
since the birth of mankind, no one has ever succeeded in doing so.
Thus,
you will have no enemy under heaven.
One who has no enemy under heaven is an officer of Heaven.
Under such circumstances, that he should not become King
is something that has never happened."
3.6 Mèngzǐ said:
"All human beings have a mind that cannot bear to see the suffering of others.
The ancient kings had this mind that could not bear to see the suffering of others,
and thus they had a government that could not bear to see the suffering of others.
Running a government that cannot bear to see the suffering of others
with a mind that cannot bear to see the suffering of others,
governing the world is as easy as turning something in the palm of one's hand.
"Why do I say that all human beings have a mind that cannot bear to see the suffering of others?
If people were suddenly to see a young child about to fall into a well,
they would all experience a feeling of alarm and distress.
This is not because they want to seek the favor of the child's parents,
nor because they seek praise from their neighbors and friends,
nor because they dislike the child's cries.
"From this we can see that
without a mind of compassion,
one is not human;
without a mind of shame and dislike,
one is not human;
without a mind of deference and compliance,
one is not human;
without a mind of right and wrong,
one is not human.
"The mind of compassion is the sprout of benevolence;
the mind of shame and dislike is the sprout of righteousness;
the mind of deference and compliance is the sprout of propriety;
the mind of right and wrong is the sprout of wisdom.
"Human beings having these four sprouts
is like having their four limbs.
To have these four sprouts and yet say one is unable to develop them
is to rob oneself;
to say that one's ruler is unable to develop them
is to rob one's ruler.
"For all who have these four sprouts within themselves,
if they know how to expand and fully develop them,
they will be like a fire that has just started to burn,
or a spring that has just begun to gush forth.
If they can be fully developed,
they are sufficient to protect all within the four seas;
if they are not developed,
they will not even be sufficient to serve one's parents."
3.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"Is the arrow-maker less benevolent by nature than the armor-maker?
Yet the arrow-maker only fears lest his arrows should not wound people,
while the armor-maker only fears lest people should be wounded.
It is the same with the healer and the coffin-maker.
Therefore, one cannot but be careful in choosing one's profession.
"Kǒngzǐ said:
'To dwell in benevolence is beautiful.
If one chooses not to dwell in benevolence,
how can one be wise?'
Now, benevolence is the most honorable rank given by Heaven,
and the peaceful dwelling of mankind.
When nothing prevents one from being benevolent, and yet one is not,
this is to be unwise.
"Lacking benevolence and wisdom,
lacking propriety and righteousness,
one becomes a servant to others.
To be a servant to others and yet feel ashamed of being a servant
is like a bow-maker being ashamed of making bows,
or an arrow-maker being ashamed of making arrows.
If one is ashamed of it,
there is nothing better than to practice benevolence.
"One who is benevolent is like an archer:
the archer aligns himself before shooting;
if he shoots and misses the mark,
he does not resent the one who wins against him,
but simply turns inward and seeks the cause in himself."
3.8 Mèngzǐ said:
"When anyone told Zǐlù
that he had a fault, he was glad.
When Yǔ heard good words, he bowed.
The great Shùn was even greater:
he regarded goodness as something to be shared with others;
he would set aside his own views to follow others,
and gladly learned from others in order to practice goodness.
From farming, pottery-making, and fishing,
all the way to becoming Emperor,
there was nothing he did not learn from others.
To learn from others in order to practice goodness
is to help others do good.
Therefore, for the gentleman, there is nothing greater than helping others do good."
3.9 Mèngzǐ said:
"Bóyí would not serve a prince whom he did not approve of,
nor befriend anyone whom he did not approve of.
He would not stand in the court of an evil man,
nor would he speak with an evil man;
to stand in the court of an evil man
and to speak with an evil man
was, to him, like sitting in mud and charcoal while wearing court robes and a court cap."
Extending his mind of hating evil,
if he thought of standing with a villager
whose cap was not straight,
he would leave him with a look of displeasure,
as if he would be defiled.
Therefore, although there were feudal lords who sent invitations with fine messages,
he would not accept them.
His not accepting them
was because he did not deign to go to them.
Liǔxià Huì was not ashamed of a corrupt ruler,
and did not look down on a low office;
when in office, he did not hide his worth,
and always acted according to his principles;
when passed over and left in obscurity, he did not harbor resentment,
and when in distress and poverty, he did not grieve.
Therefore he said:
‘You are you,
and I am I.
Even if you should stand by my side with your shoulders bare or completely naked,
how could you defile me?’
Therefore, in a self-possessed manner, he stayed in their company
without losing his self-possession,
and if held back, he would stay.
His staying when held back
was because he did not deign to leave.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“Bóyí was narrow-minded,
and Liǔxià Huì was lacking in respect.
Narrow-mindedness and lack of respect
are what the gentleman does not follow.”
4.1 Mèngzǐ said:
“Opportunities of time granted by Heaven are not equal to advantages of situation afforded by the Earth,
and advantages of situation afforded by the Earth are not equal to the union of human hearts.
An inner city wall of three lǐ,
and an outer city wall of seven lǐ,
may be surrounded and attacked, yet not be taken.
Now, to surround and attack it,
there must have been favorable opportunities of Heaven;
yet if it is not taken,
this shows that opportunities of Heaven are not equal to advantages of Earth.
It is not that the walls are not high,
nor that the moats are not deep,
nor that the weapons and armor are not sharp and strong,
nor that the stores of grain are not abundant;
yet the defenders abandon it and flee.
This shows that advantages of Earth are not equal to the union of human hearts.
Therefore it is said:
‘People are not kept within boundaries by the limits of frontiers,
a state is not secured by the obstacles of mountains and valleys,
and the world is not awed by the strength of arms.’
He who finds the Way receives abundant help,
and he who loses the Way receives little help.
When help is at its lowest,
even his own relatives will rebel against him;
when help is at its highest,
the whole world will yield obedience to him.
When one whom the whole world obeys
attacks one whom even his own relatives rebel against,
thus, the gentleman may not fight, but if he does,
he is sure to conquer.”
4.2 Mèngzǐ was about to go to court to see the King,
when the King sent a messenger to say to him:
“I was wishing to come and see you,
but I have caught a cold,
and cannot expose myself to the wind.
Tomorrow morning I will hold court;
I do not know whether I might have the pleasure of seeing you there?”
He replied:
“Unfortunately, I am ill,
and cannot go to court.”
The next day, he went out to pay a visit of condolence to the Dōngguō family.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
“Yesterday you declined on the ground of illness,
and today you go to pay a visit of condolence;
is this not perhaps improper?”
He said:
“Yesterday I was ill,
today I am well;
why should I not pay a visit of condolence?”
The King sent a messenger to inquire about his illness,
and a physician came.
Mèng Zhòngzǐ replied to them, saying:
“Yesterday, when the King’s order came,
he was suffering from a slight indisposition,
and was unable to go to court.
Today his illness is a little better,
and he has hastened to the court;
I do not know whether he will be able to reach it or not.”
He then sent several men to intercept him on the way, saying:
“Please do not return home,
but go straight to the court!”
Mèngzǐ was obliged to go and spend the night with the family of Jǐng Chǒu.
Jǐngzǐ said:
“In the family, there are father and son;
abroad, there are ruler and minister;
these are the great relations of humanity.
Between father and son, affection is the chief thing;
between ruler and minister, respect is the chief thing.
I, Chǒu, have seen the King show respect to you,
but I have not seen how you respect the King.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“Oh! What words are these!
Among the people of Qí, there is no one who speaks to the King about benevolence and righteousness.
Is it because they think benevolence and righteousness are not beautiful?
No, but in their hearts they say:
‘How is he worthy to be spoken with about benevolence and righteousness?’
Thus, there is no disrespect greater than this.
As for me, I dare not present anything before the King that is not the way of Yáo and Shùn.
Therefore, among the people of Qí, there is no one who respects the King as much as I do.”
Jǐngzǐ said:
“No,
that is not what I mean.
The Book of Rites says:
‘When a father calls, his son must not merely answer "Yes";’
‘when the ruler summons, he must not wait for his carriage to be yoked.’
You were indeed intending to go to court,
but on hearing the King’s summons, you desisted from your purpose.
This indeed seems not to be in accordance with that rite.”
He replied:
“How can you say that?
Céngzǐ said:
‘The wealth of Jìn and Chǔ cannot be equaled.
Let them use their wealth,
I will use my benevolence.
Let them use their rank,
I will use my righteousness.
In what way am I inferior to them?’
Now, would Céngzǐ have said this
if it were not right?
It is because they are of the same path.
There are three things universally honored in the world:
rank is one,
age is one,
and virtue is one.
In the court, rank is first;
in the village, age is first;
and for assisting the world and ruling the people, virtue is first.
How can one who possesses one of these treat the other two with neglect?
Therefore, a ruler who is to accomplish great things
must have ministers whom he does not summon.
When he wishes to consult with them, he goes to them.
If he does not honor virtue and delight in the Way in this manner,
he is not fit to accomplish great things.
Therefore, Tāng’s relation to Yī Yǐn was such
that he first learned from him and then made him his minister;
hence, without labor, he became king.
Duke Huán’s relation to Guǎn Zhòng was such
that he first learned from him and then made him his minister;
hence, without labor, he became leader of the princes.
Today, the states of the world are equal in territory and equal in virtue,
and none can surpass the others.
This is for no other reason than that
they love to make ministers of those whom they can teach,
and do not love to make ministers of those from whom they might receive instruction.
Tāng in relation to Yī Yǐn,
and Duke Huán in relation to Guǎn Zhòng,
dared not summon them.
If even Guǎn Zhòng could not be summoned,
how much less may one who would not be a Guǎn Zhòng be summoned?”
4.3 Chén Zhēn asked, saying:
“Formerly, when you were in Qí,
the King sent you a present of one hundred yī of fine gold, and you would not receive it.
When you were in Sòng,
you were presented with seventy yī, and you received it.
When you were in Xuē,
you were presented with fifty yī, and you received it.
If your not receiving it on the former occasion was right,
then your receiving it on these latter occasions was wrong.
If your receiving it on these latter occasions was right,
then your not receiving it on the former occasion was wrong.
You must have been in one of these errors.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“All were right.
When I was in Sòng,
I was about to make a long journey.
To travelers, a present for expenses is always made.
The message was:
‘A present for your journey.’
Why should I not have received it?
When I was in Xuē,
I had reason to be on my guard.
The message was:
‘I have heard you are on your guard,
and therefore present this to buy weapons.’
Why should I not have received it?
But as for the case in Qí,
I had no occasion for money.
To make a present of it when there is no occasion for it,
is to bribe.
How can a gentleman be bought with a bribe?”
4.4 Mèngzǐ went to Pínglù,
and said to its governor:
“If one of your spear-men
should lose his place in the ranks three times in one day,
would you dismiss him or not?”
He said,
"I would not wait for a third time."
"In that case," [said Mèngzǐ], "your own failures to maintain your ranks have also been many.
In years of famine and scarcity,
of your people, the old and weak have rolled into ditches and valleys,
while the strong have scattered and fled to all four quarters,
by the thousands."
He replied,
"This was not within the power of me, Jùxīn, to prevent."
[Mèngzǐ] said,
"If there is a man who receives another person's cattle and sheep
to pasture them for him,
he must certainly seek pasturage and fodder for them.
If he seeks pasturage and fodder but cannot find them,
should he return them to their owner,
or should he stand by and watch them die?"
He replied,
"In this, it is indeed the fault of me, Jùxīn."
On another day, having an audience with the King, [Mèngzǐ] said,
"Of your Majesty's governors of districts,
I know five.
The only one who knows his own fault
is Kǒng Jùxīn."
He then recounted the conversation to the King.
The King said,
"This is indeed the fault of me, the Solitary One."
4.5 Mèngzǐ said to Chí Wā,
"Your resigning the governorship of Língqiū
to request the office of Chief Justice
seemed reasonable,
because in that position you could speak to the King.
Now, several months have passed.
Have you still not found an opportunity to speak?"
Chí Wā remonstrated with the King, but his counsel was not accepted.
He therefore resigned his office and departed.
The people of Qí said,
"What he did for Chí
Wā was indeed excellent;
but what he has done for himself,
we do not know."
Gōngdūzǐ told this to Mèngzǐ.
[Mèngzǐ] said,
"I have heard this:
He who holds an official duty,
if he cannot perform his office, should resign;
he who has the responsibility of giving counsel,
if his counsel is not followed, should resign.
As for me, I have no official duty,
and I have no responsibility of giving counsel.
Therefore, in my advancing or retreating,
do I not have ample room and abundant leeway?"
4.6 Mèngzǐ served as a minister in Qí
and went on a mission of condolence to Téng.
The King appointed Wáng Huān, the Grand Officer of Gài, to accompany him as an assistant envoy.
Wáng Huān saw him morning and evening,
but on the entire road from Qí to Téng and back,
[Mèngzǐ] never once spoke to him about the business of the mission.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"The position of a minister of Qí
is not a minor one;
the road between Qí and Téng
is not a short one.
Yet during the journey there and back,
you never once spoke to him about the business of the mission.
Why was this?"
[Mèngzǐ] replied,
"Since those matters were already being managed by others,
what was there for me to say?"
4.7 Mèngzǐ went from Qí to Lǔ to bury his mother.
On returning to Qí,
he stopped at Yíng.
Chōng Yú made a request, saying,
"The other day, despite my unworthiness,
you put me in charge of supervising the coffin-makers.
In the midst of the urgent burial preparations,
I did not dare to ask.
Today, I would like to make a humble request:
It seemed to me that the wood was too beautiful."
[Mèngzǐ] said,
"In ancient times, there was no fixed standard for inner and outer coffins.
In middle antiquity, the inner coffin was made seven inches thick,
and the outer coffin was of corresponding thickness.
From the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
this was not merely to make them look beautiful,
but so that they might fully satisfy the filial heart of man.
If one is not permitted [by ritual law],
one cannot find satisfaction in it;
if one does not have the means,
one cannot find satisfaction in it.
But if one is permitted and has the means,
the ancients all used them;
why should I alone not do so?
Furthermore, to prevent
the earth from coming into contact with the body of the deceased,
does this not give satisfaction to the human heart?
I have heard this:
A gentleman does not, for the sake of the world, skimp on his parents."
4.8 Shěn Tóng, in his private capacity, asked,
"May Yān be attacked?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Yes.
Zǐkuài had no right to give Yān to another,
and Zǐzhī had no right to receive Yān from Zǐkuài.
Suppose there were an officer here
whom you liked,
and without informing the King,
you privately gave him your own salary and rank,
and that officer,
also without any royal command, privately received them from you—
would that be permissible?
How is the case of Yān any different from this?"
The people of Qí attacked Yān.
Someone asked,
"Did you encourage Qí to attack Yān?
Is this true?"
[Mèngzǐ] replied,
"No.
Shěn Tóng asked me, 'May Yān be attacked?'
and I answered him,
'Yes.'
Thereupon they went and attacked it.
If he had asked, 'Who may attack it?'
I would have answered,
'He who is a Minister of Heaven
may attack it.'
Suppose there were a murderer,
and someone asked,
'May this person be put to death?'
I would answer, 'Yes.'
If he then asked,
'Who may put him to death?'
I would answer,
'He who is the Chief Justice
may put him to death.'
Now, for one Yān-like state to attack another Yān-like state,
why should I have encouraged them?"
4.9 The people of Yān rebelled.
The King said,
"I am deeply ashamed before Mèngzǐ."
Chán Jiǎ said,
"Your Majesty, do not be distressed.
Between your Majesty and the Duke of Zhōu,
who do you think was more benevolent and wise?"
The King said,
"Ah!
What kind of words are these?"
[Chán Jiǎ] said,
"The Duke of Zhōu sent Guǎn Shū to supervise Yīn,
but Guǎn Shū rebelled with Yīn.
If the Duke knew he would do so and still sent him,
that was a lack of benevolence.
If he did not know and sent him,
that was a lack of wisdom.
Even the Duke of Zhōu
did not fully possess benevolence and wisdom,
how much less then can your Majesty be expected to?
I, Jiǎ, beg permission to see Mèngzǐ and explain this to him."
He saw Mèngzǐ and asked,
"What kind of man was the Duke of Zhōu?"
[Mèngzǐ] replied,
"A sage of antiquity."
[Chán Jiǎ] said,
"He sent Guǎn Shū to supervise Yīn,
and Guǎn Shū rebelled with Yīn. Is this true?"
[Mèngzǐ] replied,
"Yes."
[Chán Jiǎ] asked,
"Did the Duke of Zhōu know that he would rebel
when he sent him?"
[Mèngzǐ] replied,
"He did not know."
"If so, then even a sage can make mistakes?"
[Mèngzǐ] replied,
"The Duke of Zhōu was the younger brother;
Guǎn Shū was the older brother.
Was not the Duke of Zhōu's mistake
a very natural one?
Moreover, the gentlemen of antiquity,
when they made mistakes, they corrected them;
but the gentlemen of today,
when they make mistakes, they persist in them.
The mistakes of the gentlemen of antiquity
were like eclipses of the sun and moon:
all the people saw them;
and when they corrected them,
all the people looked up to them in admiration.
The gentlemen of today,
do they merely persist in their mistakes?
No, they go on to make excuses for them."
4.10 Mèngzǐ resigned his office as minister and prepared to return home.
The King went to see Mèngzǐ
and said:
"Formerly, I wished to see you but had no opportunity;
then I obtained the privilege of standing by your side in the same court, and was very glad.
Now you are again abandoning this lonely one and returning home.
I do not know if I may be allowed to see you again after this?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"It is what I do not dare to request,
but it is certainly what I desire."
On another day, the King said to Shízǐ:
"I wish to give Mèngzǐ a residence in the center of the kingdom,
and to support his disciples with ten thousand zhōng,
so that the officers and people may all have an exemplar to respect and imitate.
Why do you not speak to him about this for me?"
Shízǐ commissioned Chénzǐ to inform Mèngzǐ of this,
and Chénzǐ told Mèngzǐ what Shízǐ had said.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Indeed.
But how should Shízǐ know that this cannot be?
If I had wished to be rich,
would I have declined one hundred thousand and now accepted ten thousand,
as if that were the way to wish for wealth?
Jì Sūn said:
'How strange was
Zǐshū Yí!
He pushed himself into the administration,
and when he was not employed,
he should have stopped,
but he went on to have his sons and younger brothers made ministers.
Who indeed does not desire wealth and honor?
But he alone, in the midst of wealth and honor,
monopolized a commanding mound.'
In ancient times, those who carried on market trade
exchanged what they had
for what they had not,
and the officers only supervised them.
But there was a mean fellow,
who would surely search out a commanding mound and climb onto it,
looking to the right and left,
to corner all the profits of the market.
Everyone thought his conduct mean,
and therefore they proceeded to tax him.
The taxing of merchants
began with this mean fellow."
4.11 Mèngzǐ left Qí
and halted at Zhòu.
There was one who wished to detain him on behalf of the King;
he sat down and spoke with him.
Mèngzǐ did not respond,
but leaned on his arm-rest and slept.
The visitor was displeased and said:
"I, your disciple, fasted and purified myself before I dared to speak to you,
