but you, Master, sleep and do not listen to me.
I beg that I may never dare to see you again."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Sit down!
I will explain it to you clearly.
In former times, if Duke Mù of Lǔ
had no one at the side of Zǐsī,
he could not keep Zǐsī at ease;
while Xiè Liǔ and Shēn Xiáng,
if they had no one at the side of Duke Mù,
could not keep themselves at ease.
You, in planning for an elder,
have not reached the level of those who planned for Zǐsī.
Are you breaking off with the elder,
or is the elder breaking off with you?"
4.12 Mèngzǐ left Qí.
Yǐn Shì said to someone:
"If he did not know that the King could not become a Tāng or a Wǔ,
then he was lacking in understanding.
If he knew that he could not,
and yet came to him,
then he was seeking for favors.
He came a thousand li to see the King;
and because he did not meet with success, he is leaving.
Yet he stayed three nights before he left Zhòu.
Why this lingering delay?
I, Shì, am displeased with this."
Gāozǐ told this to Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
"How should Yǐn Shì know me?
To come a thousand li to see the King
was my own desire.
Because I did not meet with success, I am leaving—
how could that be my desire?
It is because I have no alternative.
My staying three nights before leaving Zhòu
still seems to my mind to have been too rapid.
Perhaps the King may change!
If the King should change,
he will certainly recall me.
When I left Zhòu,
and the King did not send to pursue me,
only then did I have a resolute mind to return home.
Even though this is so,
how should I abandon the King?
The King is still capable of doing good.
If the King would use me,
would it be only the people of Qí who would be at peace?
The people of the whole world would all be at peace.
Perhaps the King may change!
I am looking for it daily!
How could I be like one of those petty fellows?
Who, when they remonstrate with their prince and are not accepted,
become angry,
with resentment showing on their faces,
and when they leave, travel with all their might for a whole day before they will halt?"
Yǐn Shì heard of this
and said:
"I am indeed a petty man."
4.13 Mèngzǐ left Qí.
Chōng Yú questioned him on the road, saying:
"Master, you seem to have a look of dissatisfaction.
Yet formerly I, Yú, heard you say:
'The gentleman does not murmur against Heaven,
nor does he grudge against men.'"
Mèngzǐ said:
"That was one time,
and this is another.
It must be that in five hundred years a true king should arise,
and that in the interval there should be those illustrious in their generation.
From the rise of the Zhōu dynasty to the present
it is more than seven hundred years.
By that number, the time is past;
by examining the times, it is indeed suitable.
But Heaven
does not yet wish to bring peace and order to the world.
If it did wish to bring peace and order to the world,
in this present age,
who is there besides me?
Why should I be dissatisfied?"
4.14 Mèngzǐ left Qí and dwelt in Xiū.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked, saying:
"To take office and not receive salary,
is this the ancient way?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"No.
At Chóng,
I had an interview with the King,
and on retiring had the intention of leaving.
Because I did not wish to change my purpose,
I therefore would not receive salary.
Afterward, there came a call to military operations,
and I could not ask leave to go.
To remain so long in Qí
was not my desire."
5.1 When Duke Wén of Téng was the Crown Prince,
he was going to Chǔ,
and passed through Sòng, where he saw Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ discoursed to him on the goodness of human nature,
and in his speaking always referred to Yáo and Shùn.
When the Crown Prince returned from Chǔ,
he saw Mèngzǐ again.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Does the Crown Prince doubt my words?
The path is one, and only one.
Chéng Jiàn said to Duke Jǐng of Qí:
'They were men,
and I am a man;
why should I stand in awe of them?'
Yán Yuān said:
'What kind of man was Shùn?
What kind of man am I?
He who exerts himself will also be like him.'
Gōngmíng Yí said:
'King Wén is my teacher;
how could Zhōugōng deceive me?'
Now, Téng, taking its length and cutting off its excess to make up its deficiency,
is nearly fifty li square.
It is still sufficient to make a good state.
The Book of History says:
'If a medicine does not confuse and distress the patient,
it will not cure his sickness.'"
5.2 Duke Dìng of Téng died.
The Crown Prince said to Rán Yǒu:
"Formerly, Mèngzǐ spoke with me in Sòng,
and in my heart I have never forgotten it.
Now, unfortunately, I have this great cause of grief.
I wish you to go and consult Mèngzǐ,
before I carry out the funeral rites."
Rán Yǒu went to Zōu
and consulted Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Is this not excellent?
In mourning for parents, one should indeed exert oneself to the utmost.
Zēngzǐ said:
'While they are alive,
serve them according to propriety;
when they are dead,
bury them according to propriety,
and sacrifice to them according to propriety;
this may be called filial piety.'"
"As for the rites of the feudal lords,
I have not studied them;
nonetheless,
I have heard of them.
The three years' mourning,
the wearing of coarse hemp garments,
and the eating of thin congee,
from the Son of Heaven down to the commoners,
were shared by all three dynasties."
Rán Yǒu returned and reported this,
and the Duke decided on the three years' mourning.
The elder relatives and all the officials did not wish for it,
so they said:
"None of the former rulers of Lǔ, our ancestral state, practiced this,
nor did any of our own former rulers practice it.
For you to reverse this practice in your own person
is unacceptable."
Furthermore, the *Zhì* states:
‘In mourning and sacrifice, follow the ancestors.’
It also says:
‘We have received this from our predecessors.’"
The Crown Prince said to Rán Yǒu:
"In former days, I did not apply myself to study,
but was fond of galloping horses and fencing.
Now my elder relatives and officials are not satisfied with me,
and I fear I may not be able to carry out this great matter to the fullest.
Please ask Mèngzǐ on my behalf!"
Rán Yǒu went back to Zōu
to consult Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Indeed;
this is not something that can be sought from others.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘When a ruler dies,
he leaves the administration to the prime minister,
sips congee,
his face becomes deep dark,
he takes his place and weeps,
and the officials and officers
do not dare not to grieve,
because he leads them by example.’
When those above favor something,
those below will certainly exceed them in it.
The virtue of the gentleman
is the wind;
the virtue of the petty people
is the grass.
When the wind blows over the grass, it must bend.
This depends entirely on the Crown Prince."
Rán Yǒu returned and reported this.
The Crown Prince said:
"Indeed;
this truly rests with me."
For five months he lived in a mourning shed,
and issued no orders or prohibitions.
The officials and clan members
approved of this,
and said he was wise.
When it came to the burial,
people came from all directions to observe it.
The grief of his countenance
and the sorrow of his weeping
made those who came to condole deeply pleased.
5.3 Duke Wén of Téng asked about governing a state.
Mèngzǐ said:
"The affairs of the people must not be delayed.
The *Shī* says:
‘By day, go gather thatch-grass;
by night, twist it into ropes.
Quickly climb up to repair the roof;
then we shall begin sowing the various grains.’
The way of the people is this:
those who have a constant livelihood have a constant heart;
those who do not have a constant livelihood do not have a constant heart.
If they do not have a constant heart,
abandonment, deviancy, wickedness, and extravagance—
there is nothing they will not do.
When they have fallen into crime,
and only then to follow up and punish them,
is to entrap the people.
How could a benevolent man be in authority
and allow the entrapment of the people to be practiced?
Therefore, a worthy ruler must be respectful, frugal, and polite to his subordinates,
and there must be a regulation for taking from the people.
Yáng Hǔ said:
‘He who seeks to be wealthy will not be benevolent;
he who seeks to be benevolent will not be wealthy.’
Under the sovereign of the Xià dynasty, fifty *mǔ* were allotted, and the tribute system was used.
Under the people of the Yīn, seventy *mǔ* were allotted, and the aid system was used.
Under the people of the Zhōu, one hundred *mǔ* were allotted, and the share system was used.
In reality, all of these amounted to a tax of one-tenth.
The word *chè* means
to share;
the word *zhù* means
to rely upon.
Lóngzǐ said:
‘For administering the land, nothing is better than the aid system,
and nothing is worse than the tribute system.’
As for the tribute system,
it takes the average of several years as a constant standard.
In years of abundance,
when grain is scattered about in abundance,
they could take much without being oppressive,
yet they take little;
in bad years,
when they cannot even get enough to manure their fields,
they must still take the full amount.
Being the parents of the people,
and yet making the people look with glares of distress,
so that they toil and labor all year long,
yet cannot support their own parents,
and moreover must borrow to make up the deficit,
causing the old and the young to roll into the gutters and ditches—
where is their being the parents of the people?
As for hereditary salaries,
Téng indeed practices this.
The *Shī* says:
‘May it rain upon our public field,
and then extend to our private ones.’
Only in the aid system is there a public field.
From this we can see that
although Zhōu used the share system, they also had the aid system.
Establish *xiáng*, *xù*, *xué*, and *xiào* to educate them.
*Xiáng* means to nourish;
*xiào* means to instruct;
*xù* means archery.
The Xià dynasty called them *xiào*;
the Yīn dynasty called them *xù*;
the Zhōu dynasty called them *xiáng*.
As for *xué*, all three dynasties used this term;
they were all for clarifying human relations.
When human relations are clarified by those above,
the common people will love one another below.
Should a true king arise,
he will surely come to take you as a model;
thus you will become the teacher of a true king.
"The *Shī* says:
‘Although Zhōu is an ancient state,
its mandate is newly made.’
This refers to King Wén.
If you vigorously practice this,
you will also make your state new!"
The Duke sent Bì Zhàn to ask about the well-field system.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Your ruler wishes to practice benevolent government,
and has selected and sent you.
You must exert yourself!
Benevolent government must begin with the defining of boundaries.
If the boundaries are not correct,
the division of land into well-fields will not be equal,
and the grain-revenues for salaries will not be fair.
Therefore, tyrannical rulers and corrupt officials are sure to neglect the defining of boundaries.
Once the boundaries are corrected,
the division of fields and the regulation of salaries
can be settled while sitting down.
"Now Téng is a narrow and small territory,
yet there will be gentlemen there,
and there will be countrymen there.
Without gentlemen, there is no one to govern the countrymen;
without countrymen, there is no one to support the gentlemen.
I propose that in the countryside,
a tax of one-ninth be levied under the aid system;
in the capital,
a tax of one-tenth be paid by the people themselves.
From the ministers downward, all must have sacrificial fields,
of fifty *mǔ*;
and extra supernumerary males should have twenty-five *mǔ*.
In matters of death or migration, people do not leave their home village.
Those of the same village and well-field
are friendly in their comings and goings,
help each other in keeping watch,
and support each other in sickness,
so that the common people live in harmony.
A square *lǐ* constitutes a well-field,
which contains nine hundred *mǔ*.
The center is the public field.
Eight families each have a private hundred *mǔ*,
and together they cultivate the public field.
Only when the public work is finished
do they dare to attend to their private affairs,
which is how the countrymen are distinguished.
This is the general outline;
as for polishing and refining it,
that rests with your ruler and you."
5.4 There was a man, Xǔ Xíng, who spoke on behalf of the teachings of Shénnóng.
He came from Chǔ to Téng,
and coming to the gate, he announced to Duke Wén, saying:
"A man from afar,
having heard that you practice benevolent government,
wishes to receive a dwelling place and become one of your subjects."
Wéngōng assigned him a place to dwell.
His disciples, numbering several dozen,
all wore coarse haircloth clothing,
and wove sandals and made mats to earn their living.
Chén Xiāng, a disciple of Chén Liáng, and his younger brother Xīn,
carrying their ploughshares on their backs, went from Sòng to Téng,
and said:
"We have heard that the ruler is practicing the government of the sages,
and thus he must be a sage himself.
We wish to become subjects of the sage."
Chén Xiāng saw Xǔ Xíng and was greatly pleased,
and completely abandoned his former learning to study under him.
Chén Xiāng went to see Mèngzǐ,
and reported the words of Xǔ Xíng, saying:
"The ruler of Téng is indeed a worthy ruler;
nevertheless,
he has not yet heard the true Way.
A worthy ruler tills the soil along with his people to feed himself,
and rules while preparing his own morning and evening meals.
Now, Téng has granaries and treasuries;
this means he oppresses the people to support himself.
How can he be considered worthy?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Does Master Xǔ indeed plant grain before he eats?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"Does Master Xǔ indeed weave cloth before he wears clothes?"
He replied:
"No;
Master Xǔ wears coarse haircloth."
"Does Master Xǔ wear a cap?"
He replied:
"He wears a cap."
Mèngzǐ asked:
"What kind of cap?"
He replied:
"A cap of plain silk."
Mèngzǐ asked:
"Does he weave it himself?"
He replied:
"No;
he exchanges grain for it."
Mèngzǐ asked:
"Why does Master Xǔ not weave it himself?"
He replied:
"It would interfere with his farming."
Mèngzǐ asked:
"Does Master Xǔ cook with iron pots and earthenware steamers,
and does he till with iron tools?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"Does he make them himself?"
He replied:
"No;
he exchanges grain for them."
"If exchanging grain for tools and utensils
does not cause hardship to the potters and blacksmiths,
and if the potters and blacksmiths exchanging their tools and utensils for grain
does not cause hardship to the farmers,
then why does Master Xǔ not set up as a potter and blacksmith,
obtaining everything he needs from within his own home and using it?
Why does he busily engage in exchange with all kinds of artisans?
Why is Master Xǔ not averse to such trouble?"
He replied:
"The work of the various artisans
indeed cannot be carried on along with farming."
"If that is so,
can governing the realm alone be carried on along with farming?
There is the work of great men,
and there is the work of lesser men.
Moreover, for the needs of a single individual,
the products of all kinds of artisans are required.
If everyone had to make everything themselves before using them,
it would lead the whole world to exhaustion.
Therefore it is said:
'Some labor with their minds,
some labor with their strength.
Those who labor with their minds govern others;
those who labor with their strength are governed by others.
Those who are governed by others support them;
those who govern others are supported by them.'
This is a universal principle throughout the world.
"In the time of Yáo,
the world was not yet at peace.
The great floodwaters overflowed,
inundating the whole world.
Vegetation grew thick and wild,
and wild beasts and birds multiplied.
The five grains did not ripen,
and beasts and birds pressed upon human beings.
The tracks of beasts and birds
crisscrossed Zhōngguó.
Yáo alone was deeply grieved by this,
so he raised up Shùn to bring order to it.
Shùn put Yì in charge of fire;
Yì set fire to the mountains and marshlands, burning them,
and the beasts and birds fled into hiding.
Yǔ dredged the nine rivers,
cleared the Jì and Tà rivers and channeled them into the sea,
opened up the Rǔ and Hàn rivers,
and directed the Huái and Sì rivers into the Jiāng.
Only after this was it possible for the people of Zhōngguó to cultivate the land and feed themselves.
During that time,
Yǔ spent eight years away from home;
thrice he passed his own door but did not enter.
Even if he had wished to farm,
would he have been able to?
"Hòujì taught the people agriculture,
sowing and cultivating the five grains.
When the five grains ripened, the people were nourished.
The way of human beings is such that:
if they are well fed, warmly clothed,
and dwell in comfort without education,
they will be close to beasts.
The Sage was grieved by this,
and appointed Qiè as the Sītú,
to teach them the human relationships:
that there should be affection between father and son,
righteousness between ruler and minister,
distinction between husband and wife,
order between old and young,
and trust between friends.
Fàngxūn said:
'Encourage them, lead them on,
rectify them, straighten them,
assist them, give them wings,
cause them to find themselves,
and then stimulate them with benefits.'
When the sages cared for the people in this way,
did they have leisure to farm?
"Yáo took it as his own worry that he might not find Shùn,
and Shùn took it as his own worry that he might not find Yǔ and Gāoyáo.
But to take it as one's worry that one's hundred mǔ of land is not well cultivated—
that is the part of a farmer.
To share one's wealth with others is called generosity;
to teach others what is good is called loyalty;
to find suitable people for the world is called benevolence.
Therefore, to give the empire to someone else is easy;
but to find suitable people for the empire is difficult.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'How great
was Yáo as a ruler!
Only Heaven is great,
and only Yáo modeled himself after it.
So vast was he, the people could find no words to describe him!
What a ruler was Shùn!
How sublime was he, possessing the empire yet remaining aloof from it!'
When Yáo and Shùn governed the empire,
did they indeed have no use for their minds?
They simply did not use them for farming.
"I have heard of using the culture of Xià to transform the barbarians,
but I have never heard of being transformed by the barbarians.
Chén Liáng
was a native of Chǔ,
who delighted in the Way of Zhōugōng and Zhòngní.
He traveled north to study in Zhōngguó,
and among the scholars of the north,
there was none who could surpass him.
He was what we call an outstanding man of talent.
You and your brother
served him for decades,
yet as soon as your master died, you turned your backs on him!
Formerly, when Kǒngzǐ died,
after the three years of mourning,
his disciples packed their bags to return home.
They went in and bowed to Zǐgòng,
and wept looking at each other,
until they lost their voices,
and then they returned home.
Zǐgòng returned,
built a hut near the tomb,
and lived there alone for another three years,
and only then did he return.
Later, Zǐxià, Zǐzhāng, and Zǐyóu,
because Yǒu Ruò resembled the Sage,
wished to serve him as they had served Kǒngzǐ,
and tried to force Céngzǐ to agree.
Céngzǐ said:
'It must not be done.
Washed by the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
and dried by the autumn sun,
his purity was so dazzling that nothing could be added to it.'
Now, here is this shrike-tongued barbarian of the south,
who speaks against the Way of the former kings.
You turn your back on your master and learn from him!
This indeed makes you different from Céngzǐ.
I have heard of birds leaving the dark valleys
and moving to tall trees,
but I have never heard of them leaving tall trees to enter dark valleys.
The 'Lǔ Sòng' says:
'He smote the Róng and Dí,
and punished Jīng and Shū.'
Since Zhōugōng even smote them,
while you are learning from them,
you are indeed making a bad change."
"If one follows the way of Xǔ Zǐ,
then there will be no two prices in the market,
and there will be no deceit in the state.
Even if a youth of five feet were sent to the market,
no one would cheat him.
If pieces of cloth and silk of the same length,
their prices would be the same;
if bundles of hemp, thread, silk, and floss of the same weight,
their prices would be the same;
if quantities of the five grains of the same amount,
their prices would be the same;
if shoes of the same size,
their prices would be the same."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Now, that things are unequal
is in the nature of things.
Some are twice or five times as valuable as others,
some ten or a hundred times,
some a thousand or ten thousand times.
If you align them and make them all equal,
this will throw the world into chaos.
If coarsely made shoes and finely made shoes are of the same price,
why would anyone make them?
To follow the way of Xǔ Zǐ
is to lead one another into deceit.
How can one govern a state in this way?"
5.5 Yí Zhī, a Mohist,
sought an interview with Mèngzǐ through Xú Bì.
Mèngzǐ said,
"I indeed wish to see him,
but at present I am still ill.
When I recover,
I will go and see him;
Yí Zǐ need not come!"
On another day, he again sought an interview with Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said,
"Now I can see him.
If I am not direct, the Way will not be made clear;
I will speak directly to him.
I have heard that Yí Zǐ is a Mohist.
Mohists, in conducting funerals,
take simplicity as their principle.
Yí Zǐ thinks to change the world in this way;
surely he must think that anything else is wrong and not to be valued.
Yet Yí Zǐ buried his parents handsomely;
this is serving his parents with what he holds in low esteem."
Xú Zǐ reported this to Yí Zǐ.
Yí Zǐ said,
"According to the way of the Confucians,
the ancients said,
'Act as if you were protecting a newborn baby.'
What does this saying mean?
I believe it means that love has no gradations,
though its application begins with one's parents."
Xú Zǐ reported this to Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said,
"Does Yí Zǐ truly believe
that a man loves his brother's son
just as he loves his neighbor's newborn baby?
There is a specific point to be taken from that saying:
if a baby is crawling and about to fall into a well,
it is not the baby's fault.
Furthermore, when Heaven gives life to things,
It makes them have one source,
whereas Yí Zǐ makes them have two sources.
In ancient times, there were those who did not bury their parents.
When their parents died,
they took them up and threw them into a ditch.
Passing by them on a later day,
they saw foxes and wildcats eating them,
and flies and gnats biting them.
Sweat broke out on their foreheads,
and they looked askance, unable to look at them directly.
That sweat
was not for others to see;
it was the feelings of their inner hearts showing on their faces.
So they went back, got baskets and shovels, and covered them.
If covering them
was indeed right,
then the covering of their parents by filial sons and benevolent men
must also have its proper basis."
Xú Zǐ reported this to Yí Zǐ.
Yí Zǐ looked dejected for a moment and said,
"He has enlightened me."
6.1 Chén Dài said,
"Not to go and see the feudal lords
seems like a small matter.
If you go and see them now,
at best you may cause them to become kings,
and at least you may cause them to become hegemons.
Moreover, the 'Record' says:
'To bend a foot to make a fathom straight'
is something that seems worth doing."
Mèngzǐ said,
"In the past, Duke Jǐng of Qí was hunting,
and summoned his gamekeeper with a banner.
The gamekeeper did not come,
and the Duke was about to kill him.
'A determined scholar does not forget that his end may be in a ditch;
a brave man does not forget that he may lose his head.'
What did Kǒngzǐ take from this?
He approved of his not going because it was not the proper summons.
If one goes without waiting for the proper summons,
what is that like?
Moreover, 'bending a foot to make a fathom straight'
is spoken in terms of profit.
If profit is the motive,
then if bending a fathom to make a foot straight were profitable,
would that also be acceptable?
Formerly, Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ
made Wáng Liáng drive for his favorite, Xī.
Throughout the day they did not catch a single beast.
The favorite, Xī, returned and reported,
'He is the worst driver in the world.'
Someone told this to Wáng Liáng.
Wáng Liáng said,
'Please let me try again.'
Only after much urging did the favorite agree,
and in one morning they caught ten beasts.
The favorite, Xī, returned and reported,
'He is the best driver in the world.'
Jiǎn Zǐ said,
'I will make him drive for you regularly.'
He spoke to Wáng Liáng.
Wáng Liáng refused,
saying,
'When I drove for him according to the rules
and managed my driving,
all day they did not catch one;
but when I used deceitful ways to intercept the game,
in one morning they caught ten.
The Book of Odes says:
"They do not fail in their driving,
and the arrows they let go pierce the target."
I am not accustomed to driving for a petty man.
Please permit me to decline.'
If even a driver is ashamed to associate with an unprincipled archer,
and would not associate with him even to get game
piled up like hills,
and would not do so;
if I bend my principles to follow those lords,
why should I do so?
Moreover, you are mistaken:
one who bends himself
has never been able to make others straight."
6.2 Jǐng Chūn said,
"Are Gōngsūn Yǎn and Zhāng Yí
not truly great men?
Once they are angry, the feudal lords are afraid;
when they live quietly, the fires of war under heaven are extinguished."
Mèngzǐ said,
"How can they be considered great men?
Have you not studied the rites?
At a young man's capping ceremony,
his father instructs him.
At a young woman's marriage,
her mother instructs her.
Escorting her to the door,
she cautions her, saying:
'Go to your home,
you must be respectful, you must be cautious,
and never disobey your husband!'
To make compliance one's correct path
is the way of a concubine or wife.
To dwell in the wide house of the world,
to stand in the correct position of the world,
and to walk in the great path of the world;
when finding favor, to practice it along with the people;
when not finding favor,
to practice one's principles alone.
Riches and honors cannot corrupt him,
poverty and humble condition cannot swerve him,
power and force cannot bend him—
this is what is called a great man."
6.3 Zhōu Xiāo asked, saying,
"Did the gentlemen of old take office?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"They did.
The tradition says:
'If Kǒngzǐ were three months without a ruler,
he would look anxious and distracted.
When he left the boundaries of a state, he would be sure to carry his introductory gifts.'
Gōngmíng Yí said:
'The ancients,
if they were three months without a ruler,
would send condolences.'"
"To send condolences if one is three months without a ruler,
is that not being a bit too urgent?"
He replied,
"A scholar losing his office
is like a feudal lord losing his state."
The *Lǐ* says:
"The feudal lords plough the helper-plots
to supply the sacrificial grain;
the rulers' wives raise silkworms and unwind the cocoons,
to make the ritual garments.
If the sacrificial animals are not perfect,
the sacrificial grain is not clean,
or the ritual garments are not complete,
they do not dare to perform the sacrifice.
If an officer has no land,
then he also does not perform the sacrifice."
If the sacrificial animals, vessels, and garments are not complete,
and they do not dare to perform the sacrifice,
then they would not dare to hold banquets.
Is this not indeed cause for condolence?"
"When leaving the borders of his state, an officer must carry his introductory gift.
Why is this?"
He said:
"An officer's taking office
is like a farmer's ploughing.
Would a farmer, because he crosses the borders of his state,
leave behind his plough and plowshare?"
The other said:
"The State of *Jìn* is also a state where men take office,
yet I have never heard of office-seeking being so urgent.
If office-seeking is so urgent,
why does a gentleman find it difficult to take office?
Why is this?"
He said:
"When a boy is born, his parents wish for him to have a wife;
when a girl is born, they wish for her to have a husband.
This heart of parents
is shared by all people.
But if, without waiting for the parents' command
and the matchmaker's word,
they bore holes in the walls to peep at each other,
or climb over the wall to follow each other,
then both their parents and countrymen will despise them.
The men of antiquity never failed to wish to hold office,
but they also hated not doing so by the proper *dào*.
Going to seek office without following the proper *dào*
is of the same class as boring holes in walls."
6.4 *Péng Gēng* asked, saying:
"With dozens of carriages following behind,
and hundreds of attendants in your train,
to be supported by the feudal lords as you travel from one to another—
is this not too extravagant?"
*Mèngzǐ* said:
"If it is not according to the *dào*,
then one cannot accept even a single basket of rice from another.
If it is according to the *dào*,
then *Shùn* accepting the world from *Yáo*
was not considered extravagant.
Do you consider that extravagant?"
*Péng Gēng* said:
"No;
but for an officer to be supported without performing service
is not proper."
*Mèngzǐ* said:
"If you do not exchange the products of your labors and trade services,
so as to supplement insufficiency with surplus,
then the farmer will have surplus grain,
and the woman will have surplus cloth.
If you do exchange them,
then carpenters, carriage-makers, wheelwrights, and coach-builders can all obtain food from you.
Now, here is a man
who is filial at home,
respectful to his elders abroad,
who preserves the *dào* of the former kings
to hand it down to future students,
yet he cannot obtain food from you.
Why do you honor carpenters, carriage-makers, wheelwrights, and coach-builders,
while looking down upon those who practice benevolence and righteousness?"
*Péng Gēng* said:
"The carpenters, carriage-makers, wheelwrights, and coach-builders
have the intention of seeking a livelihood.
When a gentleman practices the *dào*,
is his intention also to seek a livelihood?"
*Mèngzǐ* said:
"Why do you focus on his intention?
If he performs service for you,
he deserves to be fed, and so you feed him.
Moreover, do you feed him for his intention,
or do you feed him for his service?"
*Péng Gēng* said:
"I feed him for his intention."
*Mèngzǐ* said:
"Suppose there is a man here
who breaks tiles and scratches the plaster on walls,
but his intention is to seek a livelihood;
would you feed him?"
*Péng Gēng* said:
"No."
*Mèngzǐ* said:
"In that case, you do not feed him for his intention,
but for his service."
6.5 *Wàn Zhāng* asked, saying:
"*Sòng*
is a small state.
If it now prepares to practice kingly governance,
and *Qí* and *Chǔ* dislike this and attack it,
what should be done?"
*Mèngzǐ* said:
"When *Tāng* dwelt in *Bó*,
he was neighbor to *Gě*.
The Earl of *Gě* was dissolute and did not perform sacrifices.
*Tāng* sent someone to ask him, saying,
'Why do you not perform sacrifices?'
He replied,
'I have nothing with which to supply the sacrificial animals.'
*Tāng* sent him cattle and sheep.
The Earl of *Gě* ate them,
and still did not perform sacrifices.
*Tāng* sent someone to ask him again, saying,
'Why do you not perform sacrifices?'
He replied,
'I have nothing with which to supply the sacrificial grain.'
*Tāng* then sent the people of *Bó* to go and plough for them,
and the old and weak carried food to feed them.
The Earl of *Gě* led his people
to intercept those who had wine, food, millet, and rice,
and plundered them,
and those who would not surrender them
they killed.
There was a young boy carrying millet and meat to the workers;
they killed him and plundered him.
The *Shū* says:
'The Earl of *Gě* treated those who carried food as enemies.'
This refers to this incident.
Because they killed this boy, *Tāng* marched to punish them,
and all within the four seas said,
'It is not that he wishes to enrich himself with the world;
he is avenging ordinary men and women.'
'When *Tāng* began his punitive expeditions,
he started with *Gě*.'
After eleven expeditions, he had no enemy in the world.
When he marched to the east,
the western tribes complained;
when he marched to the south,
the northern tribes complained,
saying,
'Why does he leave us for last?'
The people looked for him
as they would look for rain in a great drought.
Those going to market did not stop;
those weeding the fields made no change.
He executed their rulers
and consoled their people,
like the falling of timely rain.
The people were greatly pleased.
The *Shū* says:
'We await our sovereign;
when our sovereign comes, there will be no more punishment!'
'There were some who would not submit;
he marched to the east,
and pacified its men and women.
They filled their baskets with dark and yellow silks,
saying, "We welcome our King of *Zhōu* to receive the blessing,"
and declared their submission to the great city of *Zhōu*.'
Their gentlemen filled baskets with dark and yellow silks
to welcome his gentlemen,
and their common people filled baskets with food and vessels with drink
to welcome his common people.
They rescued the people from fire and water,
taking away only their oppressors.
The *Tàishì* says:
'Our martial power is displayed,
we invade his borders,
we take away the oppressor,
and execution is widely carried out;
this is even more glorious than *Tāng*.'
It is simply that they do not practice kingly governance.
If they were to practice kingly governance,
all within the four seas would lift up their heads
and look towards them,
wishing to have their ruler as their sovereign.
Though *Qí* and *Chǔ* are large,
what would there be to fear from them?"
6.6 *Mèngzǐ* said to *Dài Bùshèng*:
"Do you wish your king to be good?
I will tell you plainly.
Suppose there is an officer of *Chǔ* here,
who wishes his son to learn the language of *Qí*.
Would he employ a man of *Qí* to tutor him,
or would he employ a man of *Chǔ* to tutor him?"
*Dài Bùshèng* said:
"He would employ a man of *Qí* to tutor him."
*Mèngzǐ* said:
"If there is one man of *Qí* tutoring him,
but many men of *Chǔ* are clamoring around him,
even if you beat him daily to make him speak *Qí*,
you will not succeed.
But if you take him and place him in the busy district between *Zhuāng* and *Yuè* for several years,
even if you beat him daily to make him speak *Chǔ*,
you will not succeed either.
You said of Xuē Jūzhōu
that he is a virtuous scholar,
and so you caused him to reside at the King's place.
If among those at the King's place,
old and young, low and high, were all Xuē Jūzhōus,
with whom would the King do what is not good?
But if among those at the King's place,
old and young, low and high, are all unlike Xuē Jūzhōu,
with whom will the King do what is good?
What can a single Xuē Jūzhōu
do on his own with the King of Sòng?"
6.7 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"What is the principle behind not going to see the feudal lords
Mèngzǐ said,
"In ancient times, if one was not a minister, one did not go to see them.
Duàngān Mù leaped over a wall to avoid him,
and Xiè Liǔ shut his door and would not admit him.
These actions were extreme.
When pressed,
then it is acceptable to meet.
Yáng Huò wished to see Kǒngzǐ,
but disliked violating propriety.
When a great officer makes a gift to a scholar,
if the scholar cannot receive it at his home,
he must go and bow at the donor's gate.
Yáng Huò watched for a time when Kǒngzǐ was away
and sent him a roasted piglet.
Kǒngzǐ also watched for a time when Yáng Huò was away
and went to pay his respects.
At that time,
since Yáng Huò had taken the initiative,
how could Kǒngzǐ have avoided seeing him?
Zēngzǐ said,
'To shrug one's shoulders and flatter with a sycophantic smile
is more wearisome than working in the summer fields.'
Zǐlù said,
'To talk with those with whom one does not agree,
and to look at their faces
blushing with shame—
this is something that I, Yóu, do not understand.
Looking at it from this perspective,
what the gentleman cultivates
can indeed be known.'"
6.8 Dài Yíngzhī said,
"To institute a tax of one-tenth,
and to abolish the customs and marketplace duties—
we cannot do this immediately.
I propose to reduce them slightly,
wait until next year,
and then completely abolish them.
What do you think of this?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Suppose there is a man who steals his neighbor's chickens every day.
Someone tells him,
'This is not the way of a gentleman.'
He replies,
'I propose to reduce it:
I will steal only one chicken a month,
wait until next year,
and then stop.'
If one knows that it is unrighteous,
one should stop it immediately.
Why wait until next year?"
6.9 Gōngdūzǐ said,
"People outside all say that you, Master, are fond of disputation.
May I venture to ask why?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Am I fond of disputation?
I cannot do otherwise.
The world has existed for a long time,
now in order, now in chaos.
In the time of Yáo,
the waters flowed backward,
overflowing throughout the Middle Kingdom.
Snakes and dragons inhabited the land,
and the people had no settled place to live.
Those in the lowlands made nests on trees,
and those in the highlands dug caves.
The *Book of Documents* says,
'The overflowing waters warned us.'
'Overflowing waters' refers to the great flood.
Yáo employed Yǔ to regulate it.
Yǔ dug channels through the earth and directed the waters into the sea,
and drove the snakes and dragons into the marshes.
The waters flowed within their beds;
these are the Jiāng, the Huái, the Hé, and the Hàn.
Once the dangers and obstacles were removed,
the wild beasts and birds that harmed people disappeared,
and only then could people live on the flat land.
After Yáo and Shùn passed away,
the way of the sages declined.
Tyrannical rulers arose one after another,
destroying homes to make ponds and pools,
so that the people had no place to rest in peace.
They abandoned cultivated fields to make gardens and parks,
leaving the people unable to obtain food and clothing.
Heterodox doctrines and violent deeds arose again.
Gardens, parks, ponds, pools, marshes, and wetlands became numerous,
and wild beasts arrived.
By the time of Zhòu,
the world was again in great chaos.
Zhōugōng assisted King Wǔ
in executing Zhòu and attacking Yǎn.
For three years he campaigned against its ruler,
drove Fēilián to the edge of the sea and put him to death.
He extinguished fifty states,
and drove the tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, and elephants far away.
The whole world was greatly pleased.
The *Book of Documents* says,
'How illustrious were the plans of King Wén!
How grandly did King Wǔ carry on his achievements!
They assist and guide us, their descendants,
that we may all walk in the correct path without deficiency.'
"As generations declined and the Way weakened,
heterodox doctrines and violent deeds arose again.
There were ministers who murdered their rulers,
and sons who murdered their fathers.
Kǒngzǐ was afraid,
and so he composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* deals with the affairs of the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ said,
'Those who understand me
will do so only through the *Spring and Autumn Annals*!
Those who condemn me
will do so only through the *Spring and Autumn Annals*!'
Sage-kings do not arise,
the feudal lords are dissolute,
scholars without office express unwarranted views,
and the words of Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí fill the world.
The doctrines of the world,
if they do not incline toward Yáng, incline toward Mò.
Mr. Yáng advocates 'everyone for himself,'
which is to have no ruler.
Mr. Mò advocates 'impartial love,'
which is to have no father.
To have no father and no ruler
is to be like beasts.
Gōngmíng Yí said,
'In the kitchens, there is fat meat;
in the stables, there are fat horses.
But the people have the look of hunger,
and in the wilds, there are bodies of those starved to death.
This is leading beasts to devour men.'
If the ways of Yáng and Mò are not stopped,
and the way of Kǒngzǐ is not made clear,
then these heterodox doctrines will deceive the people,
blocking the path of benevolence and righteousness.
When benevolence and righteousness are blocked,
it leads beasts to devour men,
and men will eventually devour one another.
I am alarmed by this,
and so I defend the way of the former sages,
oppose Yáng and Mò, banish depraved talk,
so that heterodox doctrines cannot arise.
If they arise in their minds,
they will harm their affairs;
if they arise in their affairs,
they will harm their governance.
Should a sage arise again,
he would not alter my words.
"In former times, Yǔ controlled the great flood
and the world became peaceful.
Zhōugōng subjugated the eastern and northern barbarians,
drove away wild beasts,
and the common people found rest.
Kǒngzǐ completed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
and rebellious ministers and villainous sons were struck with fear.
The *Book of Odes* says,
'He smote the Róng and the Dí;
he punished Jīng and Shū;
so that none dared to oppose us.'
Those who have no father and no ruler
are those whom Zhōugōng would have smitten.
I also wish to rectify the hearts of men,
put an end to heterodox doctrines,
oppose biased conduct,
and banish depraved talk,
in order to carry on the work of the three sages.
Am I fond of disputation?
I cannot do otherwise.
Those who can speak to oppose Yáng and Mò
are disciples of the sages."
6.10 Kuāng Zhāng said,
"Is Chén Zhòngzǐ not truly an incorruptible scholar?
While living in Wūlíng,
he went without food for three days,
until his ears had no hearing
and his eyes had no sight.
Beside a well there was a plum tree,
and the worms had eaten more than half of its fruit.
He crawled to it, wishing to eat it.
He swallowed three mouthfuls,
and only then did his hearing and sight return."
Mèngzǐ said,
"Among the scholars of the State of Qí,
I must look upon Zhòngzǐ as the thumb.
Although this is so,
how can Zhòngzǐ be considered incorruptible?
To carry out Zhòngzǐ's principles to their full extent,
one would have to become an earthworm before one could do so.
Now, an earthworm eats dry earth above
and drinks from the yellow springs below.
Was the house in which Zhòngzǐ lives
built by Bóyí?
Or was it built by the robber Zhí?
Was the millet which he eats
planted by Bóyí?
Or was it planted by the robber Zhí?
These are things that cannot be known."
He said,
"What harm is there in that?
He himself weaves sandals, and his wife spins hemp,
in order to exchange them."
Mèngzǐ said,
"Zhòngzǐ
belongs to an ancient noble family of Qí;
his elder brother Dài
received a salary of ten thousand zhōng;
yet he considered his brother's salary as unrighteous salary
and would not eat of it;
he considered his brother's house as an unrighteous house
and would not dwell in it;
avoiding his brother and leaving his mother,
he went to live in Wūlíng.
On a subsequent day, he returned home,
and someone made a present of a live goose to his brother,
at which he frowned and said,
'What use is there for this cackling thing?'
On another day, his mother killed the goose
and gave him some of it to eat.
His brother came in from outside
and said,
'That is the meat of the cackling thing.'
Upon this, he went out and vomited it.
With respect to his mother, he would not eat,
but with respect to his wife, he eats;
with respect to his brother's house, he would not dwell in it,
but with respect to Wūlíng, he dwells there.
Can this still be considered as being able
to fully carry out his principles?
A person like Zhòngzǐ
must become an earthworm before he can fully carry out his principles."
7.1 Mèngzǐ said,
"The clear vision of Lí Lóu
and the skill of Gōngshū Zǐ,
without the compass and square,
cannot form squares and circles;
the acute hearing of Shī Kuàng,
without the six pitch-pipes,
cannot correctly tune the five notes;
the Way of Yáo and Shùn,
without benevolent government,
cannot bring peace and order to the world.
Now there may be those who have a benevolent heart and a reputation for benevolence,
yet the people do not receive their benefits,
and they cannot serve as a model for future generations,
because they do not practice the Way of the ancient kings.
Therefore it is said,
'Virtue alone is not sufficient to govern,
laws alone cannot carry themselves into practice.'
The Book of Odes says:
'Without error, without forgetfulness,
following the ancient statutes.'
One who follows the laws of the ancient kings and yet errs—
there has never been such a person.
When the sages had exhausted their power of vision,
they followed it up with the compass, square, level, and plumb-line,
to make things square, round, level, and straight,
which could then be used inexhaustibly;
when they had exhausted their power of hearing,
they followed it up with the six pitch-pipes to correct the five notes,
which could then be used inexhaustibly;
when they had exhausted their power of mind,
they followed it up with a government that cannot bear to see the sufferings of others,
and benevolence covered the whole world.
Therefore it is said,
'To build high, one must base it on hills and mounds;
to dig deep, one must base it on rivers and marshes.'
In conducting government,
if one does not base it on the Way of the ancient kings,
can he be called wise?
Therefore, only the benevolent should be in high positions.
If an unbenevolent man is in a high position,
he will only disseminate his wickedness among the people.
When those above have no principles of righteousness to measure by,
and those below have no laws to maintain;
when the court does not believe in righteousness,
and the craftsmen do not trust the measures;
when superiors violate righteousness,
and the common people violate the penal laws;
for such a state to survive is
sheer luck.
Therefore it is said,
'That the inner and outer walls are not complete,
and the weapons and armor are not numerous,
is not the disaster of a state;
that the fields are not reclaimed,
and goods and wealth are not accumulated,
is not the harm of a state.'
But when those above lack propriety,
and those below lack education,
rebellious people will arise,
and the ruin of the state is close at hand.
The Book of Odes says:
'When Heaven is about to overthrow the state,
do not be so talkative and complacent.'
'Talkative and complacent'
is the same as being garrulous and lazy.
To serve one's ruler without righteousness,
to advance and retreat without propriety,
and to speak to the disparagement of the Way of the ancient kings,
is just like being garrulous and lazy.
Therefore it is said,
'To urge difficult duties on one's ruler is called respect;
to set forth good principles and bar the way against wickedness is called reverence;
to say "My ruler is not capable of it" is called being a thief to him.'
7.2 Mèngzǐ said,
"The compass and square
are the perfection of squares and circles.
The sage
is the perfection of human relations.
He who wishes to be a ruler
must fully discharge the duties of a ruler;
he who wishes to be a minister
must fully discharge the duties of a minister.
Both of them have only to model themselves on Yáo and Shùn
and nothing more.
He who does not serve his ruler as Shùn served Yáo
does not respect his ruler;
he who does not govern the people as Yáo governed them
is a thief to his people.
Kǒngzǐ said,
'There are but two paths:
that of benevolence and that of its opposite.'
If a ruler oppresses his people to the extreme,
he himself will be assassinated and his state will perish;
if he does not do so to the extreme,
his person will still be in danger and his state will be weakened.
He will be posthumously named
'Yōu' or 'Lì'.
Even though he has filial sons and affectionate grandsons,
for a hundred generations they will not be able to alter it.
The Book of Odes says:
'The warning for Yīn is not far off;
it is in the age of the sovereign of Xià.'
This is what is meant."
7.3 Mèngzǐ said,
"The Three Dynasties gained the world through benevolence,
and lost it through the lack of benevolence.
It is the same with the rise, fall, preservation, and ruin of states.
If the Emperor is not benevolent,
he cannot preserve the four seas;
if the feudal lords are not benevolent,
they cannot preserve their altars of state;
if the ministers and great officers are not benevolent,
they cannot preserve their ancestral temples;
if the scholars and common people are not benevolent,
they cannot preserve their four limbs.
Now to hate death and ruin,
and yet to delight in what is not benevolent,
is like hating to be drunk,
and yet forcing oneself to drink wine."
7.4 Mèngzǐ said,
"If you love others and they do not respond with affection,
examine your own benevolence;
if you govern others and they are not governed,
examine your own wisdom;
if you treat others with propriety and they do not return it,
examine your own reverence.
Whenever you do not succeed in what you do,
turn inward and seek the cause in yourself.
When one's own person is correct,
the whole world will turn to him.
The Book of Odes says:
'Forever strive to be in harmony with Heaven's mandate,
and seek for yourself much happiness.'"
7.5 Mèngzǐ said,
"People have a common saying; they all say:
'The empire, the state, the family.'
The foundation of the empire lies in the state;
the foundation of the state lies in the family;
the foundation of the family lies in the individual."
7.6 Mèngzǐ said,
"Governing is not difficult;
it lies in not offending the great families.
What the great families admire,
the whole state will admire;
what the whole state admires,
the whole world will admire.
Therefore, the influence of virtue will flow copiously, overflowing the four seas."
7.7 Mencius said,
"When the world possesses the Way,
those of lesser virtue serve those of greater virtue,
and those of lesser worth serve those of greater worth.
When the world is without the Way,
the small serve the large,
and the weak serve the strong.
These two conditions
are determined by Heaven.
Those who accord with Heaven survive;
those who rebel against Heaven perish.
Duke Jǐng of Qí said,
'Since I can neither issue commands
nor receive orders,
this is to cut myself off from others.'
With tears flowing, he gave his daughter in marriage to Wú.
Nowadays, small states emulate large states,
yet they are ashamed to receive orders from them.
This is like a disciple being ashamed to receive instruction from his master.
If they are ashamed of this,
there is nothing better than to emulate King Wén.
If they emulate King Wén,
a large state in five years,
and a small state in seven years,
will surely govern the world.
The *Book of Odes* says,
'The descendants of Shāng,
their numbers were more than hundreds of thousands.
But when the Lord on High issued His decree,
they became submissive to Zhōu.
They became submissive to Zhōu;
the mandate of Heaven is not constant.
The officers of Yīn, handsome and quick,
poured libations in the capital.'
Confucius said,
'Benevolence cannot be opposed by mere numbers. If
the ruler of a state loves benevolence,
he will have no enemy in the world.'
Now, to wish to have no enemy in the world
while not practicing benevolence
is like holding something hot without using water to cool it.
The *Book of Odes* says,
'Who can hold something hot
without wetting his hands?'"
7.8 Mencius said,
"Those who are not benevolent,
can they be reasoned with?
They feel secure in their danger and profit from their disasters,
taking pleasure in that which leads to their ruin.
If those who are not benevolent could be reasoned
with,
then how could there be ruined states and destroyed families?
There was a child singing:
'When the water of the Cānglàng is clear,
it can be used to wash my hat-strings;
when the water of the Cānglàng is muddy,
it can be used to wash my feet.'
Confucius said,
'Listen to this, my disciples!
When clear, it washes the hat-strings;
when muddy, it washes the feet.
The water brings this on itself.'
Indeed, a person must first demean himself,
and only then do others demean him.
A family must first destroy itself,
and only then do others destroy it.
A state must first strike itself,
and only then do others strike it.
The *Tàijiǎ* says,
'Calamities sent by Heaven
may still be avoided;
but calamities brought on by oneself
cannot be survived.'
This is what is meant."
7.9 Mencius said,
"The reason Jié and Zhòu lost the world
was because they lost their people;
and losing their people
meant losing their hearts.
There is a way to gain the world:
gain their people, and the world is gained.
There is a way to gain their people:
gain their hearts, and the people are gained.
There is a way to gain their hearts:
what they desire,
gather and provide for them;
what they dislike,
do not impose on them. It is simply that.
"The people turning to benevolence
is like water flowing downward,
or wild beasts running to the wilderness.
Thus, what drives the fish into the deep pool
is the otter;
what drives the birds into the thicket
is the hawk;
what drove the people to Tāng and Wǔ
were Jié and Zhòu.
Today, if there were a ruler in the world who loved benevolence,
all the other lords would drive the people to him.
Even if he wished not to rule as king, he could not avoid it.
Those who now wish to rule as king
are like someone who has been sick for seven years
seeking three-year-old mugwort.
If they have not accumulated it beforehand,
they will never obtain it in their whole life.
If they do not set their minds on benevolence,
they will suffer anxiety and disgrace all their lives,
ending in ruin and death.
The *Book of Odes* says,
'How can they do good?
They only bring ruin upon each other and drown together.'
This is what is meant."
7.10 Mencius said,
"Those who do violence to themselves
cannot be spoken with;
those who abandon themselves
cannot be acted with.
To speak in contradiction to ritual propriety and righteousness
is what is meant by doing violence to oneself.
To say 'I cannot dwell in benevolence and follow righteousness'
is what is meant by abandoning oneself.
Benevolence
is the peaceful dwelling of human beings;
righteousness
is the proper path of human beings.
To leave the peaceful dwelling empty and not reside there,
and to abandon the proper path and not follow it—
how lamentable!"
7.11 Mencius said,
"The Way lies near,
yet people seek it afar;
duties lie in what is easy,
yet people seek them in what is difficult.
If everyone would love their parents and respect their elders,
the world would be at peace."
7.12 Mencius said,
"For one who occupies an inferior position,
if he does not obtain the confidence of his superiors,
he cannot hope to govern the people.
There is a way to obtain the confidence of superiors:
if one is not trusted by his friends,
he will not obtain the confidence of his superiors.
There is a way to be trusted by friends:
if one, in serving his parents, does not please them,
he will not be trusted by his friends.
There is a way to please parents:
if, on examining himself, he is not sincere,
he will not please his parents.
There is a way to make oneself sincere:
if one does not understand what is good,
he cannot make himself sincere.
Therefore, sincerity
is the Way of Heaven;
to strive for sincerity
is the way of human beings.
There has never been one who possessed utmost sincerity and yet failed to move others;
it has never happened.
If one lacks sincerity,
they will never be able to move anyone."
7.13 Mencius said,
"Bóyí avoided Zhòu
and lived on the coast of the Northern Sea.
When he heard that King Wén had arisen, he stood up
and said,
'Why not return to him?
I have heard that the Chief of the West takes good care of the aged.'
Tàigōng avoided Zhòu
and lived on the coast of the Eastern Sea.
When he heard that King Wén had arisen, he stood up
and said,
'Why not return to him?
I have heard that the Chief of the West takes good care of the aged.'
These two old men
were the greatest elders in the world, and they turned to him.
This was like the fathers of the world turning to him.
When the fathers of the world turn to him,
where else would their sons go?
If any of the feudal lords were to practice the governance of King Wén,
within seven years,
they would surely govern the world."
7.14 Mencius said,
"When Qiú
served as steward to the Jì family,
he was unable to improve their virtue,
yet he doubled the taxes in grain compared to former days.
Confucius said,
'Qiú
is no disciple of mine.
You, my disciples, may beat the drum and assail him.'
From this we can see:
when a ruler does not practice benevolent governance,
to enrich him
is to be rejected by Confucius.
How much more so, then, to wage war on his behalf?
To fight for territory,
killing people until the fields are filled with corpses;
to fight for a city,
killing people until the city is filled with corpses—
this is what is called leading the land to devour human flesh.
Death is not sufficient punishment for such crimes."
Therefore, those who are skilled in war should suffer the highest punishment;
those who unite the feudal lords in alliances come next;
those who reclaim wild lands
and impose tax burdens on the land come next after them.”
7.15 Mèngzǐ said:
“Of all that is within a person,
nothing is better than the pupil of the eye.
The pupil cannot hide a person's evil.
If the heart within is upright,
then the pupil is bright and clear;
if the heart within is not upright,
then the pupil is dim and cloudy.
Listen to their words,
look at their pupils—
how can a person hide who they are?”
7.16 Mèngzǐ said:
“Those who are respectful do not insult others,
and those who are frugal do not rob others.
A ruler who insults and robs others,
fearing only that people will not submit to him,
how can he be considered respectful and frugal?
How can respectfulness and frugality be made of mere tones of voice and smiling faces?”
7.17 Chúnyú Kūn said:
“That men and women should not touch hands when giving or receiving things—
is this the rule of propriety?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“It is the rule of propriety.”
The other said:
“If one's sister-in-law is drowning, should one rescue her with one's hand?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“If one's sister-in-law is drowning and one does not rescue her,
that is to be a wolf.
That men and women should not touch hands when giving or receiving things is
the rule of propriety;
to rescue a drowning sister-in-law with one's hand is
a matter of expediency.”
The other said:
“Now the whole world is drowning;
that you, Master, do not rescue it—
why is this?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“When the world is drowning,
one rescues it with the Way;
when a sister-in-law is drowning,
one rescues her with the hand.
Do you wish me to rescue the world with my hand?”
7.18 Gōngsūn Chǒu said:
“Why does a gentleman not teach his own son,
why is this?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“The circumstances make it impracticable.
He who teaches must do so with what is correct;
when correct behavior is not followed,
he follows it with anger.
When he follows it with anger,
it backfires and causes estrangement.
The son says, ‘My father teaches me with what is correct,
yet he himself does not proceed from what is correct.’
Thus, father and son alienate each other.
When father and son alienate each other, it is bad.
In ancient times, people exchanged sons and taught them;
between father and son, there was no demanding of goodness.
To demand goodness leads to estrangement,
and there is no greater misfortune than estrangement.”
7.19 Mèngzǐ said:
“Of services, which is the greatest?
Serving one's parents is the greatest.
Of preservations, which is the greatest?
Preserving oneself is the greatest.
Not losing one's integrity
and being able to serve one's parents—
I have heard of such cases.
Losing one's integrity and yet being able to serve one's parents—
I have never heard of such a thing.
What is not a service?
Serving one's parents
is the root of all service.
What is not a preservation?
Preserving oneself
is the root of all preservation.
When Zēngzǐ supported Zēng Xī,
he always had wine and meat for him.
When about to clear the table,
he would ask to whom the leftovers should be given.
If asked if there was any left,
he would always say, ‘There is.’
After Zēng Xī died,
Zēng Yuán supported Zēngzǐ,
and also always had wine and meat;
but when about to clear the table,
he did not ask to whom the leftovers should be given.
If asked if there was any left,
he would say,
‘There is none,’
meaning to serve them again later.
This is what is called merely nourishing the mouth and body.
As for Zēngzǐ,
he may be said to have nourished his parent's will.
To serve one's parents as Zēngzǐ did—
that is the proper way.”
7.20 Mèngzǐ said:
“The men in office are not worth censuring,
nor is the administration worth finding fault with.
Only a great person can rectify what is wrong in the ruler's heart.
If the ruler is benevolent, everyone is benevolent.
If the ruler is righteous, everyone is righteous.
If the ruler is upright, everyone is upright.
Once the ruler is rectified, the state is settled.”
7.21 Mèngzǐ said:
“There are cases of unexpected praise,
and there are cases of blame where perfection was sought.”
7.22 Mèngzǐ said:
“People speak lightly of things
simply because they have not been held responsible for their words.”
7.23 Mèngzǐ said:
“The trouble with people
is that they love to be teachers of others.”
7.24 Yuèzhèngzǐ followed Zǐ'áo to the state of Qí.
Yuèzhèngzǐ came to see Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
“So, you have also come to see me?”
He said:
“Sir, why do you speak in this way?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“How many days have you been here?”
He said:
“Since yesterday.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“Since yesterday?
Then, that I should speak in this way—
is it not quite reasonable?”
He said:
“My lodging was not yet settled.”
Mèngzǐ said: “Have you heard that
only after one's lodging is settled
should one seek to visit an elder?”
He said:
“Kè is guilty.”
7.25 Mèngzǐ said to Yuèzhèngzǐ:
“Your following Zǐ'áo here
was merely for the sake of eating and drinking.
I did not expect that you, who study the ways of the ancients,
would do so for the sake of eating and drinking.”
7.26 Mèngzǐ said:
“There are three things which are unfilial,
and to have no posterity is the greatest of them.
Shùn married without informing his parents,
lest he should have no posterity;
gentlemen, therefore, consider that it was just as if he had informed them.”
7.27 Mèngzǐ said:
“The reality of benevolence
is the service of one's parents.
The reality of righteousness
is obedience to one's elder brothers.
The reality of wisdom
is to understand these two things and not depart from them.
The reality of propriety
is the ordering and adorning of these two things.
The reality of music
is the rejoicing in these two things.
When they are rejoiced in, they grow.
Once they grow, how can they be stopped?
When they cannot be stopped,
then, without one realizing it, the feet begin to dance
and the hands to move.”
7.28 Mèngzǐ said:
“When the whole world was greatly pleased
and turning to him,
to look upon the world being pleased and turning to him
as if it were straw—
only Shùn was capable of this.
If one does not obtain the favor of one's parents,
one cannot be considered a human being.
If one is not obedient to one's parents,
one cannot be considered a son.
Shùn exhausted the way of serving his parents,
and his father Gǔsǒu was brought to find pleasure in him.
When Gǔsǒu was brought to find pleasure,
the whole world was transformed.
When Gǔsǒu was brought to find pleasure,
the relations between fathers and sons throughout the world were settled.
This is what is called great filial piety.”
8.1 Mèngzǐ said:
“Shùn was born in Zhūféng,
moved to Fùxià,
and died in Míngtiáo;
he was a man of the Eastern Yi.
Wénwáng was born in Qízhōu,
and died in Bìyǐng;
he was a man of the Western Yi.
The distance between their birthplaces
was more than a thousand lǐ;
the time between their lives
was more than a thousand years.
Yet, when they realized their ambitions and acted in the Middle Kingdom,
their actions matched like the two halves of a tally.
The former sage and the later sage
had the same standard.”
8.2 When Zǐchǎn governed the state of Zhèng,
he used his personal carriage to ferry people across the Zhēn and Wěi rivers.
Mèngzǐ said:
“He was kind, but did not understand how to govern.
In the eleventh month of the year, if footbridges are completed;
and in the twelfth month, carriage bridges are completed,
the people will not suffer from wading across.
If a gentleman manages his government in an orderly way,
he may even have the streets cleared when he travels,
so how could he ferry every single person across?
Therefore, if a ruler
tries to please every individual person,
the days will not be enough.”
8.3 Mèngzǐ said to King Xuān of Qí:
“If a ruler regards his ministers as his own hands and feet,
then the ministers will regard the ruler as their own heart and mind;
if the ruler regards his ministers as dogs and horses,
then the ministers will regard the ruler as a common citizen;
if the ruler regards his ministers as dirt and weeds,
then the ministers will regard the ruler as a bandit and enemy.”
The King said:
“According to ritual,
mourning is worn for a former ruler.
What must a ruler be like for one to wear mourning for him?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“If his remonstrances were acted upon, his words were listened to,
and his bountiful favors flowed down to the people;
and if, when he left for some reason,
the ruler sent someone to guide him out of the borders,
and also sent someone ahead to his destination to recommend him;
and only if, after three years of departure, he did not return,
did the ruler reclaim his fields and residence;
this is what is called the ‘three-fold courtesy.’
If it is like this,
then mourning will be worn for him.
But nowadays, when one is a minister,
his remonstrances are not acted upon,
and his words are not listened to;
no bountiful favors flow down to the people;
if he leaves for some reason,
the ruler arrests and binds him,
and also tries to ruin him at his destination;
and on the very day of his departure,
the ruler reclaims his fields and residence.
This is what is called acting as a bandit and enemy.
What mourning can there be for a bandit and enemy?”
8.4 Mèngzǐ said:
“If scholars are killed without crime,
then the great officers may leave the state;
if the people are slaughtered without crime,
then the scholars may migrate.”
8.5 Mèngzǐ said:
“If the ruler is benevolent, no one will not be benevolent;
if the ruler is righteous, no one will not be righteous.”
8.6 Mèngzǐ said:
“A ritual that is not truly ritual,
righteousness that is not truly righteousness,
the great person will not perform.”
8.7 Mèngzǐ said:
“Those who are balanced cultivate those who are not balanced,
and those who are talented cultivate those who are untalented;
therefore, people delight in having worthy fathers and elder brothers.
But if those who are balanced abandon those who are not balanced,
and those who are talented abandon those who are untalented,
then the distance between the worthy and the unworthy
cannot be measured by even an inch.”
8.8 Mèngzǐ said:
“Only when people refuse to do certain things,
can they be capable of doing great things.”
8.9 Mèngzǐ said:
“If one speaks of the faults of others,
what will they do about the subsequent consequences?”
8.10 Mèngzǐ said:
“Zhòngní did not go to extremes.”
8.11 Mèngzǐ said:
“A great person
does not necessarily insist that their words be literal,
nor that their actions be inflexible,
but only aligns them with what is righteous.”
8.12 Mèngzǐ said:
“A great person
is one who does not lose their infant heart.”
8.13 Mèngzǐ said:
“Supporting the living
is not sufficient to be considered a great matter,
whereas mourning the dead is indeed a great matter.”
8.14 Mèngzǐ said:
“A gentleman makes deep advancements in learning through the proper Way,
wishing to attain it by himself.
Having attained it by himself, he dwells in it securely;
dwelling in it securely, he relies on it deeply;
relying on it deeply, he finds its source wherever he turns;
therefore, a gentleman wishes to attain it by himself.”
8.15 Mèngzǐ said:
“One studies broadly and explains in detail,
in order to return to the essential points.”
8.16 Mèngzǐ said:
“He who tries to win people over through his own goodness
has never been able to win them over;
but he who nurtures people with goodness
will then be able to win over the world.
That anyone could rule as king without the hearts of the world being won over,
has never happened.”
8.17 Mèngzǐ said:
“Speech without substance
is ominous.
The actual consequence of such an omen
falls upon those who obscure the worthy.”
8.18 Xúzǐ said:
“Zhòngní repeatedly praised water,
saying:
‘Water,
O water!’
What did he see in water to praise?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“A spring gushes forth,
ceasing not day or night,
filling every hollow before flowing onward,
and reaching the four seas.
Those that have a source are like this,
and that is what he praised.
If it has no source,
then during the seventh and eighth months,
when the rain gathers,
the channels and ditches are all filled;
yet their drying up
can be awaited in a moment.
Therefore, a reputation that exceeds reality
is a thing of shame to a gentleman.”
8.19 Mèngzǐ said:
“That by which humans differ from birds and beasts
is very slight;
the common people discard it,
while the gentleman preserves it.
Shùn understood the nature of things,
and was perceptive in human relations;
he acted from benevolence and righteousness,
rather than merely practicing benevolence and righteousness.”
8.20 Mèngzǐ said:
“Yǔ detested fine wine but loved good words.
Tāng held to the middle course,
and employed the worthy without regard to their background.
King Wén looked upon the people as if they were wounded,
and gazed toward the Way as if he had not yet seen it.
King Wǔ did not neglect those who were near,
nor did he forget those who were far away.
The Duke of Zhōu desired to combine the virtues of
the three kings,
in order to practice these four things;
where there was something that did not fit,
he would look up and ponder it,
continuing from day into night;
and when he was fortunate enough to resolve it,
he would sit and wait for the dawn.”
8.21 Mèngzǐ said:
“When the traces of the true kings were extinguished,
the *Shī* ceased;
and after the *Shī* ceased,
then the *Chūnqiū* was written.
The *Chèng* of Jìn,
the *Táowù* of Chǔ,
and the *Chūnqiū* of Lǔ
were one and the same:
their subjects were Huán of Qí
and Wén of Jìn,
and their style was historical.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘As for their moral meaning, Qiū has ventured to adopt it.’”
8.22 Mèngzǐ said:
“The influence of a gentleman
ends after five generations,
and the influence of a petty person
ends after five generations.
I was not able to be a disciple of Kǒngzǐ myself,
but I have privately cultivated myself through others.”
8.23 Mèngzǐ said:
“If one can take,
and can also not take,
taking harms one's integrity;
if one can give,
and can also not give,
giving harms one's generosity;
if one can die,
and can also not die,
dying harms one's courage.”
Féng Méng studied archery under Yì.
When he had completely mastered Yì’s way,
he thought that in the whole world, only Yì was superior to himself,
and so he killed Yì.
Mèngzǐ said:
“In this, Yì was also at fault.”
Gōngmíng Yí said:
“He would seem to be without fault.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“His fault might have been slight,
but how could he be completely without fault?”
The people of Zhèng sent Zǐzhuó Rǔzǐ to invade Wèi,
and Wèi sent Yǔgōng Zhīsī to pursue him.
Zǐzhuó Rǔzǐ said,
"Today my illness has flared up,
and I cannot hold my bow.
I am a dead man!"
He asked his carriage driver,
"Who is it that is pursuing me?"
His driver said,
"It is Yǔgōng Zhīsī."
He said,
"Then I shall live!"
His driver said,
"Yǔgōng Zhīsī
is the best archer in Wèi;
yet you, Master, say you will live.
What do you mean?"
He replied,
"Yǔgōng Zhīsī learned archery
from Yǐngōng Zhītā,
and Yǐngōng Zhītā learned archery from me.
Now, Yǐngōng Zhītā
was an upright man,
and his choice of friends must likewise be upright."
When Yǔgōng Zhīsī arrived,
he said,
"Master, why do you not hold your bow?"
He replied,
"Today my illness has flared up,
and I cannot hold my bow."
The other said,
"I, your humble servant, learned archery from Yǐngōng Zhītā,
and Yǐngōng Zhītā learned archery from you, Master.
I cannot bear to use the Master's own art
to harm the Master.
Nevertheless, today's business
is my ruler's business,
and I dare not neglect it."
He drew out his arrows, tapped them against his carriage wheel
to knock off their metal tips,
shot off a set of four, and then returned."
8.25 Mèngzǐ said,
"If Xīzǐ were covered with filth,
everyone would cover their noses and pass her by.
But even an ugly person,
if they fast and bathe,
may offer sacrifices to the Lord on High."
8.26 Mèngzǐ said,
"When people in the world speak of human nature,
they refer only to what is fundamental.
And what is fundamental
takes following its natural course as its basis.
What is disliked in cleverness
is its forced maneuvering.
If clever people
behaved like Yǔ in guiding the waters,
then there would be nothing to dislike in cleverness.
When Yǔ guided the waters,
he guided them by doing what caused no disruption.
If clever people would also do what requires no forced effort,
their cleverness would indeed be great.
High as the heavens are,
and distant as the stars and constellations are,
if we only seek out their fundamental laws,
the summer and winter solstices of a thousand years hence
can be calculated while sitting down."
8.27 Gōngxíngzǐ had a mourning for his son,
and the Right Marshal went to offer his condolences.
When he entered the gate,
some stepped forward to speak with the Right Marshal,
while others approached the Right Marshal's seat
and spoke with him.
Mèngzǐ alone did not speak with the Right Marshal.
The Right Marshal was displeased and said,
"All the other gentlemen spoke with Huān,
yet Mèngzǐ alone did not speak with Huān.
This is treating Huān with neglect!"
Mèngzǐ heard of this
and said,
"According to the rites,
at court, one does not cross over others' places to speak to each other,
nor does one leap over steps to bow to one another.
I wished to follow the rites,
but Zǐ'áo thinks I neglected him.
Is that not strange?"
8.28 Mèngzǐ said,
"That by which the gentleman differs from other men
is that he preserves his heart.
The gentleman preserves his heart with benevolence,
and preserves his heart with propriety.
The benevolent man loves others,
and the polite man respects others.
He who loves others
is constantly loved by them;
he who respects others
is constantly respected by them.
Suppose there is a person here
who treats me in an outrageous and unreasonable manner.
In such a case, the gentleman will surely examine himself:
'I must have been lacking in benevolence,
I must have been lacking in propriety;
how else could this treatment have come upon me?'
If, upon self-examination, he finds he has been benevolent,
and has acted with propriety,
yet the outrageous and unreasonable treatment continues as before,
the gentleman will surely examine himself again:
'I must have been unfaithful.'
If, upon self-examination, he finds he has been faithful,
yet the outrageous and unreasonable treatment continues as before,
the gentleman will say,
'This is simply a wild, reckless person.
In this case, what difference is there between him and a beast?
And why should one trouble oneself over a beast?'
Therefore, the gentleman has lifelong anxieties,
but not a single morning's sudden trouble.
As for what he does worry about, it is this:
Shùn was a man,
and I too am a man.
Shùn became a model for the world,
worthy of being passed down to future generations,
yet I am still nothing more than a common villager;
this is indeed a cause for anxiety.
What is he to do about this anxiety?
Simply to become like Shùn.
As for the sudden troubles of a gentleman, there are none.
He does nothing that is not benevolent,
and takes no action that is not in accordance with propriety.
If any sudden trouble should arise,
the gentleman does not view it as a trouble."
8.29 Yǔ and Jì lived in a peaceful age,
yet three times they passed by their own doors without entering;
Kǒngzǐ praised them.
Yánzǐ lived in a chaotic age,
living in a mean alley,
with a single bamboo bowl of rice
and a single ladle of water;
others could not endure such distress,
yet Yánzǐ did not lose his joy;
Kǒngzǐ praised him.
Mèngzǐ said,
"Yǔ, Jì, and Yán Huí followed the same path.
Yǔ thought that if there was anyone in the world who drowned,
it was as if he himself had drowned them;
Jì thought that if there was anyone in the world who starved,
it was as if he himself had starved them.
Therefore,
they were so urgent in their efforts.
If Yǔ, Jì, and Yánzǐ had exchanged places,
each would have acted as the others did.
Suppose there are people in the same house fighting;
to go to save them,
even if one does so with disheveled hair and one's cap hastily tied,
is acceptable.
But if there are people in the neighborhood fighting,
and one rushes to save them with disheveled hair and one's cap hastily tied,
that is foolish;
even if he shuts his door, it is acceptable."
8.30 Gōngdūzǐ said,
"Kuāng Zhāng
is called unfilial by the whole country,
yet you, Master, associate with him
and even treat him with courtesy;
may I venture to ask why?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"There are five things commonly said in the world to be unfilial:
to be lazy in the use of one's four limbs,
not caring for the support of one's parents,
this is the first unfilial thing;
to be fond of chess, gaming, and drinking wine,
not caring for the support of one's parents,
this is the second unfilial thing;
to be fond of wealth and goods,
and to favor one's wife and children,
not caring for the support of one's parents,
this is the third unfilial thing;
to yield to the desires of one's ears and eyes,
and thereby bring shame upon one's parents,
this is the fourth unfilial thing;
to be fond of bravado, fighting, and quarreling,
thereby endangering one's parents,
this is the fifth unfilial thing.
Does Zhāngzǐ practice any one of these?
Now, Zhāngzǐ
exhorted his father to do good,
and as a result, they fell out.
Exhorting each other to do good
is the way of friends;
but for father and son to exhort each other to do good
is the greatest injury to their mutual affection.
How could Zhāngzǐ
not have wished to enjoy the family relationships of husband and wife, mother and child?
But because he had offended his father
and could not approach him,
he sent away his wife and banished his children,
and for the rest of his life did not accept their support.
In his mind, he believed that
if he did not do so,
his offense would be even greater.
Such is the case of Zhāngzǐ."
8.31 When Zēngzǐ was living in Wǔchéng,
there was an invasion by the forces of Yuè.
Someone said,
"The invaders are coming,
why not leave?"
He said,
"Do not let anyone lodge in my house,
lest they damage its firewood and trees."
When the invaders retreated,
he said,
"Repair my walls and house,
I am about to return."
When the invaders retreated,
Zēngzǐ returned.
His attendants said,
"The people here treated the Master with such
loyalty and respect;
yet when the invaders came,
he was the first to leave, setting an example for the people to flee;
and when the invaders retreated, he returned.
This seems highly improper."
Shěnyóu Xíng said,
"This is not something you understand.
In the past,
when the Shěnyóu family suffered the calamity of Fùchú,
among the seventy disciples who followed the Master,
none took part in it."
When Zǐsī was living in Wèi,
there was an invasion by the forces of Qí.
Someone said,
"The invaders are coming,
why not leave?"
Zǐsī said,
"If Jí leaves,
with whom will the ruler defend the state?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Zēngzǐ and Zǐsī followed the same path.
Zēngzǐ was a teacher,
and a father or elder brother figure;
Zǐsī was a minister,
and of lesser rank.
If Zēngzǐ and Zǐsī had exchanged places,
they would have acted in exactly the same way."
8.32 Chǔzǐ said,
"The King sent someone to spy on the Master,
to see if he is indeed different from other people."
Mèngzǐ said,
