"How should I be different from other people?
Yáo and Shùn were just the same as other people."
8.33 Among the people of Qí, there was a man who lived with his wife and a concubine.
Whenever their husband went out,
he would always return only after having sated himself with wine and meat.
When his wife asked him who his dining and drinking companions were,
they were always rich and honorable people.
The wife said to the concubine,
"Whenever our husband goes out,
he always returns only after having sated himself with wine and meat;
and when asked about those with whom he eats and drinks,
they are all rich and honorable people.
Yet no distinguished person has ever come to our home.
I am going to spy on where our husband goes."
Rising early in the morning,
she followed her husband stealthily to where he went.
Throughout the whole city, there was no one who stood and spoke with him.
Finally, he went among the graves outside the eastern wall,
and went to those who were performing sacrifices,
begging for their leftovers.
Not being satisfied,
he looked around and went to another spot.
This was his way of obtaining satiety.
The wife returned
and told the concubine, saying,
"Our husband
is the one whom we look up to and rely upon for our whole lives,
and now he is like this!"
Together with the concubine, she reviled their husband,
and they wept together in the courtyard,
while the husband, unaware of this,
came back jauntily from outside,
showing off before his wife and concubine.
Viewed from the perspective of a gentleman,
those means by which people seek wealth, honor, gain, and advancement
are such that those whose wives and concubines would not feel ashamed of them and weep together
are few indeed.
9.1 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"Shùn went to the fields,
and cried out and wept toward Míntiān,
why did he cry out and weep?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"It was because of his yearning and grief."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"It is said: 'If one's parents love him,
he rejoices and does not forget them;
if his parents dislike him,
he toils and does not resent them.'
Did Shùn then harbor resentment?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Cháng Xī asked Gōngmíng Gāo,
'As for Shùn going to the fields,
I have already heard your instruction;
but as for his crying out and weeping toward Míntiān
and to his parents,
I do not understand.'
Gōngmíng Gāo said,
'This is not something you understand.'
Now, Gōngmíng Gāo believed that the heart of a filial son
could not be so indifferent as to think:
'I exert all my strength in tilling the fields
and simply perform my duties as a son,
and if my parents do not love me,
what is that to me?'
The Emperor sent his children, nine sons and two daughters,
and prepared all the officials, oxen, sheep, granaries, and storehouses
to serve Shùn in the midst of the fields.
Most of the scholars of the world went to him,
and the Emperor was going to hand over the whole empire and transfer it to him.
Yet, because he was not in harmony with his parents,
he felt like a poor man with nowhere to go.
To be liked by the scholars of the world
is what men desire,
yet it was not enough to dispel his sorrow.
Beautiful women are what men desire,
and he married the Emperor's two daughters,
yet it was not enough to dispel his sorrow.
Wealth
is what men desire,
and he possessed the wealth of the whole empire,
yet it was not enough to dispel his sorrow.
Honor
is what men desire,
and he was as honored as the Emperor,
yet it was not enough to dispel his sorrow.
Being liked by others,
beautiful women, wealth, and honor
were none of them enough to dispel his sorrow;
only being in harmony with his parents
could dispel his sorrow.
When a person is young, he yearns for his parents;
when he begins to appreciate beauty, he yearns for young and attractive women;
when he has a wife and children, he yearns for his wife and children;
when he enters public service, he yearns for his ruler,
and if he does not gain his ruler's favor, his heart burns within him.
But a person of great filial piety yearns for his parents his entire life.
One who yearned for them even at the age of fifty—
I have seen this in the great Shùn."
9.2 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"The *Classic of Poetry* says,
'How does one take a wife?
He must inform his parents.'
If this saying is true,
no one should have conformed to it more than Shùn.
As for Shùn's marrying without informing them,
why was it?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"If he had informed them, he would not have been able to marry.
That male and female should live together in one house
is the greatest of human relations.
If he had informed them, he would have had to discard the greatest of human relations,
thereby harboring resentment against his parents.
This is why he did not inform them."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"As for Shùn marrying without informing them,
I have already heard your instruction.
But why did the Emperor marry his daughters to Shùn without informing them,
why was it?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"The Emperor also knew that if he had informed them,
he would not have been able to marry his daughters to him."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"His parents made Shùn repair a granary,
and then took away the ladder,
and Gǔsǒu set fire to the granary.
They made him dredge a well;
he escaped,
while they followed and covered it up.
Xiàng said,
'The plot to cover Dōujūn was all my merit.
The oxen and sheep shall be for my father and mother,
the granaries shall be for my father and mother,
but the shields and spears are mine,
the lute is mine,
the carved bow is mine,
and my two sisters-in-law shall manage my bed.'
Xiàng then went into Shùn's palace,
where Shùn was sitting on his bed playing the lute.
Xiàng said,
'I was feeling anxious and thinking of you!'
But he looked embarrassed.
Shùn said,
'There are these ministers and subjects of mine;
you must help me govern them.'
I do not know if Shùn was unaware that Xiàng was trying to kill him?"
He said,
"How could he not know?
When Xiàng was sorrowful, he was also sorrowful;
when Xiàng was joyful, he was also joyful."
He said,
"In that case, was Shùn pretending to be joyful?"
He said,
"No.
Formerly, someone presented a live fish to Zǐchǎn of Zhèng.
Zǐchǎn had the pond-keeper keep it in the pond.
The pond-keeper cooked it
and reported back, saying,
'When I first released it, it was rather sluggish;
after a short while, it moved about freely;
then it darted away.'
Zǐchǎn said,
'It has found its proper place!
It has found its proper place!'
The pond-keeper went out
and said,
'Who says Zǐchǎn is wise?
I have already cooked and eaten it,
yet he says,
"It has found its proper place!
It has found its proper place!"'
Therefore, a gentleman may be deceived by what seems reasonable,
but it is difficult to mislead him by what is contrary to the proper way.
Xiàng came with the appearance of brotherly love,
and Shùn sincerely believed him and was rejoiced by it.
How could there be any pretense?"
9.3 Wàn Zhāng asked,
"Xiàng made it his daily
business to kill Shùn.
Yet when Shùn was established as the Son of Heaven,
he banished him.
Why was this?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"He enfeoffed him.
Some, however, said he banished him."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"Shùn banished Gònggōng to Yōuzhōu,
exiled Huāndōu to Chóngshān,
executed the chief of Sānmiáo at Sānwēi,
and imprisoned Gǔn at Yǔshān.
By punishing these four
criminals, the whole world submitted,
because he punished the unbenevolent.
Xiàng was extremely unbenevolent,
yet he was enfeoffed in Yǒubì.
What crime did the people of Yǒubì commit?
Is a benevolent person truly like this:
punishing others,
but enfeoffing his own brother?"
He said,
"A benevolent man, in relation to his brother,
does not harbor anger
nor nurse resentment,
but simply feels affection and love for him.
Feeling affection for him,
he wishes him to be honorable;
loving him,
he wishes him to be rich.
Enfeoffing him in Yǒubì
was to make him rich and honorable.
If he himself were the Son of Heaven,
while his brother was a commoner,
could he be said to feel affection and love for him?"
"May I ask,
'what is meant by those who say
"he banished him"?'"
He said,
"Xiàng was not allowed to take any action in his state.
The Son of Heaven sent officers to govern his state
and collect its taxes and revenues.
Therefore, it was called banishing him.
How could he be allowed to tyrannize those people?
Nevertheless,
Shùn wished to see him constantly,
so they came in an uninterrupted flow.
'Without waiting for the time of tribute,
on the pretext of state business, he had dealings with Yǒubì.'
This is what that refers to."
9.4 Xiánqiū Méng asked,
"A saying goes,
'A scholar of abundant virtue
cannot be treated as a minister by a ruler,
nor as a son by a father.'
When Shùn stood facing south,
Yáo led the feudal lords facing north
to pay homage to him,
and Gǔsǒu also faced north
to pay homage to him.
When Shùn saw Gǔsǒu,
his countenance showed distress.
Kǒngzǐ said,
'At that time,
how perilous was the empire,
how unstable!'
I do not know if this saying is indeed true?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No.
This is not the saying of a gentleman;
it is the talk of an uncultivated person from the east of Qí.
When Yáo was old, Shùn acted as regent.
*The Canon of Yáo* says,
'In the twenty-eighth year,
Fàngxūn died.
The people mourned him as if they had lost a father or mother,
and for three years,
within the four seas, the eight kinds of musical instruments were silenced.'
Kǒngzǐ said,
'There are not two suns in the sky,
nor are there two kings over the people.'
If Shùn had already been the Son of Heaven,
and yet led the feudal lords of the empire
to observe three years of mourning for Yáo,
this would have meant there were two Sons of Heaven."
Xiánqiū Méng said,
"That Shùn did not treat Yáo as a minister,
I have already received your instruction.
*The Book of Odes* says,
'Under the vast heaven,
there is no land that is not the king's;
along the borders of the land,
there is no one who is not the king's subject.'
Since Shùn was already the Son of Heaven,
may I ask how it was that Gǔsǒu was not
his subject?"
He said,
"This ode
does not mean what you think.
It refers to being exhausted by the king's business
and thus unable to nourish one's father and mother.
It says,
'All this is the king's business,
yet I alone am overburdened with work.'
Therefore, those who explain the *Odes*
must not let the single words obscure the sentence,
nor the sentence obscure the intended meaning.
To meet the intended meaning with one's own understanding
is the way to grasp it.
If we take only the literal words,
the ode *Yúnhàn* says,
'Of the remaining people of Zhōu,
not a single one survived.'
If we believe these words literally,
it would mean that no people remained in Zhōu.
Of all the achievements of a filial son,
none is greater than honoring his parents.
Of all the ways of honoring parents,
none is greater than nourishing them with the whole empire.
To be the father of the Son of Heaven
is the height of honor.
To be nourished with the whole empire
is the height of nourishment.
*The Book of Odes* says,
'Think always of filial piety,
and your filial thoughts will become a model.'
This is what that refers to.
*The Book of Documents* says,
'With reverence he went to see Gǔsǒu,
full of awe and trepidation,
and Gǔsǒu also truly accorded with him.'
Is this what is meant by "a father not being able to treat him as a son"?"
9.5 Wàn Zhāng said,
"Did Yáo give the empire to Shùn?
Was there such a thing?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No.
The Son of Heaven cannot give the empire to another."
"Then, when Shùn got the empire,
who gave it to him?"
He said,
"Heaven gave it to him."
"In Heaven's giving it to him,
did Heaven give him instructions with explicit words?"
He said,
"No.
Heaven does not speak.
It simply showed its will through his conduct and the conduct of affairs."
He said,
"How did Heaven show its will
through his conduct and the conduct of affairs?"
He said,
"The Son of Heaven can present a man to Heaven,
but he cannot make Heaven give him the empire.
A feudal lord can present a man to the Son of Heaven,
but he cannot make the Son of Heaven give him the state.
A grand officer can present a man to a feudal lord,
but he cannot make the feudal lord give him the office of grand officer.
Formerly, Yáo presented Shùn to Heaven,
and Heaven accepted him;
he exposed him to the people,
and the people accepted him.
Therefore it is said,
'Heaven does not speak.
It simply showed its will through his conduct and the conduct of affairs.'"
He said,
"May I venture to ask: when he was presented to Heaven,
and Heaven accepted him;
and when he was presented to the people, and the people accepted him,
how was this done?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"He was made to preside over the sacrifices,
and all the spirits accepted them;
this was Heaven accepting him.
He was made to preside over affairs,
and affairs were well managed,
and the common people were at peace with him;
this was the people accepting him.
Heaven gave it to him,
and the people gave it to him.
Therefore it is said,
'The Son of Heaven cannot give the world to another.'
Shùn assisted Yáo
for twenty-eight years;
this was not something that man could do,
it was Heaven.
When Yáo died,
and the three years of mourning were completed,
Shùn withdrew from the son of Yáo
to the south of the Nánhé.
Yet the lords of the world who came to pay court
went not to the son of Yáo but to Shùn;
those who had litigations
went not to the son of Yáo but to Shùn;
those who sang praises
sang not the praises of the son of Yáo but of Shùn.
Therefore it is said,
'It was Heaven.'
Only after this did he go to the Middle Kingdom
and ascend the throne of the Son of Heaven.
Had he lived in the palace of Yáo
and pressured the son of Yáo,
this would have been usurpation,
and not the gift of Heaven.
The 'Dàshì' says,
'Heaven sees as my people see,
Heaven hears as my people hear.'
This is what is meant."
9.6 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"People have a saying:
'When it came to Yǔ, virtue declined,
for he did not pass it on to a worthy person,
but passed it on to his son.'
Was this so?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No,
it was not so.
When Heaven gave it to a worthy,
it was given to a worthy;
when Heaven gave it to a son,
it was given to a son.
In the past, Shùn presented Yǔ to Heaven,
and after seventeen years,
Shùn died.
When the three years of mourning were completed,
Yǔ withdrew from the son of Shùn
to Yángchéng,
and the people of the world followed him,
just as after the death of Yáo,
they had not followed the son of Yáo but followed Shùn.
Yǔ presented Yì to Heaven,
and after seven years,
Yǔ died.
When the three years of mourning were completed,
Yì withdrew from the son of Yǔ
to the north of Mount Jī.
Those who came to pay court
and those who had litigations
went not to Yì but to Qǐ,
saying,
'He is the son of our lord.'
Those who sang praises
sang not the praises of Yì but of Qǐ,
saying,
'He is the son of our lord.'
Dānzhū was unworthy,
and the son of Shùn was also unworthy.
Shùn's assisting of Yáo
and Yǔ's assisting of Shùn
lasted for many years,
and they had long bestowed benefits upon the people.
Qǐ was worthy,
and could respectfully inherit and continue the way of Yǔ.
Yì's assisting of Yǔ
lasted for few years,
and he had not long bestowed benefits upon the people.
With Shùn, Yǔ, and Yì,
the differences in the lengths of time,
and whether their sons were worthy or unworthy,
were all from Heaven,
and not something that man could do.
That which is done without anyone doing it
is Heaven.
That which comes about without anyone bringing it about
is destiny.
For a commoner to gain the world,
his virtue must be like that of Shùn and Yǔ,
and he must also have a Son of Heaven to present him;
therefore Zhòngní did not gain the world.
When the throne is inherited from generation to generation and one gains the world,
those whom Heaven discards
must be like Jié and Zhòu;
therefore Yì, Yī Yǐn, and Zhōugōng
did not gain the world.
Yī Yǐn assisted Tāng to rule as king over the world.
When Tāng died,
Tàidīng had not been established;
Wàibǐng ruled for two years,
and Zhòngrén for four years.
Then Tàijiǎ overturned the laws and standards of Tāng,
and Yī Yǐn banished him to Tóng.
After three years,
Tàijiǎ repented of his errors,
blamed himself and reformed;
while at Tóng, he dwelt in benevolence and moved toward righteousness,
and for three years he listened to Yī Yǐn's lessons to him,
and then returned to Bó.
That Zhōugōng did not gain the world
was just like Yì in relation to Xià,
and Yī Yǐn in relation to Yīn.
Kǒngzǐ said,
'Táng and Yú abdicated,
while the sovereigns of Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu inherited;
but the principle was the same.'"
9.7 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"People have a saying:
'Yī Yǐn sought an introduction to Tāng through his cooking.'
Was this so?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No,
it was not so.
Yī Yǐn farmed in the wilderness of Yǒushēn,
and delighted in the way of Yáo and Shùn.
If it was not righteous,
or if it was not in accordance with the way,
though he were offered the wealth of the world as his salary, he would not look at it;
though a thousand teams of horses were tethered for him, he would not glance at them.
If it was not righteous,
or if it was not in accordance with the way,
he would not give a single straw to others,
nor would he take a single straw from others.
Tāng sent messengers with gifts to invite him,
and he said with an air of indifference,
'What use have I for Tāng's gifts and invitation?
How can they compare with my remaining here in the midst of these fields,
and thereby delighting in the way of Yáo and Shùn?'
Tāng sent three times to invite him,
after which he suddenly changed his mind and said,
'Rather than remaining in the midst of these fields,
and thereby delighting in the way of Yáo and Shùn,
would it not be better for me to make this ruler a ruler like Yáo and Shùn?
Would it not be better for me to make this people a people like the people of Yáo and Shùn?
Would it not be better for me to see this in my own person?
When Heaven produced this people,
it made those who are first informed awaken those who are later informed,
and those who first awaken awaken those who awaken later.
I
am one of Heaven's people who has first awakened;
I will use this way to awaken this people.
If I do not awaken them, who will?'
He thought that of all the common men and common women in the world,
if there was any who did not enjoy the benefits of Yáo and Shùn,
it was as if he himself had pushed them into a ditch.
Such was the heavy responsibility he took upon himself for the world,
and so he went to Tāng
and persuaded
him to attack Xià
and save the people.
I have never heard of one who bent himself and could straighten others,
much less of one who disgraced himself to straighten the world!
The actions of sages are not all alike:
some keep at a distance, some draw near;
some leave, some do not leave;
but in the end, it all comes to keeping their own persons pure.
I have heard that he sought an introduction to Tāng through the way of Yáo and Shùn,
but I have not heard that it was through cooking.
The 'Yī Xùn' says,
'Heaven's punishment began its attack from the Mù Palace;
I began my work from Bó.'"
9.8 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"Some say
that Kǒngzǐ, when in Wèi, lodged with the ulcer-doctor Yōng Jū,
and in Qí, with the eunuch Jí Huán.
Was this so?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No,
it was not so.
Those who are fond of making up stories invented this."
In Wèi,
he lodged with Yán Chóuyóu.
The wife of Mí Zǐ and the wife of Zǐlù
were sisters.
Mí Zǐ said to Zǐlù,
"If Kǒngzǐ will lodge with me,
the position of a high minister in Wèi may be obtained."
Zǐlù reported this to him.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"There is a decree of Heaven."
Kǒngzǐ advanced according to propriety,
and withdrew according to righteousness. Whether he succeeded
or did not succeed, he said,
"There is a decree of Heaven."
But if he had lodged with Yōng Jū and the eunuch Jí Huán,
that would have been without righteousness and without regard to Heaven's decree.
Kǒngzǐ was not pleased with Lǔ and Wèi.
He encountered Marshal Huán of Sòng,
who wished to intercept and kill him,
so he passed through Sòng in disguise.
At that time, Kǒngzǐ was in difficulties,
and lodged with Sīchéng Zhēnzǐ,
serving as a minister to Zhōu, the Marquis of Chén.
I have heard that we judge the ministers near the court
by those whom they host,
and we judge the ministers from afar
by those with whom they lodge.
If Kǒngzǐ had lodged with Yōng Jū and the eunuch Jí Huán,
how could he be Kǒngzǐ?"
9.9 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"Some say that
Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself
to a keeper of cattle in Qín
for five sheepskins, and fed cattle,
in order to seek the favor of Duke Mù of Qín.
Is this true?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No,
it was not so.
It was an invention of busybodies.
Bǎilǐ Xī
was a native of Yú.
The people of Jìn, by means of the jade of Chuíjí
and the team of horses from Qū,
begged a passage through Yú to attack Guó.
Gōng Zhīqí remonstrated,
but Bǎilǐ Xī did not.
Knowing that the Duke of Yú could not be remonstrated with, he left and went to Qín.
He was already seventy years old.
If he did not know that seeking the favor of Duke Mù of Qín by feeding cattle was a base thing,
could he be called wise?
But since he did not remonstrate when remonstrance would have been useless,
can he be called unwise?
Knowing that the Duke of Yú was about to perish
and leaving beforehand,
he cannot be called unwise.
When he was raised to office in Qín,
knowing that Duke Mù was a ruler with whom he could achieve great things,
he became his prime minister.
Can this be called unwise?
He assisted Qín,
made his ruler illustrious throughout the world,
and left a name to be handed down to future generations.
Could he have done this if he were not a worthy man?
As for selling himself to advance his ruler,
even a self-respecting villager would not do it.
How could a worthy man do such a thing?"
10.1 Mèngzǐ said,
"Bó Yí's eyes would not look on an evil sight,
and his ears would not listen to an evil sound.
He would not serve a ruler of whom he did not approve,
nor command a people whom he did not approve.
When there was good government, he took office;
when there was disorder, he retired.
Where tyrannical government prevailed
and lawless people gathered,
he could not bear to dwell.
He thought that being with common villagers
was like sitting in mud and charcoal
dressed in court robes and a court cap.
In the time of Zhòu,
he dwelt on the shores of the North Sea,
waiting for the world to become clean.
Therefore, when people hear of the character of Bó Yí,
the corrupt become honest,
and the weak-willed form a firm resolve.
Yī Yǐn said,
'Whom may I not serve as my ruler?
Whom may I not employ as my people?'
When there was good government, he took office;
when there was disorder, he also took office.
He said,
'Heaven, in producing this people,
appoints those who are first informed
to awaken those who are later in knowing,
and those who are first awakened
to awaken those who are later in awakening.
I
am one of the first of Heaven's people to awaken.
I will awaken this people by means of this path.'
If he thought that among the people of the world there was any common man or common woman
who did not enjoy the benefits of the rule of Yáo and Shùn,
it was as if he himself had pushed them into a ditch.
Such was the heavy responsibility he took upon himself for the world.
Liǔxià Huì
was not ashamed to serve an impure ruler,
nor did he decline a low office.
When in office, he did not conceal his worth,
and always acted according to his principles.
When he was passed over and left in obscurity, he did not complain;
when in distress and poverty, he was not sorrowful.
When staying with common villagers,
he was quite at ease, and could not bear to leave them.
'You are you,' he said,
'and I am I.
Although you should stand by my side with shoulders bare or entirely naked,
how can you defile me?'
Therefore, when people hear of the character of Liǔxià Huì,
the narrow-minded become broad,
and the mean-spirited become generous.
"When Kǒngzǐ left Qí,
he strained the rice and set off;
when he left Lǔ,
he said,
'I will delay my departure;
this is the way to leave the state of one's parents.'
When it was proper to go quickly, he went quickly;
when it was proper to delay, he delayed;
when it was proper to keep in retirement, he kept in retirement;
when it was proper to take office, he took office.
Such was Kǒngzǐ."
Mèngzǐ said,
"Bó Yí
was the sage of purity;
Yī Yǐn
was the sage of responsibility;
Liǔxià Huì
was the sage of harmony; and
Kǒngzǐ was the sage of timeliness.
Kǒngzǐ may be said to have gathered together all these great qualities.
Gathering them together
is like beginning with the sound of bronze bells and concluding with the sound of jade chimes.
The sound of the bronze bells
begins the orderly sequence;
the sound of the jade chimes
ends the orderly sequence.
Beginning the orderly sequence
is the work of wisdom;
ending the orderly sequence
is the work of sageliness.
Wisdom
is like skill;
sageliness
is like strength.
Like shooting at a mark a hundred paces off,
that the arrow reaches it
is a matter of your strength,
but that it hits the mark
is not a matter of your strength."
10.2 Běigōng Qí asked, saying,
"How did the House of Zhōu arrange ranks and emoluments,
and how was it?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"The particulars
cannot be heard,
because the feudal lords disliked them as being injurious to themselves,
and they all destroyed the records.
However, I, Kē,
have heard the outline of it.
The Tiānzǐ constituted one rank;
the *gōng* one rank;
the *hóu* one rank;
the *bó* one rank;
and the *zǐ* and *nán* shared one rank;
making five classes in all.
The ruler constituted one rank;
the *qīng* one rank;
the *dàfū* one rank;
the *shàngshì* one rank;
the *zhōngshì* one rank;
the *xiàshì* one rank;
making six classes in all.
According to the system of the Tiānzǐ,
his territory was a thousand *lǐ* square;
a *gōng* or a *hóu* was a hundred *lǐ* square;
a *bó* was seventy *lǐ* square;
and a *zǐ* or a *nán* was fifty *lǐ* square;
making four grades in all.
Those whose territory does not reach fifty lǐ,
cannot have direct communication with the Son of Heaven.
They attach themselves to the feudal lords,
and are called attached states.
A minister of the Son of Heaven
receives land equal in size to that of a hóu;
a great officer
receives land equal in size to that of a bó;
a chief scholar
receives land equal in size to that of a zǐ or nán.
In a great state, whose territory is one hundred lǐ square,
the ruler's income is ten times that of a minister;
a minister's income is four times that of a great officer;
a great officer's is twice that of a scholar of the first class;
a scholar of the first class has twice as much as a scholar of the middle class;
a scholar of the middle class has twice as much as a scholar of the lowest class;
a scholar of the lowest class and those of the common people who are employed in public offices have the same income,
which is sufficient to replace what they would have made by farming.
In a medium state, whose territory is seventy lǐ square,
the ruler's income is ten times that of a minister;
a minister's income is three times that of a great officer;
a great officer's is twice that of a scholar of the first class;
a scholar of the first class has twice as much as a scholar of the middle class;
a scholar of the middle class has twice as much as a scholar of the lowest class;
a scholar of the lowest class and those of the common people who are employed in public offices have the same income,
which is sufficient to replace what they would have made by farming.
In a small state, whose territory is fifty lǐ square,
the ruler's income is ten times that of a minister;
a minister's income is twice that of a great officer;
a great officer's is twice that of a scholar of the first class;
a scholar of the first class has twice as much as a scholar of the middle class;
a scholar of the middle class has twice as much as a scholar of the lowest class;
a scholar of the lowest class and those of the common people who are employed in public offices have the same income,
which is sufficient to replace what they would have made by farming.
As to what a farmer harvests,
one man has one hundred mǔ;
from the manuring of those hundred mǔ,
a farmer of the highest class can support nine people;
the next class can support eight;
the middle class can support seven;
the next class can support six;
and the lowest class can support five.
For those of the common people who are employed in public offices,
their incomes are graded according to these differences."
10.3 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying,
"May I venture to ask about friendship?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Friendship should be maintained without presuming on one's superior age,
or superior station,
or one's brothers.
Friendship with a person
is friendship with their virtue,
and there must be no presumption of superiority.
Mèng Xiànzǐ
was the head of a family of a hundred chariots,
and he had five friends:
Yuèzhèng Qiú and Mù Zhòng;
the other three I have forgotten.
When Xiànzǐ was friends with these five men,
he did not keep in mind his family status.
If these five men had kept in mind Xiànzǐ's family status,
they would not have been friends with him.
Not only is this the case with the head of a family of a hundred chariots,
but even the ruler of a small state may be like this.
Duke Huì of Fèi said,
'As for Zǐsī,
I look upon him as my teacher;
as for Yán Bān,
I look upon him as my friend;
Wáng Shùn and Cháng Xī
are those who serve me.'
Not only is this the case with the ruler of a small state,
but even the ruler of a great state may be like this.
Duke Píng of Jìn, in his relations with Hài Táng,
entered when he was told to enter,
sat when he was told to sit,
and ate when he was told to eat.
Even though it was coarse food and vegetable soup,
he never failed to eat his fill,
for indeed he did not dare not to eat his fill.
Yet he stopped there and went no further.
He did not share with him the office appointed by Heaven,
nor did he share with him the duties appointed by Heaven,
nor did he share with him the emoluments appointed by Heaven.
This is how a scholar honors a virtuous man,
not how a king or duke honors a virtuous man.
Shùn went up to see the Emperor,
and the Emperor lodged his son-in-law in a secondary palace;
he also feasted Shùn,
and they alternately acted as host and guest.
This was the Son of Heaven
making a friend of a common man.
For an inferior to show respect to a superior
is called honoring the noble;
for a superior to show respect to an inferior
is called honoring the virtuous.
Honoring the noble and honoring the virtuous,
their principle is the same."
10.4 Wàn Zhāng said,
"May I venture to ask what should be the attitude in social intercourse?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"It is respect."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"It is said, 'To refuse it,
to refuse it is disrespectful.'
Why is that?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"When a superior offers a gift,
if one thinks,
'Was the way he obtained this
righteous or unrighteous?'
and only accepts it after that,
this is considered disrespectful,
and therefore one does not refuse it."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"Please allow me to ask: if one does not refuse it in words,
but refuses it in one's heart,
saying,
'He took this unrighteously from the people,'
and then uses some other excuse to decline it,
is that not permissible?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"If the intercourse is conducted in accordance with the proper Way,
and the reception is in accordance with propriety,
then even Kǒngzǐ would have accepted it."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"Suppose there was a highwayman who robbed people outside the city gates.
If his intercourse was conducted in accordance with the proper Way,
and his gift made in accordance with propriety,
could one accept his plunder?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"No.
The *Kāng Gào* says,
'When someone kills and robs a person of his goods,
violently reckless and not fearing death,
there is no one among the people who does not detest him.'
Such a person is to be executed without waiting for instruction.
The Yīn dynasty received this rule from the Xià,
and the Zhōu received it from the Yīn;
it was never set aside.
In the present day, such practices are even more extreme;
how could one accept them?"
Wàn Zhāng said,
"The feudal lords of today take from their people
just like highwaymen.
If they only refine their polite manners and intercourse,
the gentleman accepts their gifts.
May I venture to ask how you explain this?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Do you think that if a true king were to arise,
he would immediately round up the present-day feudal lords and execute them?
Or would he first instruct them, and only execute them if they did not reform?
To say that
taking what is not one's own
is theft,
is pushing a classification to the absolute limit of righteousness.
When Kǒngzǐ held office in Lǔ,
the people of Lǔ competed for game in hunting,
and Kǒngzǐ also competed for game.
If even competing for game was permissible,
how much more so is accepting their gifts?"
Wàn Zhāng said,
"In that case, when Kǒngzǐ held office,
was it not to practice the Way?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"It was to practice the Way."
Wàn Zhāng asked, "If it was to practice the Way, why did he compete for game?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Kǒngzǐ first corrected the registers of the sacrificial vessels,
and did not use food from the four quarters to supply what was missing from the registers."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"Why did he not leave?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"He wanted to make a beginning.
If the beginning was sufficient for his principles to be practiced,
and yet they were not practiced,
only then did he leave.
Therefore, he never stayed in any place for as long as three years.
Kǒngzǐ held office when he saw that his principles could be practiced,
he held office when he was treated with proper courtesy,
and he held office when he was supported by the ruler.
Under Jì Huánzǐ,
it was holding office because he saw that his principles could be practiced;
under Duke Líng of Wèi,
it was holding office because he was treated with proper courtesy;
under Duke Xiào of Wèi,
it was holding office because he was supported by the ruler."
10.5 Mèngzǐ said,
"Taking office is not for the sake of avoiding poverty,
yet there are times when one does so for the sake of avoiding poverty.
Taking a wife is not for the sake of supporting one's parents,
yet there are times when one does so for the sake of supporting them.
If one takes office for the sake of avoiding poverty,
one should decline honorable positions and occupy humble ones,
and decline rich offices and occupy poor ones.
Declining honorable positions and occupying humble ones,
declining rich offices and occupying poor ones,
what positions are suitable?
Being a gatekeeper or a night watchman.
Kǒngzǐ was once a keeper of stores,
and he said,
"My calculations must be correct; that is all."
He was once a keeper of pastures,
and he said,
"The oxen and sheep must be fat and strong,
and growing well; that is all."
To speak of high matters when one's position is low
is a crime;
to stand in a ruler's court
and yet not have the Way practiced
is a shame."
10.6 Wàn Zhāng said,
"Why is it that a scholar does not rely upon the feudal lords,
what is the reason?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"He does not dare to do so.
For a feudal lord who has lost his state to rely on another feudal lord
is according to ritual;
but for a scholar to rely on a feudal lord
is contrary to ritual."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"If a ruler sends him a gift of grain,
does he accept it?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"He accepts it."
"On what principle of righteousness does he accept it?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"A ruler toward his people
is bound to give them relief."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"If he accepts relief,
but would not accept a gift of patronage,
why is that?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"He does not dare."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"May I ask why he does not dare?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"The gatekeepers and night watchmen
all have regular duties for which they receive sustenance from the ruler.
To receive a gift from the ruler without having a regular duty
is considered disrespectful."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"If a ruler sends him gifts,
and he accepts them,
I wonder if this can be continued indefinitely?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Mù Gōng's relation to Zǐsī was such that
he frequently sent inquiries,
and frequently sent gifts of sacrificial meat.
Zǐsī was displeased.
At last,
he waved his hand to the messenger to go out beyond the great gate,
and, facing north, bowed his head to the ground twice and declined the gift,
saying,
'Now and hereafter I know
that the ruler supports Jí as he would a dog or a horse.'
From that time, there were no more gifts sent from the palace.
If a ruler is pleased with a worthy person, but can neither raise him to office
nor support him properly,
can he be said to be pleased with worthy men?"
Wàn Zhāng said,
"May I ask how a ruler of a state should support a superior man,
so that it may indeed be called supporting him?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"At the beginning, the gift is sent by the ruler's command,
and the recipient bows twice, touching his head to the ground, and accepts it.
After this, the officer of the granary continues to send grain,
and the officer of the kitchen continues to send meat,
without any further command from the ruler.
Zǐsī felt that sacrificial meat
made him repeatedly and laboriously bow,
which was not the way to support a superior man.
Yáo's relation to Shùn was such that
he caused his nine sons to serve him,
gave his two daughters to him in marriage,
and provided all the officers, oxen and sheep, granaries and storehouses
to support Shùn in the midst of the fields;
and after that he raised him to office and placed him in the highest position.
Therefore it is said: 'This is how kings and princes honor the worthy.'"
10.7 Wàn Zhāng said,
"May I ask on what principle of righteousness it is that a scholar does not go to see the feudal lords?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"When in the city, he is called 'a minister of the marketplace';
when in the country, he is called 'a minister of the wilderness'.
Both are called commoners.
For a commoner, before presenting introductory gifts to become a minister,
not to go and see the feudal lords
is according to ritual."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"A commoner,
when called upon to do service,
goes and performs the service;
yet if the ruler wishes to see him,
and summons him,
he does not go to see him.
Why is that?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"To go and do service
is a matter of duty;
to go and see the ruler
is contrary to duty.
Moreover, when the ruler wishes to see him,
for what purpose is it?"
Wàn Zhāng said,
"It is because of his extensive information,
or because of his worthiness."
Mèngzǐ said,
"If it be because of his extensive information,
even the Emperor does not summon his teacher,
how much less may a feudal lord do so?
If it be because of his worthiness,
then I have never heard of wishing to see a worthy man and summoning him.
Mù Gōng went frequently to see Zǐsī,
and said,
'In ancient times, a state of a thousand chariots befriended scholars;
what do you think of that?'
Zǐsī was displeased,
and said,
'The ancients had a saying:
"They should be served";
did they say, "They should be befriended"?'
Was not Zǐsī's displeasure
in effect saying:
'In point of station,
you
are the ruler,
and I
am the minister;
how could I dare to be a friend with my ruler?
In point of virtue,
you are one who should serve me;
how can you be a friend with me?'
When the ruler of a state of a thousand chariots sought to be a friend with him,
he could not obtain his wish;
how much less could he summon him?
Qí Jǐng Gōng was hunting,
and summoned his gamekeeper with a banner.
The gamekeeper did not come,
and the Duke was going to kill him.
'A scholar of high purpose does not forget that his end may be in a ditch or a stream;
a brave soldier does not forget that he may lose his head.'
What did Kǒngzǐ take from this?
He took his refusing to go when not summoned with the proper signal."
Wàn Zhāng said,
"May I ask what is the proper signal for summoning a gamekeeper?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"With a leather cap.
Commoners are summoned with a plain red flag;
scholars with a flag with bells;
great officers with a banner.
When one summons a gamekeeper with the signal for a great officer,
the gamekeeper would rather die than dare to go.
When one summons a commoner with the signal for a scholar,
how could the commoner dare to go?
How much less, then,
when one summons a worthy man
with a signal inappropriate for a worthy man?
To wish to see a worthy man, and yet not to approach him according to the proper way,
is like wishing a man to enter while shutting the door against him.
Righteousness
is the road,
and propriety
is the gate.
Only the superior man can walk along this road,
and go out and in by this gate.
The Book of Poetry says:
'The way of Zhōu is like a whetstone,
and its straightness is like an arrow;
it is what the superior man treads,
and what the common people look up to.'"
Wàn Zhāng said,
"When Kǒngzǐ,
when summoned by his ruler's command,
went without waiting for his carriage to be yoked;
was Kǒngzǐ then wrong?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Kǒngzǐ was in office, holding official duties,
and he was summoned by virtue of his office."
10.8 Mèngzǐ said to Wàn Zhāng,
"A good scholar of a neighborhood
will befriend other good scholars of that neighborhood;
a good scholar of a state
will befriend other good scholars of that state;
a good scholar of the world
will befriend other good scholars of the world.
If befriending the good scholars of the world is still not enough,
he will also ascend to consider the ancients.
He recites their poems,
reads their books—
yet is it possible to be ignorant of what kind of people they were?
Therefore he considers the age in which they lived.
This is what is meant by befriending the ancients."
10.9 King Xuān of Qí asked about ministers.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Which ministers is the King asking about?"
The King said:
"Are ministers not all the same?"
He replied:
"They are not the same.
There are ministers who are of the noble lineage of the ruling family,
and there are ministers of different surnames."
The King said:
"I beg to ask about the ministers who are of the noble lineage."
He replied:
"If the ruler has great faults, they remonstrate with him.
If they do so repeatedly and he does not listen,
then they depose him and seat another."
The King suddenly changed countenance.
He said:
"May the King not find this strange.
The King asked his servant,
and his servant dared not but answer truthfully."
The King's countenance settled,
and then he begged to ask about the ministers of different surnames.
He replied:
"If the ruler has faults, they remonstrate with him.
If they do so repeatedly and he does not listen,
then they leave the state."
11.1 Gàozǐ said:
"Human nature is like the qǐ-willow tree,
and righteousness
is like cups and bowls.
To make benevolence and righteousness out of human nature
is like making cups and bowls out of the qǐ-willow tree."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Can you follow the nature of the qǐ-willow
to make it into cups and bowls?
Or must you do violence and damage to the qǐ-willow
before you can make it into cups and bowls?
If you must do violence and damage to the qǐ-willow
to make it into cups and bowls,
then must you also do violence and damage to human beings to make them benevolent and righteous?
That which leads the people of the world to bring disaster upon benevolence and righteousness
must surely be your words!"
11.2 Gàozǐ said:
"Human nature
is like rushing water.
Direct it to the east, and it flows to the east;
direct it to the west, and it flows to the west.
Human nature's lack of distinction between good and not-good
is like water's lack of distinction between east and west."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Water indeed makes no distinction between east and west,
but does it make no distinction between up and down?
The goodness of human nature
is like water flowing downward.
There is no human who is not good,
just as there is no water that does not flow downward.
Now, as for water, if you strike it and splash it,
it can be made to go over your forehead;
if you dam it and channel it,
it can be made to go up a hill.
But is this the nature of water?
It is the force of circumstances that makes it so.
That humans can be made to do what is not good,
their nature is also like this."
11.3 Gàozǐ said:
"What is inborn is called nature."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Is 'what is inborn is called nature'
like saying 'white is called white'?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"Is the whiteness of a white feather
like the whiteness of white snow,
and the whiteness of white snow
like the whiteness of white jade?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"Then is the nature of a dog
like the nature of an ox,
and the nature of an ox
like the nature of a human?"
11.4 Gàozǐ said:
"The desire for food and sex
is nature.
Benevolence
is internal,
not external;
righteousness
is external,
not internal."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Why do you say that benevolence is internal and righteousness is external?"
He replied:
"That man is older and I treat him as older.
It is not that there is a quality of being older within me;
just as that thing is white and I treat it as white,
following its whiteness which is external.
Therefore, I call it external."
He said:
"Is there any difference between the whiteness of a white horse
and the whiteness of a white man?
But I do not know, is the age of an old horse
no different from the age of an old man?
And furthermore, is it the old man who is righteous,
or the person who treats him as older who is righteous?"
He replied:
"My own younger brother, I love him,
but the younger brother of a man of Qín, I do not love him.
This is because the feeling is determined by myself,
therefore I call it internal.
I treat an old man of Chǔ as older,
and I also treat an old man of my own family as older.
This is because the age itself determines the respect,
therefore I call it external."
He said:
"Our enjoying the roast meat of a man of Qín
is no different from enjoying our own roast meat.
Since external things are also like this,
does it mean our enjoyment of roast meat is also external?"
11.5 Mèng Jìzǐ asked Gōngdūzǐ:
"Why do you say that righteousness is internal?"
He replied:
"It is because I practice my own respect,
therefore I call it internal."
"If a man of your village is one year older than your eldest brother,
whom do you respect?"
He replied:
"I respect my brother."
"When pouring wine, whom do you serve first?"
He replied:
"I pour first for the villager."
"The one you respect is the former,
but the one you treat as older is the latter.
Indeed, it is external,
and does not come from within."
Gōngdūzǐ was unable to answer,
and told Mèngzǐ about it.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Ask him: 'Do you respect your uncle,
or do you respect your younger brother?'
He will say:
'I respect my uncle.'
Then say:
'If your younger brother is personating the deceased ancestor,
then whom do you respect?'
He will say:
'I respect my younger brother.'
You should then say:
'Where is your respect for your uncle?'
He will say:
'It is because of the position he occupies.'
You should likewise say:
'It is because of the position he occupies.
Ordinary respect is due to my brother,
but temporary respect is due to the villager.'"
Jìzǐ heard this and said:
"When one respects the uncle, one respects him;
when one respects the younger brother, one respects him.
Indeed, it is external,
and does not come from within."
Gōngdūzǐ said:
"In winter we drink hot water,
in summer we drink cold water.
Does it then mean that eating and drinking are also external?"
11.6 Gōngdūzǐ said:
"Gàozǐ says:
'Human nature is neither good nor not-good.'
Some say:
'Human nature can be made to be good,
and it can be made to be not-good.
Therefore, when Wén and Wǔ arose,
the people loved what was good;
when Yōu and Lì arose,
the people loved violence.'
Some say:
'There are those whose nature is good,
and there are those whose nature is not-good.
Therefore, with Yáo as ruler, there was Xiàng;
with Gǔsǒu as father, there was Shùn;
and with Zhòu as their brother's son,
as well as their ruler,
there were Wēizǐ Qǐ and Prince Bǐgān.'
Now you say, 'Human nature is good.'
Are all those other views then wrong?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"If one refers to their genuine feelings,
they are capable of doing good.
This is what I mean by saying they are good.
As for doing what is not good,
it is not the fault of their natural endowment."
The feeling of compassion,
everyone has it;
the feeling of shame and dislike,
everyone has it;
the feeling of respect and reverence,
everyone has it;
the feeling of right and wrong,
everyone has it.
The feeling of compassion
is benevolence;
the feeling of shame and dislike
is righteousness;
the feeling of respect and reverence
is propriety;
the feeling of right and wrong
is wisdom.
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom
are not infused into us from without;
we inherently possess them,
only we do not reflect upon them.
Hence it is said,
"Seek and you will find it;
neglect and you will lose it."
That some differ from others by twice, five times, or an incalculable amount,
is because they cannot fully develop their natural talents.
The *Shī* says:
"Heaven gave birth to the multitudes of people,
where there are things, there are principles.
The people hold onto their constant nature,
and they love this admirable virtue."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The author of this poem
must indeed have known the Way!
Therefore, where there are things, there must be principles;
and since the people hold onto their constant nature,
they therefore love this admirable virtue."
11.7 Mèngzǐ said,
"In years of good harvest,
the young men are mostly dependable;
in years of famine,
the young men are mostly violent.
This is not because Heaven has endowed them with different natural talents,
but because of what has trapped and drowned their hearts.
Now, take barley:
sow the seeds and cover them with soil.
The ground is the same,
and the time of planting is also the same.
They grow up rapidly,
and by the summer solstice,
they are all ripe.
Although there may be differences,
these are due to the soil being fertile or barren,
the nourishment from rain and dew,
and the unevenness of human labor.
Therefore, whatever are of the same kind
are all similar to one another.
Why should we doubt this only when it comes to human beings?
The sages and we are of the same kind.
Hence Lóngzǐ said,
'If one weaves sandals without knowing the size of the feet,
I know they will not make them into baskets.'
Sandals are similar
because the feet of the world are alike.
In the relation of the mouth to flavors,
there are common preferences;
Yì Yá was simply the first to capture what our mouths prefer.
If the mouth's preference for flavors
were by nature different from other people's,
as if dogs and horses were of a different kind from us,
then why would the world
always follow Yì Yá's standards of flavor?
When it comes to flavor,
the world looks to Yì Yá;
this shows that mouths throughout the world are similar.
The same is true of the ears.
When it comes to sound,
the world looks to Shī Kuàng;
this shows that ears throughout the world are similar.
The same is true of the eyes.
When it comes to Zǐ Dū,
there is no one in the world who does not know his beauty.
Anyone who does not recognize the beauty of Zǐ Dū
must have no eyes.
Therefore it is said:
in the relation of the mouth to flavors,
there are common preferences;
in the relation of the ear to sounds,
there are common hearings;
in the relation of the eye to beauty,
there are common appreciations of beauty.
When it comes to the heart,
is it the only thing that has no common ground?
What is it that hearts have in common?
What is it?
It is principle
and righteousness.
The sages were simply the first to obtain
what our hearts have in common.
Therefore, principle and righteousness please our hearts,
just as fine meats please our mouths."
11.8 Mèngzǐ said,
"The trees of Niúshān were once beautiful.
But because it lies on the borders of a large state,
axes and hatchets have chopped them down.
Can they remain beautiful?
Yet, with the rest they get day and night,
and the moisture of rain and dew,
it is not that there are no new shoots growing.
But then cattle and sheep come and graze on them,
and this is why the mountain looks so bald.
People seeing its baldness
assume that trees never grew there.
But is this indeed the nature of the mountain?
Even so, in what exists in humans,
can there be a lack of the heart of benevolence and righteousness?
The way they lose their good conscience
is just like the axes and hatchets to the trees.
Chopped down day after day,
can it remain beautiful?
With the rest they get day and night,
and the Qi of the dawn,
their likes and dislikes are slightly close to those of other people,
but what they do during the day
fetters and destroys it.
When this fettering is repeated,
the Qi of the night is not sufficient to preserve it.
When the Qi of the night is not sufficient to preserve it,
then they are not far removed from beasts.
Other people, seeing them behave like beasts,
assume that they never had any talent.
But is this indeed the true nature of a human being?
Therefore, if it receives its proper nourishment,
there is nothing that will not grow;
if it loses its proper nourishment,
there is nothing that will not decay.
Kǒngzǐ said,
'Hold fast to it, and it remains;
let go of it, and it is lost.
It goes out and comes in at no set time,
and no one knows where it goes.'
Was it not the heart that he was referring to?"
11.9 Mèngzǐ said,
"Do not be surprised at the King's lack of wisdom.
Even if there is a plant in the world that is easiest to grow,
if you expose it to warmth for one day
and expose it to cold for ten days,
it will never be able to grow.
My audiences with him are rare,
and when I withdraw,
those who chill him arrive.
What can I do to help his sprouts grow?
Now, the art of go
is but a minor art;
yet if one does not focus one's mind and dedicate one's will to it,
one cannot master it.
Yì Qiū
is the best go player in the whole state.
Suppose Yì Qiū is teaching two people to play go:
one of them focuses his mind and dedicates his will,
listening only to Yì Qiū;
the other, though he listens,
has his mind set on a wild swan that is about to arrive,
and thinks of drawing his bow and arrow to shoot it.
Although he learns together with the other,
he will not be as good as him.
Is this because his intelligence is inferior?
The answer is,
'No, it is not.'"
11.10 Mèngzǐ said,
"Fish
is what I desire;
bear's paw
is also what I desire.
If I cannot have both,
I will let go of fish and choose bear's paw.
Life
is also what I desire;
righteousness
is also what I desire.
If I cannot have both,
I will let go of life and choose righteousness.
Life is indeed what I desire,
but there is something I desire more than life;
therefore, I will not obtain it by improper means.
Death is indeed what I dislike,
but there is something I dislike more than death;
therefore, there are dangers I will not avoid.
If what people desire most were nothing other than life,
then whatever means could preserve life,
why would they not use them?
If what people dislike most were nothing other than death,
then whatever means could avoid danger,
why would they not do them?
If by doing this one can survive,
yet there are times when one does not use it;
if by doing this one can avoid disaster,
yet there are times when one does not do it.
Therefore, there are things that one desires more than life,
and there are things that one dislikes more than death.
It is not only the worthy who have this heart;
all people have it,
but the worthy are able to avoid losing it.
A basket of food,
a bowl of soup—
if one gets it, one lives;
if one does not get it, one dies.
Yet if it is offered with a shout,
even a traveler on the road will not accept it;
if it is offered after being trampled on,
even a beggar will look down upon it.
But when it comes to ten thousand *zhōng* of grain, one accepts them without distinguishing whether it conforms to propriety and righteousness.
What do ten thousand *zhōng* add to me?
Is it for the beauty of mansions,
the service of wives and concubines,
or because poor acquaintances of mine feel grateful to me?
Formerly, one would rather die than accept it,
but now one accepts it for the beauty of mansions;
formerly, one would rather die than accept it,
but now one accepts it for the service of wives and concubines;
formerly, one would rather die than accept it,
but now one accepts it so that poor acquaintances of mine will feel grateful to me.
Can this not also be stopped?
This is what is called losing one's original heart."
11.11 Mèngzǐ said:
"Benevolence
is the human heart;
righteousness
is the human path.
To abandon one's path
and not follow it,
and to lose one's heart
and not know to seek it—
how lamentable!
When people have chickens or dogs that stray,
they know to seek them;
but when they have a lost heart,
they do not know to seek it.
The way of learning is none other than
seeking one's lost heart."
11.12 Mèngzǐ said:
"Suppose there is a person whose ring finger
is bent and cannot straighten,
which is neither painful nor injurious to his affairs.
If there were someone who could straighten it,
he would not consider the road to Qín or Chǔ too far,
because his finger is not like those of other people.
When his finger is not like those of other people,
he knows to dislike it;
but when his heart is not like those of other people,
he does not know to dislike it.
This is what is called not understanding the relative importance of things."
11.13 Mèngzǐ said:
"If there are paulownia and catalpa trees of one or two hand-spans in circumference,
if anyone wishes them to grow,
they all know how to cultivate them.
Yet when it comes to their own persons,
they do not know how to cultivate them.
Is it that they love their own persons less than paulownia and catalpa trees?
It is because they do not reflect upon it deeply."
11.14 Mèngzǐ said:
"A person in relation to their own body
loves all parts of it.
Loving all parts of it,
they nurture all parts of it.
There is not an inch of skin they do not love,
so there is not an inch of skin they do not nurture.
To examine whether they are good or bad,
how can there be any other way?
It is simply by looking at what they choose to prioritize in themselves.
In the body, there are parts that are noble and parts that are base,
parts that are small and parts that are great.
Do not harm the great for the sake of the small;
do not harm the noble for the sake of the base.
He who nurtures the small parts is a small man;
he who nurtures the great parts is a great man.
Suppose there is a gardener
who abandons his parasol trees and catalpas
to cultivate sour jujube shrubs;
he would be considered a worthless gardener.
He who nurtures one of his fingers
but loses his shoulders and back
without realizing it
is a muddled person.
A person who cares only for eating and drinking
is despised by others
because he nurtures the small
and loses the great.
If a person who cares only for eating and drinking
does not lose anything else,
then his mouth and stomach
are surely not merely an inch of skin, are they?"
11.15 Gōngdūzǐ asked:
"Equally being human beings,
some are great men,
and some are small men.
Why is this?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who follow their greater parts
become great men;
those who follow their smaller parts
become small men."
The other said:
"Equally being human beings,
why do some follow their greater parts,
and some follow their smaller parts,
why is this?"
He said:
"The organs of hearing and sight do not think,
and are obscured by external things.
When external things interact with external things,
they simply lead them away.
The organ of the heart thinks.
By thinking, it attains it;
by not thinking, it does not attain it.
This is what Heaven has given us.
If one first establishes the greater part,
then the smaller parts cannot snatch it away.
This is simply what makes a great man."
11.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"There is nobility of Heaven,
and there is nobility of man.
Benevolence, righteousness,
loyalty, and trustworthiness,
and untiring delight in goodness—
this is the nobility of Heaven;
dukes, ministers, and great officers—
this is the nobility of man.
The ancients
cultivated their nobility of Heaven,
and the nobility of man followed.
The people of today
cultivate their nobility of Heaven in order to seek the nobility of man;
and once they obtain the nobility of man, they abandon their nobility of Heaven.
This is the height of delusion,
and in the end they must surely lose everything."
11.17 Mèngzǐ said:
"The desire to be noble
is common to all human hearts.
Every person has what is noble within themselves,
they simply do not think about it.
What other people make noble
is not true nobility.
He whom Zhào Mèng makes noble,
Zhào Mèng can also make base.
*Shī* says:
'We are already drunk with wine,
we are already filled with virtue.'
This means being filled with benevolence and righteousness,
and therefore one does not covet the taste of others' rich food and fine grains;
a good reputation and broad praise are bestowed on one's person,
and therefore one does not covet others' embroidered garments."
11.18 Mèngzǐ said:
"Benevolence overcomes non-benevolence
just as water overcomes fire.
Those who practice benevolence today
are like someone trying to extinguish a wagon-load of burning firewood with a single cup of water.
When it is not extinguished,
they say that water cannot overcome fire.
This moreover aligns them with those who are extremely non-benevolent,
and in the end they must surely lose everything."
11.19 Mèngzǐ said:
"The five grains
are the finest of seeds;
but if they do not ripen,
they are not as good as wild tares and weeds.
Benevolence likewise lies simply in bringing it to ripeness."
11.20 Mèngzǐ said:
"When Yì taught people archery,
he always set his mind on drawing the bow to the full;
those who learn must also set their minds on drawing it to the full.
A master craftsman, in teaching people,
must use the compass and square;
those who learn must also use the compass and square."
12.1 A person of Rèn asked Wūlúzǐ, saying:
"Which is more important, propriety or food?"
He replied:
"Propriety is more important."
"Which is more important, sex or propriety?"
He replied:
"Propriety is more important."
The man said:
"If one eats according to propriety, one will starve to death;
if one eats without propriety, one will get food.
Must one still follow propriety?
If one performs the ritual of personally welcoming the bride, one will not get a wife;
if one does not personally welcome her, one will get a wife.
Must one still personally welcome her?"
Wūlúzǐ could not reply.
On the next day, he went to Zōu
and told Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said,
"What difficulty is there in answering this?
If you do not measure them at the base,
but only align their tops,
a block of wood an inch square can be made to look higher than a high tower.
When we say gold is heavier than feathers,
how could it refer to a single gold clasp
compared with a cartload of feathers?
If you take the most important aspect of food
and compare it with the least important aspect of ritual propriety,
how is it not just that food is more important?
If you take the most important aspect of sex
and compare it with the least important aspect of ritual propriety,
how is it not just that sex is more important?
Go back and answer him, saying,
'If you twist your elder brother's arm to snatch his food,
you will get food;
if you do not twist it,
you will not get food—
will you then twist it?
If you climb over your neighbor's wall and drag away his virgin daughter,
you will get a wife;
if you do not drag her away,
you will not get a wife—
will you then drag her away?'"
12.2 Cáo Jiāo asked,
"Can all people become Yáo and Shùn?
Is this true?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Yes."
"I, Jiāo, have heard that King Wén was ten feet tall,
and Tāng was nine feet tall.
Now I, Jiāo, am over nine feet four inches tall,
yet I do nothing but eat grain.
What must I do to be like them?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"What difficulty is there in this?
It is simply a matter of doing it.
Suppose there is a person here
whose strength cannot lift a single young chicken;
then he is a person of no strength.
But if today he says he can lift a hundred jūn,
then he is a person of strength.
Therefore, if one lifts the weight that Wū Huò lifted,
then one is simply a Wū Huò.
Why should a person worry about not being able to lift it?
It is just that they do not do it.
To walk slowly behind one's elders
is called being brotherly;
to walk quickly ahead of one's elders
is called being unbrotherly.
Now, walking slowly—
is that something a person cannot do?
It is just something they do not do.
The Way of Yáo and Shùn
is nothing more than filial piety and brotherly respect.
If you wear the clothes of Yáo,
recite the words of Yáo,
perform the deeds of Yáo,
you are simply a Yáo.
If you wear the clothes of Jié,
recite the words of Jié,
perform the deeds of Jié,
you are simply a Jié."
Cáo Jiāo said,
"I have obtained an audience with the ruler of Zōu,
and he may provide me with lodging.
I wish to remain and receive instruction at your gate."
Mèngzǐ said,
"The Way is like a great highway;
how is it difficult to know?
The trouble with people is simply that they do not seek it.
Go back and seek it,
and you will find teachers in abundance."
12.3 Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"Gāo Zǐ says,
'The "Xiǎo Biàn"
is the poem of a petty man.'"
Mèngzǐ asked,
"Why does he say so?"
Gōngsūn Chǒu replied,
"Because of its resentment."
Mèngzǐ said,
"How narrow-minded
old Gāo is in his interpretation of poetry!
Suppose there is a person here:
if a person of Yuè draws his bow and shoots at him,
he may talk and laugh while telling others about it;
for no other reason than
that the shooter is distant from him.
If his own brother draws his bow and shoots at him,
then he will weep and cry while telling others about it;
for no other reason than
that the shooter is close to him.
The resentment in "Xiǎo Biàn"
arises from affection for parents.
Affection for parents
is humaneness.
How narrow-minded indeed
is old Gāo in his interpretation of poetry!"
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"Why is there no resentment in 'Kǎi Fēng'?"
Mèngzǐ replied,
"'Kǎi Fēng'
deals with a minor fault of the parent.
'Xiǎo Biàn'
deals with a major fault of the parent.
To feel no resentment when a parent's fault is major
is to become even more distant;
to feel resentment when a parent's fault is minor
is to be excessively irritable.
To become more distant
is unfilial;
to be excessively irritable
is also unfilial.
Kǒngzǐ said,
'Shùn was indeed the paragon of filiality;
even at fifty, he still yearned for his parents.'"
12.4 Sòng Kēng was going to Chǔ,
and Mèngzǐ met him at Shíqiū.
Mèngzǐ asked,
"Where are you going, sir?"
Sòng Kēng replied,
"I have heard that Qín and Chǔ are raising troops against each other.
I am going to see the King of Chǔ
to persuade him to cease hostilities.
If the King of Chǔ is not pleased,
I am going to see the King of Qín
to persuade him to cease hostilities.
I shall surely find favor with one of these two kings."
Mèngzǐ said,
"I, Kē, beg not to ask for details,
but I would like to hear the main point.
How are you going to persuade them?"
Sòng Kēng replied,
"I am going to explain to them how unprofitable it is."
Mèngzǐ said,
"Your intention, sir, is indeed great,
but your slogan is unacceptable.
If you, sir, use profit to persuade the kings of Qín and Chǔ,
and the kings of Qín and Chǔ are pleased with profit
and so disband their armies,
then the soldiers of the three armies will rejoice in disbanding
and find pleasure in profit.
If ministers
cherish profit in serving their ruler,
if sons
cherish profit in serving their father,
if younger brothers
cherish profit in serving their elder brothers,
then rulers and ministers,
fathers and sons, and brothers will in the end abandon benevolence and righteousness,
and interact with one another solely out of a cherish of profit.
Under such circumstances, that a state should not perish
is something that has never happened.
But if you, sir, use benevolence and righteousness to persuade the kings of Qín and Chǔ,
and the kings of Qín and Chǔ are pleased with benevolence and righteousness
and so disband their armies,
then the soldiers of the three armies will rejoice in disbanding
and find pleasure in benevolence and righteousness.
If ministers
cherish benevolence and righteousness in serving their ruler,
if sons
cherish benevolence and righteousness in serving their father,
if younger brothers
cherish benevolence and righteousness in serving their elder brothers,
then rulers and ministers,
fathers and sons,
and brothers will abandon profit
and interact with one another solely out of a cherish of benevolence and righteousness.
Under such circumstances, that they should not bring true kingship to the world
is something that has never happened.
Why must you speak of profit?"
12.5 When Mèngzǐ was living in Zōu,
Jì Rèn was acting as regent in Rèn.
He sent gifts to cultivate a friendship;
Mèngzǐ accepted them but did not return the courtesy.
When Mèngzǐ was staying in Pínglù,
Chǔ Zǐ was the Prime Minister of Qí.
He sent gifts to cultivate a friendship;
Mèngzǐ accepted them but did not return the courtesy.
Later on, Mèngzǐ went from Zōu to Rèn,
and went to see Jì Zǐ.
But when he went from Pínglù to Qí,
he did not go to see Chǔ Zǐ.
Wūlú Zǐ was pleased and said,
"I, Lián, have found an opportunity to ask a question!"
He asked,
"When you went to Rèn, Master, you saw Jì Zǐ;
when you went to Qí, you did not see Chǔ Zǐ.
Was it because the latter is the Prime Minister?"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"No.
The *Shū* says,
'In presenting offerings, there are many rituals.
If the rituals do not match the gifts,
it is called a failure to offer,
because the mind is not directed toward the offering.'
This is because it does not constitute a true offering."
Wūlúzǐ was pleased.
Someone asked him about it.
Wūlúzǐ said,
"Jìzǐ had no way of going to Zōu,
but Chǔzǐ had a way of going to Pínglù."
12.6 Chúnyú Kūn said,
"One who puts reputation and reality first
acts for others;
one who puts reputation and reality last
acts for himself.
You, Master, were among the three highest ministers,
yet before your reputation and reality could influence
those above or below, you departed.
Is a benevolent person naturally like this?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"To dwell in a low position,
and refuse to serve the unworthy with one's worthiness,
was the way of Bóyí;
to go five times to Tāng
and five times to Jié
was the way of Yī Yǐn;
not to detest a corrupt ruler
and not to decline a minor office
was the way of Liǔxià Huì.
These three gentlemen followed different paths,
but their ultimate aim was one.
What was that one aim?
I say:
benevolence.
A gentleman seeks only benevolence.
Why must they be identical?"
(Chúnyú Kūn) said,
"In the time of Duke Mù of Lǔ,
Gōngyízǐ ran the government,
and Zǐliǔ and Zǐsī were ministers,
yet the diminution of Lǔ became even more severe.
If this is so, then worthy men are of no benefit to a state!"
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"Yú did not employ Bǎilǐ Xī and perished;
Duke Mù of Qín employed him and became hegemon.
If one does not employ the worthy, one perishes;
how could one merely suffer diminution?"
(Chúnyú Kūn) said,
"In the past,
Wáng Bào lived by the Qí River,
and the people of Héxī became skilled in singing;
Mián Jū lived in Gāotáng,
and the people of western Qí became skilled in singing;
the wives of Huá Zhōu and Qǐ Liáng
wailed so well for their husbands
that they changed the customs of the state.
When something exists within,
it must manifest without.
Performing a task
without achieving its effect—
I, Kūn, have never seen such a thing.
Therefore, there are no worthy men;
if there were, I, Kūn, would surely recognize them."
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"When Kǒngzǐ was the Minister of Justice of Lǔ,
his advice was not followed.
He participated in the sacrifice,
but the sacrificial meat was not sent to him.
He then departed without even taking off his ceremonial cap.
Those who did not understand thought he left because of the meat;
those who understood thought he left because of the breach of ritual.
But Kǒngzǐ actually wished to depart on account of a minor offense,
rather than leaving without a pretext.
What a gentleman does
is indeed not understood by the multitude."
12.7 Mèngzǐ said,
"The Five Hegemons
were sinners against the Three Kings.
The feudal lords of today
are sinners against the Five Hegemons.
The great officers of today
are sinners against the feudal lords of today.
When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords, it is called 'a tour of inspection.'
When the feudal lords present themselves to the Son of Heaven, it is called 'reporting on office.'
In the spring, he inspects the plowing and supplies what is lacking;
in the autumn, he inspects the harvest and assists those who have insufficient.
Upon entering a territory,
if the land is reclaimed,
the fields well-cultivated,
the aged cared for, the worthy honored,
and outstanding talents in office,
then there is a reward;
the reward is given in land.
Upon entering a territory,
if the land is overgrown with weeds,
the aged neglected, the worthy lost,
and rapacious officials in office,
then there is a reprimand.
If a lord fails to appear once at court,
his rank is lowered.
If he fails to appear twice,
his land is reduced.
If he fails to appear three times,
the six armies are moved against him.
Thus, the Son of Heaven punishes by decree but does not wage war;
the feudal lords wage war but do not punish by decree.
The Five Hegemons
dragged other feudal lords along to wage war against other feudal lords.
Therefore it is said,
'The Five Hegemons
were sinners against the Three Kings.'
Of the Five Hegemons,
Duke Huán was the most illustrious.
At the covenant of Kuíqiū,
the feudal lords bound the sacrificial animal and placed the covenant text upon it, but did not smear its blood on their lips.
The first decree said:
'Punish the unfilial;
do not change the designated heir;
do not make a concubine a wife.'
The second decree said:
'Honor the worthy and nurture the talented,
so as to manifest those of virtue.'
The third decree said:
'Respect the aged and cherish the young;
do not forget guests and travelers.'
The fourth decree said:
'Officers shall not hold hereditary offices;
administrative duties shall not be held concurrently;
in selecting officers, the right persons must be secured;
do not execute great officers on your own authority.'
The fifth decree said:
'Do not make crooked dikes;
do not block the sale of grain;
do not make enfeoffments without reporting them.'
It concluded,
'All of us who join in this covenant,
after this covenant is made,
pledge to return to friendly relations.'
The feudal lords of today
violate all five of these prohibitions.
Therefore it is said,
'The feudal lords of today
are sinners against the Five Hegemons.'
Encouraging a ruler's evil
is a lesser offense;
anticipating and pandering to a ruler's evil
is a greater offense.
The great officers of today all pander to their rulers' evil.
Therefore it is said,
'The great officers of today
are sinners against the feudal lords of today.'
12.8 Lǔ wished to make Shènzǐ a general.
Mèngzǐ said,
"To employ the people in war without instructing them
is called ruining the people.
One who ruins the people
would not have been tolerated in the era of Yáo and Shùn.
Even if, in a single battle, you defeat Qí
and consequently gain Nányáng,
it is still impermissible."
Shènzǐ suddenly became displeased and said,
"This is something that I, Huálí, do not understand."
(Mèngzǐ) said,
"I will tell you clearly.
The territory of the Son of Heaven is one thousand lǐ square;
if it were not one thousand lǐ,
it would not be sufficient to receive the feudal lords.
The territory of a feudal lord is one hundred lǐ square;
if it were not one hundred lǐ,
it would not be sufficient to preserve the ritual archives of the ancestral temple.
When Zhōugōng was enfeoffed in Lǔ,
his territory was one hundred lǐ square;
it was not that the land was insufficient,
but he was restricted to one hundred lǐ.
When Tàigōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
his territory was also one hundred lǐ square;
it was not that the land was insufficient,
but he was restricted to one hundred lǐ.
Now Lǔ is five times one hundred lǐ square.
If a true King were to arise,
do you think Lǔ would have its territory reduced
or increased?
Merely taking from one to give to another
is something a benevolent person would not do,
how much less killing people to seek it!
In serving his ruler,
a gentleman must strive to lead his ruler onto the right path,
setting his mind only on benevolence."
12.9 Mèngzǐ said,
"Those who serve rulers today
all say,
'I can open up territories for my ruler
and fill his treasuries.'
Those who are called 'excellent ministers' today
are what in ancient times were called 'plunderers of the people.'"
If a ruler is not directed toward the Way
and does not set his mind on benevolence,
yet one seeks to enrich him,
this is to enrich a Jié.
"I can form alliances with other states for my ruler,
and in war we are sure to win."
Those who are called "good ministers" today
were called "plunderers of the people" in ancient times.
If a ruler is not directed toward the Way,
and does not set his mind on benevolence,
yet one seeks to fight violently for him,
this is to assist a Jié.
Following today's way
without changing today's customs,
even if you gave them the empire,
they could not hold it for a single morning."
12.10 Bái Guī said,
"I wish to take a tax of one in twenty;
how would that be?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Your way
is the way of the Mó.
In a state of ten thousand households,
if there were only one potter, would that do?"
He said,
"No,
there would not be enough utensils for use."
Mèngzǐ said,
"Now, in the territory of the Mó,
the five grains do not grow;
only millet grows.
They have no city walls,
palaces,
ancestral temples,
or ritual ceremonies.
They have no exchange of gifts or feasts among feudal lords,
nor do they have various officials and bureaucrats.
Therefore, taking one in twenty is sufficient for them.
But now, living in the Middle Kingdom,
to discard human relations
and do away with superior men—
how could that be possible?
If potters are too few,
a state cannot be run;
how much less so if there are no superior men?
Those who want to make taxes lighter than the way of Yáo and Shùn
are either major Mó or minor Mó.
Those who want to make them heavier than the way of Yáo and Shùn
are either major Jié or minor Jié."
12.11 Bái Guī said,
"My management of the waters is superior to that of Yǔ."
Mèngzǐ said,
"You are mistaken.
Yǔ's management of the waters
followed the natural course of water.
Therefore, Yǔ used the four seas as his drainage basins.
Now you, sir, use your neighboring states as drainage basins.
When water flows in a reverse direction,
it is called overflowing water.
Overflowing water
is a flood,
which is detested by benevolent men.
You, sir, are mistaken."
12.12 Mèngzǐ said,
"If a gentleman is not trustworthy,
what can he hold onto?"
12.13 Lǔ wished to make Yuèzhèngzǐ the administrator of government.
Mèngzǐ said,
"When I heard of it,
I was so happy I could not sleep."
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"Is Yuèzhèngzǐ strong-willed?"
He replied,
"No."
"Is he wise and deliberative?"
He replied,
"No."
"Has he wide learning and knowledge?"
He replied,
"No."
"Then why are you so happy you cannot sleep?"
He replied,
"Because as a person, he loves what is good."
"Is loving what is good sufficient?"
He replied,
"Loving what is good is more than sufficient for the whole empire,
how much more so for the state of Lǔ?
If a ruler truly loves what is good,
then from within the four seas,
everyone will make light of traveling a thousand li
to come and tell him of what is good.
But if he does not love what is good,
then people will say with self-complacency,
'I already know it.'
That self-complacent tone of voice and look on the face
will keep people a thousand li away.
