When scholars stay a thousand li away,
then slanderers, flatterers, and sycophants will arrive.
Dwelling with slanderers, flatterers, and sycophants,
even if one wishes to govern the state well,
can it be achieved?"
12.14 Chénzǐ asked,
"Under what circumstances did the ancient superior men
take office?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"There were three cases in which they took office,
and three in which they left it.
When they were welcomed with the utmost respect and courtesy,
and it was indicated that their words would be put into practice,
they took office.
Although the respectful courtesy had not declined,
if their words were not put into practice,
they left office.
Next,
even though their words were not yet put into practice,
if they were welcomed with the utmost respect and courtesy,
they took office.
When the respectful courtesy declined,
they left office.
In the lowest case,
if they had no food in the morning
and no food in the evening,
and were so starved they could not go out of their door,
and the ruler, hearing of this,
said,
'I was unable to practice his Way in great matters,
nor could I follow his words,
and now to let him starve in my territory—
I am ashamed of this.'
If the ruler came to their relief,
they could accept it,
but only to escape death."
12.15 Mèngzǐ said,
"Shùn rose from among the channeled fields;
Fù Yuè was raised from his building frames and earth-beaters;
Jiāo Gé was raised from fish and salt;
Guǎn Yíwú was raised from the prison official;
Sūnshū Áo was raised from the seashore;
Bǎilǐ Xī was raised from the marketplace.
Therefore, when Heaven is about to place a great responsibility on a person,
it must first embitter his heart and mind,
toil his muscles and bones,
starve his body and skin,
subject his person to poverty,
and disrupt and throw into disarray his actions.
By these means, it stimulates his mind, hardens his nature,
and increases his abilities.
A person constantly makes mistakes
and only then can reform;
he is distressed in his mind
and frustrated in his thoughts,
and only then does he rise up;
it is manifested in his countenance
and expressed in his voice,
and only then do others understand him.
If domestically a state has no law-abiding families or assisting scholars,
and externally has no hostile states or foreign threats,
that state will constantly face ruin.
From this we know that life springs from sorrow and calamity,
and death from ease and pleasure."
12.16 Mèngzǐ said,
"There are many methods of teaching.
My refusing to teach someone
is itself a way of teaching him."
13.1 Mèngzǐ said,
"He who exhausts his mind
knows his nature.
Knowing his nature,
he knows Heaven.
To preserve one's mind
and nourish one's nature
is the way to serve Heaven.
Whether a premature death or long life, he does not doubt,
but cultivates himself and waits for it—
this is how he establishes his destiny."
13.2 Mèngzǐ said,
"There is nothing that is not destiny,
but one should submissively receive what is correct.
Therefore, he who knows destiny
does not stand under a precariously leaning wall.
He who dies after exhausting his way
dies a correct destiny.
He who dies in fetters and handcuffs
does not die a correct destiny."
13.3 Mèngzǐ said,
"Seek and you shall find it,
neglect and you shall lose it;
in this case, seeking is beneficial to finding,
because what we seek is within ourselves.
Seeking it according to the proper way,
but finding it depends on destiny;
in this case, seeking is of no benefit to finding,
because what we seek is external to ourselves."
13.4 Mèngzǐ said,
"All things are complete within me.
To turn inward and find oneself sincere,
there is no greater joy than this.
To act with vigorous effort at empathy,
there is no closer way to seek benevolence."
13.5 Mèngzǐ said:
"To act in accordance with it without being conscious of it,
to practice it habitually without examining it,
and to follow it all one's life without knowing its Way—
such are the multitude."
13.6 Mèngzǐ said:
"A person cannot be without shame.
If one is ashamed of having no shame,
then one will be free from shame."
13.7 Mèngzǐ said:
"Shame is of great importance to a person.
Those who engage in clever schemes and transformations
have no use for shame.
If one is not ashamed of not being equal to others,
how can one ever be equal to others?"
13.8 Mèngzǐ said:
"The worthy kings of antiquity
loved goodness and forgot their own power and status.
How could the worthy scholars of antiquity
have been any different?
They delighted in their own Way
and forgot the power and status of others.
Therefore, if kings and dukes did not show them the utmost respect and observe full courtesy,
they could not obtain frequent interviews with them.
If even seeing them could not be frequent,
how much less could they make them their ministers?"
13.9 Mèngzǐ said to Sòng Gōujiàn:
"Do you like traveling to counsel rulers?
Let me speak to you about such traveling.
If people understand you, be content and easy;
if people do not understand you, be content and easy as well."
Sòng Gōujiàn asked:
"How can one be content and easy?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"Honor virtue and delight in righteousness,
and then you can be content and easy.
Therefore, when in adversity, a scholar does not lose righteousness;
when in prosperity, he does not depart from the Way.
Because in adversity he does not lose righteousness,
the scholar preserves his self-possession;
because in prosperity he does not depart from the Way,
the expectations of the people are not disappointed.
When the ancients
achieved their ambitions,
their bounty was extended to the people;
when they did not achieve their ambitions,
they cultivated themselves and became manifest to the world.
In adversity, they perfected their own personal goodness;
in prosperity, they shared their goodness with the whole world."
13.10 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who wait for a Wén Wáng to arise before they arouse themselves
are ordinary people.
As for outstanding and heroic scholars,
they arouse themselves even without a Wén Wáng."
13.11 Mèngzǐ said:
"If one is enriched with the wealth of the families of Hán and Wèi,
yet still looks upon oneself as unsatisfied,
then one far surpasses ordinary men."
13.12 Mèngzǐ said:
"If one employs the people with a view to their ease,
though they toil, they will not complain.
If one puts the people to death with a view to preserving their lives,
though they die, they will not feel resentment toward those who kill them."
13.13 Mèngzǐ said:
"The people of a hegemon
are happy and cheerful;
the people of a true king
are self-possessed and vast-minded.
They are put to death without resentment,
and benefited without acknowledging the favor.
Every day they move toward goodness,
without knowing who it is that makes them do so.
Wherever a superior person passes, transformation occurs;
wherever he abides, his influence is divine,
flowing in harmony with Heaven and Earth above and below.
How can this be said to be merely a minor benefit?"
13.14 Mèngzǐ said:
"Benevolent words
do not sink so deeply into people as a reputation for benevolence.
Good government
does not win the people so well as good instruction.
With good government, the people fear it;
with good instruction, the people love it.
Good government gains the people's wealth;
good instruction gains the people's hearts."
13.15 Mèngzǐ said:
"What people are capable of doing without having learned it
is their intuitive ability;
what they know without having to reflect on it
is their intuitive knowledge.
Among children carried in arms,
there are none who do not know how to love their parents;
when they grow up,
there are none who do not know how to respect their elder brothers.
Loving one's parents
is benevolence;
respecting one's elders
is righteousness.
There is no other reason for these:
they extend throughout the whole world."
13.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"When Shùn lived deep in the mountains,
dwelling among trees and stones,
and wandering with deer and swine,
the way he differed from the rustic folk of the deep mountains
was very slight.
But when he heard a single good word,
or saw a single good deed,
it was like the bursting of the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers,
overflowing with a force that nothing could resist."
13.17 Mèngzǐ said:
"Do not do what you should not do;
do not desire what you should not desire.
Just be like this, and that is all."
13.18 Mèngzǐ said:
"That people possess virtue, wisdom, skill, and intelligence
is constantly due to their having lived through adversity and suffering.
The friendless minister and the concubine's son—
their keeping of their minds is always full of precaution,
and their consideration of dangers is deep.
Therefore, they succeed."
13.19 Mèngzǐ said:
"There are those who serve the ruler,
who, in serving this ruler,
aim only at pleasing and flattering him.
There are ministers who bring peace to the altars of state,
who find their pleasure in bringing peace to the altars of state.
There are the people of Heaven,
who, only when they see that their principles can be put into practice throughout the world,
go forth to practice them.
There are great men,
who rectify themselves, and thereby all things are rectified."
13.20 Mèngzǐ said:
"The superior person has three delights,
and ruling over the empire is not among them.
That his parents are both alive,
and his brothers are free from harm—
this is the first delight.
That, looking up, he has no occasion for shame before Heaven,
and, looking down, he has no occasion to blush before men—
this is the second delight.
That he gets the most talented people in the world
and educates them—
this is the third delight.
The superior person has three delights,
and ruling over the empire is not among them."
13.21 Mèngzǐ said:
"To possess a vast territory and a numerous population
is what the superior person desires,
but his delight does not consist in this.
To stand in the center of the world
and bring peace to the people within the four seas,
is what the superior person delights in,
but his true nature does not depend on this.
What belongs by nature to the superior person
is not increased by his great achievements,
nor is it diminished by his dwelling in poverty and retirement;
for his portion is fixed.
What belongs by nature to the superior person,
namely, benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, are rooted in his heart.
Their outward manifestation is
a mild harmony; they are revealed in his face,
filled in his back,
and extended to his four limbs;
the four limbs reveal them without needing words."
13.22 Mèngzǐ said:
"Bó Yí, to avoid Zhòu,
dwelt on the shores of the Northern Sea.
When he heard that Wén Wáng had arisen, he arose and
said:
'Why not go and follow him?
I have heard that Xībó well supports the aged.'
Tài Gōng, to avoid Zhòu,
dwelt on the shores of the Eastern Sea.
When he heard that Wén Wáng had arisen, he arose and
said:
'Why not go and follow him?
I have heard that Xībó well supports the aged.'
When there is one in the world who well supports the aged,
then benevolent people look to him as their refuge.
Around a homestead of five mu,
if mulberry trees are planted beneath the walls,
and women raise silkworms on them,
then the aged will have sufficient silk to wear.
If five brood hens
and two brood sows
are not allowed to miss their breeding seasons,
then the aged will have a constant supply of meat to eat.
If a hundred mu of land
is cultivated by a single husbandman,
then a family of eight mouths
will have sufficient to escape hunger.
What is meant by saying that Xībó well supported the aged is this:
he regulated their fields and homesteads,
taught them how to plant trees and raise animals,
and guided their wives and children
to support their elders."
At fifty, without silk one is not warm;
at seventy, without meat one is not full.
Being neither warm nor full
is called being cold and hungry.
That among the people of King Wén (Wén Wáng)
there were no elderly who suffered from cold and hunger,
this is what is meant."
13.23 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"If their fields are well-cultivated,
and their taxes and levies are lightened,
the people can be made rich.
If they consume food according to the seasons
and use resources according to ritual propriety,
wealth and resources will be inexhaustible.
The people cannot live without water and fire;
yet if someone knocks on another's door at dusk
to ask for water or fire,
there is no one who would refuse them,
because these things are extremely abundant.
When a sage rules the world,
he ensures that pulse and grain are as abundant as water and fire.
When pulse and grain are as abundant as water and fire,
how could there be any among the people who are not benevolent?"
13.24 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"When Confucius (Kǒngzǐ) climbed the East Mountain (Dōngshān),
he looked down on Lǔ and felt it was small;
when he climbed Mount Tài (Tàishān),
he looked down on the world and felt it was small.
Therefore, for one who has contemplated the ocean, it is difficult to be impressed by other waters;
for one who has studied at the gate of a sage, it is difficult to be satisfied by other teachings.
There is a method to contemplating water:
one must observe its ripples.
The sun and moon possess brightness;
even the smallest crevice will certainly be illuminated by them.
Flowing water, as a thing,
does not proceed until it has filled every hollow;
the gentleman’s mind, set on the Way,
does not advance until he has mastered each stage of accomplishment."
13.25 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"One who rises at cockcrow
and applies himself diligently to doing good
is of the class of Shùn;
one who rises at cockcrow
and applies himself diligently to pursuing profit
is of the class of Zhí.
If you wish to know the difference between Shùn and Zhí,
there is no other distinguishing factor
than the difference between profit and goodness."
13.26 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"Yangzi (Yángzǐ) chose 'everyone for himself.'
Even if plucking out a single hair would benefit the whole world,
he would not do it.
Mozi (Mòzǐ) practiced universal love.
Even if he had to rub himself smooth from crown to heel to benefit the world,
he would do it.
Zǐmò held to the middle course.
Holding to the middle is close to the right way.
But to hold to the middle without flexibility
is just like holding to a single extreme.
Why one dislikes holding to a single extreme
is because it ruins the Way,
elevating one thing while discarding a hundred others."
13.27 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"To the hungry, any food is sweet;
to the thirsty, any drink is sweet.
Thus they do not get the true flavor of food and drink,
because hunger and thirst distort their taste.
Is it only the mouth and belly that suffer from the distortion of hunger and thirst?
The human mind also has its distortions.
If a person can prevent the distortions of hunger and thirst from becoming distortions of the mind,
then falling short of others will not be a source of worry."
13.28 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"Liǔxià Huì would not have exchanged his integrity
for the office of the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng)."
13.29 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"An undertaking
is like digging a well.
If you dig a well to a depth of nine rèn
but do not reach the spring,
it is still just an abandoned well."
13.30 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"Yáo and Shùn
possessed it by nature;
Tāng and Wǔ
embodied it in their persons;
the Five Hegemons (Wǔbà)
feigned it.
If they feigned it for a long time without returning it,
how could anyone know they did not truly possess it?"
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"Yī Yǐn said,
'I will not be familiar with those who are not compliant.'
He banished Tàijiǎ to Tóng,
and the people were greatly pleased.
When Tàijiǎ became virtuous
and Yī Yǐn restored him,
the people were again greatly pleased.
When a virtuous man serves as a minister,
and his ruler is not virtuous,
may he indeed banish him in this way?"
Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"If he has the intention of Yī Yǐn,
then it is permissible;
but if he lacks the intention of Yī Yǐn,
then it is usurpation."
13.32 Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"The *Shījīng* (Book of Odes) says,
'He does not eat the bread of idleness.'
As for a gentleman eating without farming,
why is that?"
Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"When a gentleman resides in a state,
if the ruler employs him,
the state will be secure, wealthy, respected, and glorious;
if the young men follow him,
they will become filial, brotherly, loyal, and trustworthy.
As for 'not eating the bread of idleness,'
what could be greater than this?"
Prince Diàn (Wángzǐ Diàn) asked,
"What is the business of a scholar?"
Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"To elevate his resolve."
The prince asked,
"What does it mean to elevate one's resolve?"
Mencius replied,
"It is simply benevolence and righteousness.
To kill one innocent person
is not benevolent;
to take what is not one's own
is not righteous.
Where should one dwell?
In benevolence.
Where is the path?
In righteousness.
Dwelling in benevolence and proceeding along righteousness—
with this, the business of a great man is complete."
13.34 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"As for Zhòngzǐ, if offered the state of Qí unrighteously
he would not accept it,
and everyone believes this of him.
This is like declining a basket of food and a bowl of soup
sort of righteousness.
A person can commit no greater offense than to discard relatives,
rulers and ministers,
superiors and inferiors.
Using his small virtue
to gain trust in major matters,
how can that be acceptable?"
13.35 Táo Yìng asked,
"If Shùn were the Emperor,
Gāoyáo were the minister of justice,
and Gǔsǒu killed someone,
what would have been done?"
Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"He would simply have apprehended him."
"But then, would Shùn not have forbidden it?"
Mencius replied,
"How could Shùn have forbidden it?
Gāoyáo had received the law from a proper authority."
"Then what would Shùn have done?"
Mencius replied,
"Shùn would have viewed casting aside the empire
as if casting away a worn-out sandal.
He would have secretly taken him on his back and fled,
dwelling along the seacoast,
cheerful and happy for the rest of his life,
forgetting the empire in his joy."
13.36 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) went from Fàn to Qí.
Looking at the son of the King of Qí from a distance,
he sighed and said,
"One's position changes one's air;
one's nourishment changes one's body.
Great indeed is the influence of position!
Is he not, after all, a human being's son just like anyone else?"
Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"The prince's apartments, carriages, horses, and clothing
are mostly the same as those of other men,
yet the prince looks like that
because his position makes him so.
How much more so for one who dwells in the wide house of the world!
When the Lord of Lǔ went to Sòng,
he called out at the Diézé Gate.
The gatekeeper said,
'This is not our ruler,
yet how is it that his voice sounds so much like our ruler?'
This was due to nothing else
than that their positions were similar."
13.37 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"To feed someone without loving them
is to treat them like a pig;
to love them without respecting them
is to keep them like a domestic animal.
Reverence and respect
should exist before gifts are presented.
If there is reverence and respect without reality,
a gentleman cannot be retained by empty gestures."
13.38 Mencius (Mèngzǐ) said,
"Our physical form and appearance
are of our heavenly nature;
only a sage is able to fully realize his physical form."
13.39 King Xuān of Qí wished to shorten the period of mourning.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"To have a mourning period of one year,
is that not still better than stopping it altogether?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"This is like someone who is twisting his older brother's arm,
and you say to him,
'Just do it a little more gently.'
One should simply teach him filial piety and brotherly love, and that is all."
There was a prince whose mother died,
and his tutor requested for him a mourning period of several months.
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"How is a case like this?"
He replied,
"In this case, he wished to complete the full term but was not allowed to do so.
Even adding a single day
is better than stopping it altogether.
What I said before was referring to someone who is not forbidden to do it but still does not do it."
13.40 Mèngzǐ said,
"There are five ways in which the gentleman teaches:
there are those whom he transforms like a timely rain;
there are those whose virtue he helps to complete;
there are those whose talents he helps to develop;
there are those whose questions he answers;
and there are those who privately cultivate themselves through him.
These five
are the ways in which the gentleman teaches."
13.41 Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"The Way is indeed lofty and beautiful,
but it is as if one were ascending to heaven,
seemingly impossible to reach.
Why not make it so that it seems within reach,
so that people may strive after it daily with diligence?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"A master carpenter does not alter or discard the plumb-line for the sake of an awkward apprentice;
Yì did not change his standard for drawing the bow for the sake of an unskilled archer.
The gentleman draws the bow but does not release the arrow;
he poised himself as if about to leap.
He stands in the middle of the Way,
and those who are able follow him."
13.42 Mèngzǐ said,
"When the Way prevails in the world,
the Way follows the person;
when the Way does not prevail in the world,
the person sacrifices oneself for the Way;
I have never heard of sacrificing the Way to follow other men."
Gōngdūzǐ said,
"When Téng Gēng was studying with you,
he seemed to be someone who should be treated with courtesy,
yet you did not answer his questions.
Why was that?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"To ask questions relying on one's high rank,
relying on one's own worthiness,
relying on one's seniority,
relying on one's past merits,
or relying on old acquaintance—
these are all things to which I do not reply.
Téng Gēng was guilty of two of these."
13.44 Mèngzǐ said,
"He who stops where he ought not to stop,
will stop at nothing.
He who treats coldly those whom he ought to treat generously,
will treat everyone coldly.
He who advances eagerly,
retreats quickly."
13.45 Mèngzǐ said,
"In regard to things, the gentleman
loves them but does not show benevolence toward them;
in regard to the people,
he shows benevolence toward them but does not feel intimate affection.
He is affectionate to his parents and benevolent to the people;
he is benevolent to the people and loves things."
13.46 Mèngzǐ said,
"The wise know everything,
but they consider what is most urgent as the priority;
the benevolent love everyone,
but they consider cultivating intimacy with the worthy as their urgent task.
The wisdom of Yáo and Shùn did not extend to knowing every single thing,
because they prioritized what was most urgent;
the benevolence of Yáo and Shùn
did not extend to loving everyone individually,
because they prioritized cultivating intimacy with the worthy.
If a person cannot observe the three years of mourning,
yet is meticulous about the details of the three-month and five-month mourning periods;
if he gulps down his food and swills down his soup,
yet asks about the rule of not tearing meat with his teeth—
this is what is called not knowing what is urgent."
14.1 Mèngzǐ said,
"How unbenevolent was
King Huì of Liáng!
The benevolent person
extends his love for those he loves to those he does not love.
The unbenevolent person, on the other hand,
extends his lack of love for those he does not love to those he does love."
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"What does that mean?"
"King Huì of Liáng, for the sake of territory,
sacrificed and slaughtered his people in war.
Suffering a great defeat,
he wished to fight again;
fearing he could not win,
he therefore drove his beloved sons and younger brothers to sacrifice themselves in battle.
This is what is called
extending his lack of love for those he does not love to those he does love."
14.2 Mèngzǐ said,
"In the Spring and Autumn period, there were no righteous wars.
That one was better than this one,
indeed there were such cases.
As for 'punitive campaigns' (zhēng),
they are campaigns waged by a superior against a subordinate.
Equal states do not wage punitive campaigns against each other."
14.3 Mèngzǐ said,
"It would be better to have no Book of History
than to believe everything in it.
In the chapter 'Wǔchéng',
I accept only two or three passages.
The benevolent man has no enemy in the world.
When the most benevolent campaigned against the most unbenevolent,
how could the blood have flowed so copiously as to float the pestles?"
14.4 Mèngzǐ said,
"If someone says,
'I am skilled at arranging battle formations;
I am skilled at waging war,'
this is a great crime.
If the ruler of a state loves benevolence,
he will have no enemy in the world.
When he marched to the south, the northern Dí murmured;
when he marched to the east, the western Yí murmured,
saying,
'Why does he leave us for last?'
When King Wǔ campaigned against Yīn,
he had three hundred war-chariots
and three thousand tiger-like guards.
The King said,
'Be not afraid!
I come to bring you peace,
not to be enemies to the common people.'
Thereupon they bowed their heads to the ground, with a sound like the falling of a mountain.
'To wage a campaign' (zhēng) means to rectify (zhèng);
when everyone wishes to rectify themselves,
what need is there for war?"
14.5 Mèngzǐ said,
"A carpenter or carriage-maker
can give others the compass and the square,
but he cannot make them skillful."
14.6 Mèngzǐ said,
"When Shùn was eating parched grain and wild herbs,
he lived as if he would do so for his entire life.
Yet when he became the Emperor,
wearing fine robes,
playing the lute,
and having the two daughters of Yao
to serve him, he was as at ease as if he had always possessed these things."
14.7 Mèngzǐ said,
"From now on I know
how serious a thing it is to kill another's relatives:
if you kill another's father,
others will also kill your father;
if you kill another's older brother,
others will also kill your older brother.
In that case, although you did not kill them yourself,
it is only one step removed."
14.8 Mèngzǐ said,
"In ancient times, frontier passes were established
to guard against violence;
nowadays, passes are established
to perpetrate violence."
14.9 Mèngzǐ said,
"If you do not practice the Way yourself,
it will not be practiced even by your wife and children.
If you command others not in accordance with the Way,
you will not be able to get even your wife and children to follow your commands."
14.10 Mèngzǐ said,
"One who has laid up a rich store of material goods
cannot be killed even in years of famine;
one who has laid up a rich store of virtue
cannot be corrupted even in a degenerate age."
14.11 Mèngzǐ said,
"A person who loves fame
may be able to yield a state of a thousand chariots;
but if he is not truly that kind of person,
his true feelings will show on his face over a basket of rice or a bowl of soup."
14.12 Mèngzǐ said,
"If a state does not trust the benevolent and worthy,
it will become empty and hollow;
without ritual propriety and righteousness,
the relationship between superiors and inferiors will fall into chaos;
without proper administration,
there will not be sufficient wealth and resources for use."
14.13 Mèngzǐ said,
"There have been cases of those who were unbenevolent gaining a state;
indeed there have.
But of those who were unbenevolent gaining the empire,
there has never been such a thing."
14.14 Mèngzǐ said:
"The people are of the supreme importance,
the altars of the soil and grain come next,
and the ruler is the least important.
Therefore, winning the favor of the common people is the way to become the Son of Heaven;
winning the favor of the Son of Heaven is the way to become a feudal lord;
winning the favor of a feudal lord is the way to become a grand officer.
When a feudal lord endangers the altars of the soil and grain,
he should be replaced.
When the sacrificial beasts are sleek,
the millet in the vessels is pure,
and sacrifices are offered in due season,
yet there is still drought or flood,
then the altars of the soil and grain should be replaced."
14.15 Mèngzǐ said:
"Sages are
teachers of a hundred generations;
Bóyí and Liǔxià Huì are examples of this.
Therefore, when people hear of the character of Bóyí,
the corrupt become honest,
and the weak-willed establish their resolve.
When they hear of the character of Liǔxià Huì,
the narrow-minded become generous,
and the mean become broad-minded.
They exerted themselves a hundred generations ago,
and a hundred generations later, all who hear of them are inspired to rise.
Could anyone but a sage do this?
How much more so for those who personally received their warmth?"
14.16 Mèngzǐ said:
"Benevolence
is humanity.
When spoken of together,
they constitute the Way."
14.17 Mèngzǐ said:
"When Kǒngzǐ left Lǔ,
he said:
'Slowly, slowly do I go;
this is the proper way to leave the state of one's parents.'
When he left Qí,
he took the washed rice out of the water and immediately set off;
this is the proper way to leave another state."
14.18 Mèngzǐ said:
"The distress of the superior man between Chén and Cài
was because he had no relations with either the rulers above or the people below."
14.19 Hé Jī said:
"I, Jī, am greatly slandered by many mouths."
Mèngzǐ said:
"No harm.
A scholar is hated for having many mouths talking about him.
The *Shī* says:
'My heart is full of anxious sorrow,
and I am hated by the crowd of small men.'
This refers to Kǒngzǐ.
'Though he did not eliminate their anger,
neither did he let his own reputation fail.'
This refers to King Wén."
14.20 Mèngzǐ said:
"The worthy, using their own clarity,
make others clear-sighted;
today, people use their own obscurity
to try and make others clear-sighted."
14.21 Mèngzǐ said to Gāozǐ:
"A footpath through mountain passes, if used
continuously for a short while, becomes a road;
but if it is not used for a short while,
weeds will choke it up.
Now, weeds have choked up your mind."
14.22 Gāozǐ said:
"The music of Yǔ
was superior to the music of King Wén."
Mèngzǐ said:
"On what grounds do you say that?"
He replied:
"Because the hangers of his bells were worn out."
Mèngzǐ said:
"How is that sufficient?
Are the deep ruts at a city gate
made by the strength of only two horses?"
14.23 There was a famine in Qí.
Chén Zhēn said:
"The people of the state all think that you, Master,
will once again cause the granary of Táng to be opened for them,
but it is likely you cannot do so again."
Mèngzǐ said:
"That would be acting like Féng Fù.
There was a man of Jìn named Féng Fù,
who was skilled at fighting tigers;
in the end, he became a refined scholar.
Once, when he went to the countryside,
there was a crowd of people chasing a tiger.
The tiger put its back against a corner,
and no one dared to attack it.
Catching sight of Féng Fù,
they rushed to welcome him.
Féng Fù bared his arms and got down from his carriage.
The crowd was all delighted with him,
but those who were refined scholars laughed at him."
14.24 Mèngzǐ said:
"The mouth's relation to flavors,
the eye's relation to colors,
the ear's relation to sounds,
the nose's relation to odors,
and the four limbs' relation to ease and comfort,
these belong to human nature;
yet there is a decree of Heaven in them,
and so the superior man does not call them nature.
Benevolence between father and son,
righteousness between ruler and minister,
propriety between guest and host,
wisdom in the worthy,
and the sage's relation to the Way of Heaven,
these belong to the decree of Heaven;
yet there is human nature in them,
and so the superior man does not call them destiny."
14.25 Hàoshēng Bùhài asked, saying:
"What kind of man is
Yuèzhèngzǐ?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"He is a good man,
a trustworthy man."
"What do you mean by 'good'?
What do you mean by 'trustworthy'?"
He replied:
"One who is desirable is called 'good.'
One who possesses this goodness in himself is called 'trustworthy.'
One who is filled with it is called 'beautiful.'
One who is filled with it and radiates it is called 'great.'
One who is great and transforms others is called a 'sage.'
A sage who is beyond comprehension is called 'divine.'
Yuèzhèngzǐ
is in the middle of the first two,
and below the other four."
14.26 Mèngzǐ said:
"Those who escape from the School of Mò must return to the School of Yáng;
those who escape from the School of Yáng must return to Confucianism.
When they return,
they should simply be received.
But those who nowadays debate with the followers of Yáng and Mò
act as if they were chasing a stray pig:
once it has entered the pen,
they proceed to tie its legs."
14.27 Mèngzǐ said:
"There is the levy of cloth,
the levy of grain,
and the levy of labor-service.
A wise ruler employs only one of these,
while deferring the other two.
If he employs two of them,
there will be corpses of starved people among the citizenry.
If he employs all three,
fathers and sons will be separated."
14.28 Mèngzǐ said:
"The treasures of a feudal lord are three:
land, people, and the administration of government.
Those who treasure pearls and jade
will surely bring disaster upon themselves."
Pénchéng Kuò took office in Qí.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Pénchéng Kuò is a dead man!"
When Pénchéng Kuò was indeed killed,
the disciples asked:
"Master, how did you know he would be killed?"
He replied:
"He was a man
of small ability,
who had never heard of the great Way of the superior man.
This was just enough to get himself killed."
14.30 When Mèngzǐ went to Téng,
he stayed at the Upper Palace.
An unfinished pair of hemp sandals had been left on a window sill,
and the keeper of the lodging sought but could not find them.
Someone asked him:
"Is it likely that your followers should have hidden them?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Do you think they came here to steal sandals?"
The other replied:
"Probably not."
"But in my method of establishing instruction,
I do not pursue those who leave,
nor do I reject those who come.
If they come with a mind to learn,
they are simply received."
14.31 Mèngzǐ said:
"All people have things that they cannot bear to do.
To extend this feeling to what they can bear to do
is benevolence;
all people have things that they will not do.
To extend this to what they actually do
is righteousness.
If a person can fully develop the heart that is free from any desire to harm others,
their benevolence will be more than can ever be put into practice;
if a person can fully develop the heart that refuses to break through or leap over walls,
their righteousness will be more than can ever be put into practice;
if a person can fully develop the reality of not accepting being addressed familiarly as 'thee' and 'thou',
there is nowhere they can go where they will not act righteously.
If a scholar speaks when he should not speak,
he is trying to entice people with his words;
if he does not speak when he should speak,
he is trying to entice people by his silence.
Both of these are in the same category as breaking through and leaping over walls."
14.32 Mèngzǐ said,
"Words that are near at hand but whose meaning is far-reaching
are good words.
To hold to what is essential and to apply it broadly
is the good Way.
The words of a gentleman
do not go below the belt,
yet the Way is preserved in them.
The holding to what is essential of a gentleman
is to cultivate his own person,
and the whole world is brought to peace.
The fault of people is that they abandon their own fields
to weed the fields of others.
What they demand from others is heavy,
while that which they take upon themselves is light."
14.33 Mèngzǐ said,
"Yáo and Shùn
possessed it by nature;
Tāng and Wǔ
returned to it.
For one's every movement and turn to conform to propriety
is the height of abundant virtue.
To wail for the dead with grief
is not for the sake of the living.
To follow virtue constantly without deviating
is not in order to seek emolument.
For one's words to be necessarily trustworthy
is not in order to project a righteous conduct.
The gentleman acts according to the standard
and simply awaits his destiny."
14.34 Mèngzǐ said,
"When counseling men of high station,
one should look upon them with disregard,
and not look at their imposing grandeur.
Their halls are several rén high,
their rafters and eaves several feet wide—
were I to achieve my ambition, I would not have them.
Their food is spread out before them over ten square feet,
with hundreds of concubines in attendance—
were I to achieve my ambition, I would not have them.
They indulge in pleasure and drink wine,
galloping and hunting,
followed by a thousand chariots—
were I to achieve my ambition, I would not have them.
What is in their possession
are all things I would not do;
what is in my possession
are all the institutions of antiquity.
Why should I be in awe of them?"
14.35 Mèngzǐ said,
"For nurturing the mind, there is nothing better than reducing desires.
If a person has few desires,
even if there are moments when his goodness is not preserved,
they will be few;
if a person has many desires,
even if there are moments when his goodness is preserved,
they will be few."
14.36 Zeng Xī was fond of jujubes,
and Zēngzǐ could not bear to eat jujubes.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked,
"Which is more delicious, minced and roasted meat or jujubes?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Minced and roasted meat!"
Gōngsūn Chǒu said,
"Then why did Zēngzǐ eat minced and roasted meat
but would not eat jujubes?"
He said,
"Minced and roasted meat is what is liked in common;
jujubes are what was liked by him alone.
One avoids pronouncing a personal name but does not avoid pronouncing a family name.
The family name is what is shared in common;
the personal name is what is unique to the individual."
14.37 Wàn Zhāng asked,
"When Kǒngzǐ was in Chén,
he said,
'Why not return?
The young disciples of my school are wild and impulsive,
forging ahead,
but they have not forgotten their initial purpose.'
When Kǒngzǐ was in Chén,
why did he think of the wild scholars of Lǔ?"
Mèngzǐ said,
"Kǒngzǐ
said, 'Since I cannot obtain those who follow the Middle Way to associate with,
I must choose the wild or the cautious!
The wild forge ahead,
while the cautious have things they will not do.'
Could it be that Kǒngzǐ did not desire those who follow the Middle Way?
Since he could not be sure of obtaining them,
he therefore thought of the next best."
"May I ask what kind of people can be called 'wild'?"
He said,
"Those like Qín Zhāng, Zēng Xī, and Mù Pí
are those whom Kǒngzǐ called 'wild'."
"Why are they called 'wild'?"
He said,
"Their ambitions are grand,
and they say,
'The ancients!
The ancients!'
But when we examine their actions,
they do not live up to their words.
When even the wild could not be obtained,
he wished to find those who disdain what is impure to associate with.
These are the cautious,
and they are next in order.
Kǒngzǐ said,
'To pass by my door and not enter my room,
without my feeling any regret—
surely this is only the village honest man!
The village honest man
is the thief of virtue.'"
Wàn Zhāng asked,
"What kind of person can be called a 'village honest man'?"
He said,
"They ask: 'Why are those others so grand?
Their words do not look to their actions,
and their actions do not look to their words,
yet they say,
"The ancients! The ancients!"
And why do they act in such a solitary and cold manner?
Living in this age,
we should act for this age.
As long as we are good, that is enough.'
Eunuch-like, they flatter the world—
such is the village honest man."
Wànzǐ said,
"An entire village calls them honest men,
and wherever they go they act as honest men;
yet Kǒngzǐ regarded them as the thieves of virtue.
Why is this?"
He said,
"If you wish to criticize them, there is nothing to point to;
if you wish to censure them, there is nothing to censure.
They agree with the current customs
and align with a corrupt world.
In their dwelling, they seem loyal and trustworthy;
in their actions, they seem upright and pure.
Everyone is pleased with them,
and they consider themselves right.
Yet they cannot be brought to enter the Way of Yáo and Shùn.
Therefore they are called
'the thieves of virtue.' Kǒngzǐ said,
'I hate that which seems to be but is not:
I hate weeds,
for fear they will confuse the sprouts;
I hate the sycophants,
for fear they will confuse righteousness;
I hate the glib-tongued,
for fear they will confuse trustworthiness;
I hate the music of Zhèng,
for fear it will confuse proper music;
I hate purple,
for fear it will confuse vermillion;
I hate the village honest man,
for fear he will confuse virtue.'
The gentleman simply returns to the standard.
If the standard is correct,
then the common people will be aroused;
when the common people are aroused,
then there will be no wickedness and evil."
14.38 Mèngzǐ said,
"From Yáo and Shùn down to Tāng,
there were over five hundred years.
As for Yǔ
and Gāoyáo, they knew them by having seen them.
As for Tāng, he knew them by hearsay.
From Tāng down to King Wén,
there were over five hundred years.
As for Yī Yǐn and Lái Zhū, they knew him by having seen him.
As for King Wén, he knew him by hearsay.
From King Wén down to Kǒngzǐ,
there were over five hundred years.
As for Tàigōng Wàng and Sànyí Shēng,
they knew him by having seen him.
As for Kǒngzǐ, he knew him by hearsay.
From Kǒngzǐ down to the present day,
there are over one hundred years.
We are from the era of the sage
not so very far removed,
and to the dwelling place of the sage
exceedingly close.
Yet if there is no one who has it,
then there is indeed no one."
